https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/brist: Parking charges coming to the Downs under Bristol City Council budget plansThe new pay-and-display meters are expected to bring in £200,000 a yearCommentsNewsAdam Postans Local democracy reporter16:34, 17 Oct 2025View ImageVan dwellers and caravans on sides of roads in Bristol(Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach PLC)Parking charges will be introduced on the Downs under plans to raise money in Bristol City Council’s annual budget.‌The new pay-and-display meters are expected to bring in £200,000 a year after their introduction from April 2027, while another proposal to charge drivers across the city a standard fixed hourly parking rate instead of the current mishmash of fees, especially for evening and overnight stays, is forecast to generate £500,000 annually.‌Both plans have gone out to public consultation in the organisation’s draft financial plans for 2026/27 – and they have been previously controversial when discussed by Bristol city councillors.‌Last December, members on the transport and connectivity committee warned the proposed new parking charges on Clifton and Durdham Downs could “inflame tensions” between residents and van dwellers, so the idea was sent to a cross-party taskforce looking into a wider parking and kerbside strategy to assess the pros and cons.Concerns were also raised about displacing parking onto neighbouring streets which would remain free to park.Article continues belowThen in March 2025, the committee narrowly voted in favour of fixed “linear” hourly fees in Bristol city centre and some council-owned car parks but members were split 5-3.The decision, which now forms part of the council’s budget, will increase charges from 6pm to 10pm to £6.80 from the current £4.50 flat fee, but this was less than the initial proposed hike of £2.70 an hour, totalling £10.80 from 6pm to 10pm, following a pushback at the meeting.Residents can give their views on these and the authority’s other cuts and money-raising ideas at the consultation which is open for six weeks here.

possible”. Article continues below components.molecules.ReadMore: [More deaths in Bristol from pollution than car crashes, Centre for Cities report finds](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/more-deaths-bristol-pollution-car-3809538) School communities across the city were invited to trial the initiative and Wansdyke Primary School in [Hartcliffe](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/hartcliffe) and St Peter's C of E Primary School in [Bishopsworth](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bishopsworth) were chosen. Pilot schemes outside both schools will start on Monday, February 24 - the first day back after the half term. ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article3816951.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_St-Peters-C-of-E-SchoolJPG.jpg) View 3 Images St Peter's C of E Primary School in Bristol(Image: Google Maps) ‌ Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. It will see the streets the schools are located on temporarily become a ‘School Street zone’ for pedestrians and cyclists at the beginning and end of the school day. Article continues below Vehicles will not be allowed to enter the street between these times unless they have been granted an exemption. Exemptions will be granted to residents and businesses living or working within the zone so they can still move freely. Special exemptions will also be granted to blue badge holders. In relation to Wansdyke Primary School, vehicles would be prohibited from driving within School Close for 45 minutes in morning and 45 minutes in the afternoon. ‌ ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article3816952.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Wansdyke-SchoolJPG.jpg) View 3 Images Wansdyke Primary School in Bristol(Image: Google Maps) ‌ For St Peter’s C of E School, vehicles will be banned from entering Ellfield Close, for the same amount of time. centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre) that is set to be adopted after May’s [mayoral election.](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-mayoral-election-2020) ‌ The idea is not new, having been pushed by community groups in the past and promised by former mayor George Ferguson in his unsuccessful re-election campaign of 2016. Now [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) officials have briefed councillors on progress being made towards the pedestrianisation of the small triangular area between Castle Park and the A38. Cork**](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/authors/tristan-cork/) Chief Reporter 16:29, 02 Mar 2020 Updated 16:19, 03 Mar 2020 In January, the embankment wall separating the River Avon New Cut and Cumberland Road collapsed, taking with it the Chocolate Path and the ground underneath the Harbour Railway. Article continues below Cumberland Road, the only road that runs from one end of Spike Island to the other, [was closed, and remains closed](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/cumberland-road-closed-update-traffic-3867731). ‌ Anyone looking at a map might think this road closure, while inconvenient for the people who live on Spike Island, and for the tourist attractions like the SS Great Britain and the caravan site nearby, has not had much effect on the rest of Bristol. Article continues below But while the road is closed, the knock-on effects have been felt for miles around, some obvious, some unforeseen, some surprising. **Get all your local traffic news, powered by [In Your Area](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/):** ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) With Bristol City Council [saying it will be at least until the end of March](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/cumberland-road-closed-update-traffic-3867731) before they will know if the road can reopen, Bristol, its commuters, bus passengers, cyclists and motorists are getting used to these. ### 1) Traffic congestion on Coronation Road If you are coming to the city centre from the south west, or west of Bristol, then Cumberland Road is one of three options to get from the west end of the floating harbour and river to the middle of town. So while the road is, according to the road network, a relatively minor one compared to the A4 Hotwell Road or the A370 Coronation Road, it was a well-used, very busy rat run, with traffic flowing west to east in the morning, and east to west in the evening. ‌ So it’s no surprise that the other two roads, Coronation Road especially, have been very busy since the riverbank collapse - not helped in the first few weeks, by roadworks there. Coronation Road was already one of Bristol’s busiest roads, and is now, in rush hour, busier than ever. components.molecules.ReadMore: [Wife of Bristol Rovers legend has car vandalised after 'road rage' incident](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/sport/football/wife-bristol-rovers-legend-ex-3901083) ### 2) The m2 Metrobus becoming a bus again Cumberland Road was the route for the m2 metrobus from Long Ashton park and ride to the city centre. ‌ It was launched with a huge fanfare and the first part of its route from the park and ride car park in North Somerset took it up and over a special flyover next to Ashton Gate Stadium, and over a refurbished Ashton Avenue Swing Bridge. The first bit of regular road the bus goes on to is Cumberland Road, just yards from where the collapse happened. ![Image 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article3905497.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_WhatsApp-Image-2020-03-02-at-124558jpeg.jpg) View 3 Images Notice on the m2 metrobus about re-routing and tickets ‌ The collapse has meant the metrobus m2 service has had to be re-routed along Coronation Road - so it now joins the very traffic queue the multi-million-pound investment in a bus-only link from the park and ride to Cumberland Road was created to avoid. The knock-on effect has been a challenge for FirstBus, the metrobus m2 operators. During the worst of the congestion in the first few weeks of the closure, First Bus sometimes had to abandon some m2 services because they caught up with the bus in front. Passengers were decanted onto the bus in front, and the second bus returned to Long Ashton. ### 3) The pay-before-you-board metrobus project has been abandoned - temporarily ### Today's top stories ![Image 8: Swingers club reopens](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4514475.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/0_Route-2.jpg) [### Swingers club reopens](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/whats-on-news/swingers-club-weston-super-mare-4514412) ![Image 9: Residents hit back at scathing reviews](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4514039.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/1_JMP_SWA_140920kingswood_Bristol_015_JPG.jpg) [### Residents hit back at scathing reviews](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/kingswood-staple-hill-residents-hit-4513805) ![Image 10: Nightclub gets three police call outs](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article2387469.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/0_party-the-night-277172.jpg) [### Nightclub gets three police call outs](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/nightclub-gets-three-police-call-4513949) ![Image 11: Flight in emergency over Bristol Channel](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4515264.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/0_EmeregncyPlane.jpg) [### Flight in emergency over Bristol Channel](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/british-airways-flight-declares-emergency-4515262) ‌ The metrobus project was the first in Bristol to stop the practice of being able to pay the driver for a ticket. Instead, all the metrobus stops were fitted with ticket machines and, as well as the usual phone app tickets and passes, passengers had to buy a ticket from a machine before they got on board. But because the metrobus m2 bus now runs along the other side of the river, and uses temporary bus stops that are basically just poles in the pavement with a bus stop sign on them, FirstBus has announced it is now accepting people buying tickets from the driver with a contactless bank card, which officially ends - albeit temporarily - the biggest difference between metrobus and regular bus services - between Ashton Gate and Redcliffe, at least. ### 4) People waited for buses that never came ![Image 12](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article3905460.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_Cumberland-Road-tweet-bus-waitJPG.jpg) View 3 Images Dan Roddy's tweet about metrobus on Cumberland Road Weeks after the road closure, and it seemed no one had thought to put signs on the metrobus ticket machines on Cumberland Road. They were still displaying bus times for buses that would, in fact, pass by on the other side of the river. It took this tweet to sort it out. ### 5) Cumberland Road is quiet For all the traffic in other parts of Bristol, if you regularly cycle or walk to work along Cumberland Road, then the lack of congestion has been seen by many as a blessing in disguise. Clear roads, cleaner air, looking smugly at the queue of traffic on the other side of the river… components.molecules.ReadMore: [Somerset town dubbed one of 'coolest' places to live in The Sunday Times](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/local-news/bruton-sunday-times-bruton-live-3885438) ### 6) The quirk of the airport bus Soon after the Long Ashton park and ride metrobus route was opened, the main A1 airport bus from[Bristol Airport](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-airport) to the city centre was re-routed so it could beat the south Bristol traffic queues and use the metrobus road too. The closure of Cumberland Road means the A1 airport bus route is also closed too, so the bus has returned to using its original route, straight out of the city centre down the A38 through Bedminster and out to the airport. A total of seven stops on the A1 route are now not being served by the airport bus. ![Image 13](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article3905459.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_Airport-A1-bus-diversionJPG.jpg) View 3 Images The A1 Airport bus has been re-routed When the A1 route was originally switched to use the Long Ashton metrobus road, people who work at the airport or live along the route in Bedminster and Bishopsworth complained. Article continues below They had chosen their homes so it was convenient for the airport bus, and mounted a brief and successful campaign for a rethink by FirstBus and the airport authorities. The result was the A2 airport bus, which runs from the city centre to the airport but along the A38 through Bedminster and out through Bridgwater Road. The collapse of the wall at Cumberland Road means now there are two airport buses, the A1 and the A2, which both go along the same route, but the first one doesn’t stop on the route, while the second one does. Lloyd Photography) The Green Party is calling for sections of roads in Bristol to be coned off to enable the widening of pavements and help social distancing. ‌ Green councillors are asking[Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) to temporarily “reclaim” roads for walkers and cyclists struggling to keep two metres apart during the [coronavirus lockdown](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/live-coronavirus-deaths-cases-updates-4060203), including shutting some residential areas to through-traffic. ‌ The Labour administration says it was already investigating the ideas but that vehicle access is vital to ensuring essential supplies can get through to vulnerable people in isolation. Article continues below Last month, residents in [Avon Crescent put their own markers down on the road to keep runners far enough from their homes](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/coronavirus-markings-encouraging-runners-practice-4007086). ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4007011.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_WhatsApp-Image-2020-04-01-at-084217-1jpeg.jpg) View 2 Images The markings on Avon Crescent(Image: Bristol Live) Green group leader Cllr Eleanor Combley said she had emailed[Mayor Marvin Rees](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/marvin-rees) and cabinet member for transport Cllr Kye Dudd urging them to take space from cars to extend pedestrian space in busy areas and near shops, filter traffic near people’s homes and temporarily widen cycle lanes. ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) She said cities around the world were taking similar measures during the coronavirus pandemic. Cllr Combley said: “We should do everything in our power to keep people safe. “During this crisis it is important that we do everything we can to reduce the burden on the NHS. Article continues below “We can do that by keeping people safe and preventing road traffic accidents. “And we can also help slow the spread of Covid-19 by ensuring people have the space to move around for exercise or essential shopping at a safe distance from each other. components.molecules.ReadMore: [This is how long you can stay outside for while exercising during lockdown](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/how-long-time-outside-exercising-4016765) “That is why I am calling on Bristol City Council to take temporary measures to make more space available to pedestrians and cyclists and reduce crowding. ‌ “Cities across the world are already doing this, from Auckland to Winnipeg and from Berlin to Bogota, and in the UK Transport for London and other councils are already actively considering what can be done. “We should do everything in our power to keep people safe.” In response, Labour Cllr Dudd said: “Like all responsible politicians, I want to echo Marvin’s thanks to all Bristolians who are staying home to slow the spread of the coronavirus and save lives. ‌ “Our streets are much safer and quieter as a result for people taking their daily exercise, with air pollution much reduced, while our inspiring NHS and other key workers continue to move around Bristol. components.molecules.ReadMore: [People asked not to go to Portbury's bluebell woods after 'deluge' of visitors](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/portbury-bluebell-woods-visit-lockdown-4064508) “After Cllr Marg Hickman and other Labour councillors raised this idea weeks ago, I directed transport officers to investigate where such measures might be necessary and feasible. “However, road access is important to ensure essential supplies are provided to people being shielded, are accessible for all and that we do not cause unforeseen consequences that damage our ability to support everyone through this pandemic. Article continues below “Like other cities, we are exploring how we might continue to build on the success of our school streets closures. “Once the lockdown is lifted, and as Bristol recovers and rebuilds, we will continue to work to make our streets safer, improve walking and cycling, and make public transport more reliable and affordable.” Follow Bristol Live: * Priority will be given to public transport, taxis, cycles and pedestrians travelling through the central area of Bristol. The route will be closed to general through-traffic * **New sustainable transport, walking and cycling upgrades in central areas.**This will include Marlborough Street, Park Row, Victoria Street, Lewins Mead, Stokes Croft and the Clifton Triangle. * **City-wide pavement widening for local shopping areas to enable social distancing.**Including Bedminster Parade, Stapleton Road, St Marks Road and Clifton Village * **Working with bus providers to ensure social distancing.**The council will look at how they prioritise key workers to give them reassurance they can get to work * **Issuing new guidelines to taxi and private vehicles, working with taxi representatives now.**Including cleaning and infection prevention measures. Many of these schemes were previously mapped out through the £400million infrastructure programme in Bristol’s element of the regional Local Cycling and Walking Infrastructure Plan. Additional funding is expected from central government, which promised £250m for regions for specific Covid-19 interventions to enable safer walking and cycling. "Action we take now will contribute to reducing air pollution, improving people movement for all Bristolians and encouraging alternative sustainable ways to travel," he said. Article continues below 138205441690 “Work on the Old City and Bristol Bridge proposals are already underway but the coronavirus means we now need to accelerate the changes that will transform the way we travel in the city centre. "For the future we need to ensure everyone has more travel options and these proposals are underpinned by the Bus Deal that we continue to progress, alongside our ongoing plans for mass transit." He added that the crisis was challenging our usual travel habits, saying: "Many of us have already embraced more walking and cycling journeys. 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4140969.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_JB_BRI_170520RedcliffeDevelopment-03JPG.jpg) View 5 Images (Image: James Beck/Freelance) Ambitious proposals to turn one of Bristol’s dual carriageways into a ‘shared space for all’ have been revealed. ‌ The plan, put forward by the local residents themselves, would see the Redcliffe Way dual carriageway from Temple Meads to St Mary Redcliffe Church completely transformed into something more like Wapping Wharf with affordable homes, local shops and a ‘playful, green public space’. ‌ The plans are being suggested to [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) and the wider citizens of Bristol, and are at an early stage, but would see a new building, up to six storeys high, to provide new affordable homes and spaces for bars, businesses and shops, on the north side of Redcliffe Way. Article continues below ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4133630.ece/ALTERNATES/s1168v/0_Parenting-main-image.jpg) ### The Great Big Lockdown Parenting Survey Hey parents, you're doing great! But we know sometimes parenting can be tough, especially under lockdown. We're trying to build a picture of what family life is really like under coronavirus - so please will you take a few moments to fill in our parenting survey [here](https://www.surveymonkey.co.uk/r/KP8MJD2)? It won't take long and will help us paint a picture of what life was like in 2020 for future generations. Just [click here](https://www.surveymonkey.co.uk/r/KP8MJD2) to take part. Thank you. At present the wide space between the buildings on either side of the road are occupied by a dual carriageway, a verge and then another road and cycleway. Those putting forward the idea said they want to ‘reconnect’ the two communities either side of the dual carriageway, which they said ‘slices the neighbourhood in half’. ‌ [![Image 9: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Put your skills to the test. Whether you love word games, tricky cryptic crosswords, Sudoku, or our other brain teasers, you'll find a new favourite today! Play Now](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games/) The plan is from the [Redcliffe](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/redcliffe)Residents Action Group & Neighbourhood Forum, and has the backing of leaders at St Mary Redcliffe Church. ![Image 10](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4140964.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_TCR_BRI_170520RedcliffeWAyBRI_JPG.jpg) View 5 Images (Image: LDA Design) The group has hired local design practice LDA, which has already worked on similar schemes on previously busy roads in London. Article continues below “The community in Redcliffe has been long campaigning to reclaim Redcliffe Way,” said local resident and member of the Redcliffe Residents Action Group, Melissa Mean. “The[Covid 19 lockdown](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/coronavirus) has meant many people are looking at their city with fresh eyes and realising just how much space had been given over to polluting, noisy, space-greedy motor traffic. ![Image 11](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4154413.ece/ALTERNATES/s1168v/0_newsletter-image.jpg) ### Want Bristol news straight to your inbox? Sign up to our daily newsletter using the box at the top of this article, or by clicking [here](https://communicatoremail.com/F/gqxNwa0hZubC9_IKKGjv78/) to see all of our newsletters ‌ “When Bristol opens up again, we want to say yes to development that prioritises clean air, and makes space for nature and people to play, walk and cycle. This is especially important in poorer neighbourhoods – like Redcliffe – where many people live in cramped flats, with no access to outdoor space, and suffer an unequal burden of air pollution, and as a consequence significantly poorer health,” she added. The group said its proposals show how development with a more ‘humane density’ can be achieved. It proposes ‘The Redcliffe Block’, a development no higher than 6 storeys, with “a layer of much needed shops and services at ground level, space for offices on the middle floors, and spacious apartments above all with access to outdoor and green space”. Those behind the scheme said it could provide more than 150 affordable homes at a scale that ‘both respects the historic urban landscape and provides a greener and gentler alternative to tall towers’. ‌ ![Image 12](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4140967.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_JB_BRI_170520RedcliffeDevelopment-02JPG.jpg) View 5 Images (Image: James Beck/Freelance) The vicar of St Mary Redcliffe Church, Dan Tyndall, said he is keen to see the plans come to fruition, and said Redcliffe Way marks the beginning of the ‘sharp divide’ between north and south Bristol. “Redcliffe is currently sliced in half by an over-sized and outdated highway,” he said. ‌ “Redcliffe Way splits the neighbourhood in half and marks the beginning of the sharp divide of inequality between North and South Bristol. “We want to stitch North and South Redcliffe back together, create a fitting setting for St Mary Redcliffe, and a welcoming breathing space that the whole of Bristol can enjoy and be proud of,” he added. components.molecules.ReadMore: [This is where the 'A House Through Time' house is in Bristol and when it's going to be broadcast](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/celebs-tv/house-through-time-bristol-bbc-4132209) To the north of Redcliffe Way, there has been a lot of development, with the Finzels Reach scheme bringing homes and businesses - and Channel 4 - to the city centre, while work on the ‘Redcliffe Quarter’ is continuing - and its aim is to turn that part of Redcliffe into a food hub with upmarket food restaurants and a food market. But to the south of Redcliffe Way is the large post-war council estate, said to be the biggest in Bristol, which has some of the highest levels of deprivation in the city. ### Is it possible? ![Image 13](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4140966.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_TCR_BRI_170520RedcliffeWAyBRI__03JPG.jpg) View 5 Images (Image: LDA Design) The current dual carriageway of Redcliffe Way has been made less vital to the city’s traffic flow in the past year by the Temple Circus project, which saw almost three years of roadworks [do away with the Temple Circus roundabout](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/temple-meads-roadworks-taxi-route-3855931) at one end. Now, through traffic is largely directed along to the Bath Road Bridges and along the River Avon New Cut. And at the other end of Redcliffe Way, there will soon be even less reason, or point, for traffic to travel in the opposite direction into the city centre. components.molecules.ReadMore: [City centre roads to shut for motorists as part of major transport plan](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/city-centre-roads-shut-motorists-4129715) The [council’s plans to trial blocking off Bristol Bridge and Baldwin Street](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/city-centre-roads-shut-motorists-4129715) to private vehicles would effectively mean the Redcliffe Bascule Bridge would provide access only to the area around Queen Square, with the only route out of that area being over Prince Street Bridge. Ending the possibility of through traffic into the city centre from Redcliffe could, in theory, mean Redcliffe Way is able to be turned into a ‘shared space’ without affecting the key flow of traffic on the ‘ring road’ around the city centre that includes Clarence Road, Temple Way and Bond Street. The aim is for people who currently walk along a dual carriageway from [Temple Meads into the city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/raft-changes-planned-temple-meads-3822971), will instead find a pedestrian-friendly avenue lined with shops and homes. ![Image 14](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4140970.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_JB_BRI_170520RedcliffeDevelopment-04JPG.jpg) View 5 Images (Image: James Beck/Freelance) Article continues below “Our vision for Redcliffe Way is to shift the focus away from motor vehicles and create a place people love to spend time in and one that wows people arriving in Bristol from Temple Meads,” said Clare Wilks, the head of the Bristol office of LDA Design. “It is a great opportunity to re-organise this incredibly wide street to provide more homes and offices, design delightful new spaces and develop hubs of activity along the route. As someone who has worked in the area for the past eight years, I believe Redcliffe Way could offer so much more for city life in Bristol,” she added. 2](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4142242.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/4_GH120818banksy.jpg) View 2 Images (Image: Western Daily Press) A series of pop-up walking and cycling routes are set to be created in parts of North Somerset, so people can follow social distancing guidelines while out and about. ‌ Clevedon seafront and Nailsea High Street could become traffic-free, as could part of Weston-super-Mare's town centre. ‌ North Somerset Council is looking to change the focus in areas of Nailsea, Clevedon and Weston-super-Mare from vehicle use to pedestrian and cycle use, creating a series of temporary walking and cycling routes. ‌ The move follows the partial easement of the Government lockdown and the need to ensure people can socially distance safely when they are out and about. ![Image 3](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article1552946.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/2_Nailsea-high-street.png) View 2 Images Nailsea High Street As part of the move, Nailsea High Street could be temporarily closed to traffic and other changes made to Clevedon seafront and Marine Parade, as well as Meadow Street in Weston-super-Mare. ‌ In Nailsea the section of High Street from the roundabout opposite Iceland to its junction with the link road could be closed to traffic to give more room for pedestrians. The top end of High Street would remain open to traffic as it is a bus route. Arrangements would also be made for businesses in the closed section of High Street. components.molecules.ReadMore: [UK hotter than California as temperatures continue to rise](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/uk-hotter-california-temperatures-continue-4144483)components.molecules.ReadMore: [Bristol Water releases statement on 'extremely dangerous' parking at Chew Valley Lake as car parks remain closed](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/local-news/bristol-water-releases-statement-extremely-4144071) It is expected the changes to Nailsea High Street could come into force in the next couple of weeks. ‌ Changes to the seafront area in Clevedon are currently being drawn up, with details announced in the coming weeks. In Weston-super-Mare, the council intends to continue with its closure of Marine Parade on the seafront to traffic to reduce pressure on the promenade at busy times. Signs will go up this week to designate the road for walking and cycling only. ‌ ![Image 4: videoHeadline](https://cf-images.eu-west-1.prod.boltdns.net/v1/static/4221396001/5ca45271-b0c9-4a78-b53d-aa6e012633c8/9b7006e7-36db-4eb3-ba2a-407d15370a48/1280x720/match/image.jpg) Boris Johnson's five stage plan to lifting lockdown restrictions - everything you need to know North Somerset Council executive member for transport Councillor James Tonkin said: “We are making these changes for local people to help them stay safe while exercising outdoors. “Please, if Marine Parade is not one of your regular exercise routes, do not to make unnecessary journeys. ‌ "We are asking everyone to explore around their homes rather than travelling and creating further social distancing problems.” It is hoped that as well as maintaining social distancing the move to pedestrianise some areas will help aid the economic recovery as more businesses prepare to re-open. issued a £70 fine straight away. ‌ Parking officers no longer have to wait two minutes to check children are not getting in or out of the vehicle before issuing the fine. Jon Kent/ Bristol Live) Weekend road closures and improved public transport have been suggested as potential solutions to Bristol's pollution problem. ‌ _Bristol Live_ wants to hear suggestions about changes people want to see in the city post-lockdown, as part of our campaign [Bristol Bounces Back.](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-bounces-back-what-could-4251117) ‌ We are seeking ideas about how to shape Bristol into an even better city for people to live and work in, using the lessons people have learnt in lockdown. Article continues below Soroptimist International Bristol has now put forward four key points of focus, which its members feel should be prioritised to improve the city's future. ### Today's top stories ![Image 8: Swingers club reopens](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4514475.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/0_Route-2.jpg) [### Swingers club reopens](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/whats-on-news/swingers-club-weston-super-mare-4514412) ![Image 9: Residents hit back at scathing reviews](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4514039.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/1_JMP_SWA_140920kingswood_Bristol_015_JPG.jpg) [### Residents hit back at scathing reviews](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/kingswood-staple-hill-residents-hit-4513805) ![Image 10: Nightclub gets three police call outs](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article2387469.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/0_party-the-night-277172.jpg) [### Nightclub gets three police call outs](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/nightclub-gets-three-police-call-4513949) ![Image 11: Flight in emergency over Bristol Channel](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4515264.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/0_EmeregncyPlane.jpg) [### Flight in emergency over Bristol Channel](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/british-airways-flight-declares-emergency-4515262) The organisation aims to empower, enable and educate women, and is part of a global network of Soroptimist International groups. ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) One of the ideas championed by the group is to close certain roads at weekends or during some points in the week, to encourage cycling and walking. Club secretary Lucy Swithinbank explained: "There was an increase in cycling and walking when roads were closed during lockdown, especially among less experienced cyclists who felt safer with less traffic around. "Exercise outdoors is known to be beneficial for physical and mental wellbeing, and I know many people are finding it valuable at the moment." Article continues below components.molecules.ReadMore: [The nicest places to cycle to on a day out from Bristol](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/nicest-places-cycle-day-out-4257033)components.molecules.ReadMore: [Popular cycle route to get upgrade as usage soars during lockdown](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/local-news/popular-cycle-route-upgrade-usage-4254378) She suggested Sea Walls and the Downs would be a good area to look at road closures, to ensure walkers and cyclists can enjoy the open space away from traffic. Public transport was also a key focus for the group's idea about cutting pollution levels. Dr Swithinbank said: "The reduction in pollution in our city has been marked during lockdown. ‌ "We should improve connected affordable and accessible public transport to discourage travel in private cars and hence reduce pollution." 'Green agenda' was top of their list of priorities, with a focus on expanding green spaces and opening up access. ‌ Dr Swithinbank continued: "COVID-19 has taught us how important this is, and not everyone is fortunate to have their own private green space. "[We should] plant trees and involve children and women in that, maintain open accessible green spaces for all, and have outside exhibitions of art work for all ages." The artwork should be varied to appeal to all tastes, she said, with a sculpture garden suggested as one example. ‌ Tackling homelessness is another aim held of high importance to Soroptimist International Bristol, particularly as homeless people have been temporarily housed to protect them from the pandemic. ![Image 12](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4269756.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Lucy-Swithinbank.jpg) View 2 Images Lucy Swithinbank (back) with other members of Soroptimists International(Image: Bristol Soroptimists International) "Going forward Bristol should strive to become a city without people sleeping on the streets", Dr Swithinbank said. Encouraging community participation and spirit was another area the group hopes Bristol will focus on as lockdown draws closer to an end. The club's secretary explained: "During lockdown we have not been able to meet in our normal ways, but club members have been making scrubs, scrub bags for care homes, crocheting hearts for COVID patients in hospital and their families, and we gave a donation of money rather than our usual food collection to the North West Bristol Food Bank. **For news tailored to your local area****, powered by [In Your Area](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/):** Article continues below **_What is happening where you live? Volunteering was cited as an example of how to encourage this, for example at food banks as demand for their services increase. general traffic next month as part of work to improve air quality. Article continues below The closure also aims to make it easier for people to catch the bus, walk and cycle in the city centre. Article continues below The changes - which will go live on Sunday, August 2 - will stop through traffic using the bridge as well as Baldwin Street and Union Street, to prevent these roads being used as an alternative route. Article continues below 138205439166 [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) said priority would be given to buses, taxis, [cyclists](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cycling) and pedestrians travelling through the central area of Bristol in order to ease congestion and pollution. **Get all your local traffic news, powered by [In Your Area](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/):** Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) The measures are being done alongside [the pedestrianisation of the Old City](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/city-centre-roads-shut-motorists-4129715), and are part of a package of major transport improvements being accelerated to help Bristolians safely navigate the city during the [coronavirus](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/coronavirus) pandemic. Mayor [Marvin Rees](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/marvin-rees) said: “We are taking bold action to create a better, more connected future for everyone in and around Bristol. "By restricting general through traffic from our central areas we will protect public health and unlock barriers to inclusive economic growth with cleaner air, safer and better public transport, and improved walking and cycling routes for everyone. The Mayor said the pandemic had huge impacts on travel habits and the city saw air pollution levels drop by almost half during the months of lockdown with big increases in walking and cycling. Article continues below "We want to capture those benefits and protect the long-term public health of the city as well as the viability of our public transport services that provide real value to our communities," he said. Camera monitored bus gates with signs and road markings to prohibit general traffic will be installed on Bristol Bridge, either end of Baldwin Street and at the bottom of Union Street. components.molecules.ReadMore: [Warning to e-scooter riders as trial scheme is set for Bristol's roads](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/warning-e-scooter-riders-trial-4333510) Article continues below Access to the city centre for loading and car parks will still remain using alternative routes. Article continues below 138205439166 School Streets is a national scheme encouraging councils to restrict traffic outside schools, to prohibit motorised vehicles from entering the vicinity at drop-off and pick-up times. It aims to create a safer and healthier environment by tackling pollution and dangerous congestion, and two [Bristol schools started trialling the initiative back in February](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/cars-banned-outside-two-bristol-3815045). [South Gloucestershire Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/south-gloucestershire-council) is now consulting on the proposals at the three schools above, and the trial will run from September 2020 until July 2021 if it goes ahead as planned. Maloney Architects) Cotham Hill should be pedestrianised to help businesses survive, says a new campaign group. ‌ Businesses and residents in the area are working together to persuade [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council)to pedestrianise a section of the road in order to help businesses survive through the [Covid-19](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/coronavirus) crisis while improving safety for pedestrians and cyclists. ‌ Dan Williams, owner of Coffee + Beer, has been liaising with the council and other local businesses. Article continues below ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4399697.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_11-cotham-hill-4-temp.jpg) View 3 Images The plans are being supported by both businesses and residents He said: “It is a golden opportunity for this vibrant and iconic street to become a flagship of pedestrianisation in Bristol. "The suggested plans would definitely be safer for families, attract more shoppers, allow some alfresco dining options and encourage people to cycle or walk to work safely. ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) "The increased footfall would be a major bonus for the local independent businesses, including all the excellent hospitality businesses on the street that have been hit hard by the Covid-19 situation." Dominic Borel, one of the owners of Pasta Loco, one of the most well-known restaurants along Cotham Hill, said pedestrianising the road would make a really big difference. ### Today's top stories ![Image 9: Swingers club reopens](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4514475.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/0_Route-2.jpg) [### Swingers club reopens](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/whats-on-news/swingers-club-weston-super-mare-4514412) ![Image 10: Residents hit back at scathing reviews](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4514039.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/1_JMP_SWA_140920kingswood_Bristol_015_JPG.jpg) [### Residents hit back at scathing reviews](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/kingswood-staple-hill-residents-hit-4513805) ![Image 11: Nightclub gets three police call outs](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article2387469.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/0_party-the-night-277172.jpg) [### Nightclub gets three police call outs](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/nightclub-gets-three-police-call-4513949) ![Image 12: Flight in emergency over Bristol Channel](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4515264.ece/ALTERNATES/s810/0_EmeregncyPlane.jpg) [### Flight in emergency over Bristol Channel](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/british-airways-flight-declares-emergency-4515262) Article continues below Mr Borel said their small restaurant is currently closed as social distancing guidelines mean they could only operate at 50 per cent capacity, adding the option to have some outdoor seating could help them make the business work. He added: "I think it is a great idea and it would help us make some decisions moving forward. "I think it would also be great for pedestrians as social distancing can not take place there and make it safer for people to walk around. ‌ "If it could happen as soon as possible while the weather is still good, that would be great." ![Image 13](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4399703.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_08-cotham-hill-3-temp.jpg) View 3 Images The pedestrianised area would stretch from The Penny/Dragon Fountain to the Jubo Raj/Clic Sargent A spokeswoman for Falafel King, a Middle-Eastern restaurant towards the top end of [Cotham](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cotham) Hill, said they supported the plans. ‌ She said: "It would be really good to see the area pedestrianised. It would be vital in helping businesses thrive in this difficult time." The plans are also supported by local residents and Harriet Brennan said that, for years, Cotham Hill has seen the encroachment of increasing two-way traffic, illegal parking and frequent speeding. She added: "All forcing pedestrians and cyclists to tolerate a smaller and smaller space to travel, walk and shop. Safe distancing is not possible on this street.” ‌ A limited amount of funding for walking and cycling improvements was made available in April, however, unlike some other local high streets, Cotham Hill was not included, said the campaign group in a statement. Provisional proposals from the local businesses involved are for the road to be closed to vehicle traffic in the afternoon and/or evening so that deliveries can still take place earlier in the day. The pedestrianised area would stretch from The Penny/Dragon Fountain to the Jubo Raj/Clic Sargent. She said: “I’ve received an incredible number of emails over the last few months asking for more space for walking and cycling in Clifton Down ward, possibly more than I have received on any other topic. "Most of these requests focused on Cotham Hill, because it is such a busy shopping street with narrow pavements and no way for people to do social distancing safely. "It has been brilliant to see such widespread support, and to see businesses and residents working together on this." "As these temporary changes are to help with social distancing it is important that they go in soon," she added. Sandy Murray, of Smith Maloney Architects, which has its practice nearby along Whiteladies Road, has produced the set of images to help bring the idea to life. Article continues below He said: “At Smith Maloney, our hope is that the catastrophic impact of the global pandemic can be used as a catalyst to transform the urban streetscape, allowing local communities and businesses to thrive whilst maintaining social distancing guidelines, whilst also promoting cleaner air and greener spaces. "I believe that Cotham Hill could be a benchmark for the sustainable city streets of the future." [**Sophie Grubb**](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/authors/sophie-grubb/) Content Editor 14:32, 07 Aug 2020 Updated 17:38, 07 Aug 2020 ![Image 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4404830.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_Avon-Crescent.jpg) View 5 Images A cyclist heading for the gap in the roadblocks along Avon Crescent(Image: Jon Kent) Residents in a Bristol street have denied moving roadblocks and traffic cones to keep people out. Article continues below Avon Crescent near the harbourside has been closed for several months, as part of[Bristol City Council's](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) repairs to Cumberland Road and the [Chocolate Path](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/river-bank-collapse-means-cumberland-3773254). Article continues below Rows of roadblocks are in place to stop vehicles from entering, with small gaps allowing pedestrians and bike riders to pass. Article continues below 138205439166 A [cyclist](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cycling)has now claimed gaps are being repeatedly blocked to prevent access, accusing residents of being to blame. However, one resident dismissed this as "rubbish" and said it was more likely the council or contractors who had been moving things about. ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4404789.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Avon-Crescent.jpg) View 5 Images A cyclist passing the closure in Avon Crescent(Image: Jon Kent) Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) Posting on the FixMyStreet problem-reporting website, the anonymous cyclist said: "Residents and pedestrians have taken to moving the cones and road blockings to stop cyclists being able to legally pass though Avon Crescent through towards Spike Island, which is both dangerous and incredibly frustrating. "This has been happening on a regular basis since Avon Crescent was shut. It means cyclists are having to stop on the wrong side of the road to move cones and bollards to pass though, increasing the risk of an accident. READ MORE: [Mum's horror as new friend turns out to be attempted child abductor and sexual offender](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/mums-horror-new-friend-turns-4401985) "Residents have also been spray painting the roads in an attempt to police people, confusing pedestrians." Article continues below 138205441690 [Bristol Live](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/) reported in April how residents had [sprayed their own social distancing markers on the road](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/coronavirus-markings-encouraging-runners-practice-4007086), reminding pedestrians and runners to keep two metres apart. It would appear tensions along the road are still running high, as a large handmade sign has also been propped up on the [traffic](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/traffic-travel) island. ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4404794.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Avon-Crescent.jpg) View 5 Images A sign demanding to know 'what part of road closed don't you understand' in Avon Crescent(Image: Jon Kent) Article continues below Along with a drawing of what appears to be a chest, it states in large capital letters: "WHAT PART OF 'ROAD CLOSED' DON'T YOU UNDERSTAND??" The cardboard sign has been attached to the back of a road sign with cable ties and remained in place today (Friday), although it is not clear how long it has been there for. There is also a message written across the width of the pavement, stating: "NO ADULT BIKES." Article continues below ![Image 10](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4404786.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Avon-Crescent.jpg) View 5 Images A message drawn on the pavement in Avon Crescent in Bristol(Image: Jon Kent) The cyclist's complaint was posted on July 26, and the council has since responded: "This enquiry has been referred to another team for action. "They will provide further updates on the issue in due course." Article continues below READ MORE: [Harbourside litter angers resident into leaving passive-aggressive note](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/harbourside-litter-angers-resident-leaving-4400838) Another passer-by [tweeted](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/twitter)about the road in June, describing it as "very aggressively signposted and not very welcoming at all." 'It's rubbish' -------------- However, [Bristol Live](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/)spoke to a resident who denied that people living in the street have anything to do with the complaint. The man, who asked not to be named, said he was frustrated too as a fellow cyclist. Article continues below He added: "The [Chocolate Path] contractors come down regularly and move things around, they are clearly monitoring it. "Residents haven't got anything to do with it, it's rubbish." ![Image 11](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4404783.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Avon-Crescent.jpg) View 5 Images Cyclists inside the road closure along Avon Crescent in Bristol(Image: Jon Kent) Article continues below He said the situation had "obviously been causing friction" but that the sign pictured above was not representative of how all residents feel. Article continues below [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) banned general traffic from the city centre route on August 2, in a bid to cut pollution and make it easier to walk and [cycle](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cycling). ‌ But we took up a spot on the bridge five days later and filmed for 20 minutes as about 116 unauthorised vehicles, by our count, appeared to travel through the bus gate. Article continues below You can watch our time-lapse footage, shot at 12pm on Friday (August 7), at the top of this page. Breaches of the closure will eventually result in [a £60 fine](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/motorists-pictured-risking-60-fine-4395773), though penalties are not yet being enforced on the route, which links Victoria Street with High Street. The council is sending out warning letters in the "initial weeks" of the ban and has not yet revealed when it will start issuing fines. ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. Changes to traffic free seafront scheme in Portishead have been announced * [](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/) * [News](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/) * [Bristol News](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/) * [North Somerset Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/north-somerset-council) North Somerset Council has carried out a review of the temporary closure of The Esplanade ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 12:30, 12 Aug 2020 Portishead seafront is to remain a traffic free zone for now following a review by council highways chiefs. ‌ Barriers were put up at both ends of Esplanade Road earlier this summer to provide more space for social distancing. ‌ The move meant all the parking spaces along The Esplanade were out of use. ‌ Following a review of the temporary restrictions, [North Somerset Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/north-somerset-council) has decided to keep them in place to support social distancing. However there will be some tweaks to the scheme with additional disabled parking put in place. Additional disabled parking spaces will be added facing the sea next to the temporary barriers at the Lake Road/Esplanade Road Junction nearest to Beach Road West. ‌ Extra disabled spaces will also be installed near to the temporary barriers at the Lake Road/Esplanade junction by the Lido Yellow lining will be installed by the corner of Lake Road/Beach Road West to stop traffic congestion in the area ‌ An exit sign will be installed at the west end of the Esplanade to deter people from turning around The Kilkenny Fields and Lido car parking will be signposted. READ MORE: [House fire near Bristol leaves woman with life-threatening injuries](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/house-fire-bristol-leaves-woman-4411698)READ MORE: [Every coronavirus symptom you need to be aware of including red toes and hiccups](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/every-coronavirus-symptom-you-need-4412876) North Somerset Council executive member for highways Councillor James Tonkin said: “Our priority continues to be the health of our residents and social distancing plays a key role in this. ‌ “As a result, the temporary road closure will remain in place for the time being but we have listened to the feedback received and acted accordingly." The review comes at the same time as people are being asked their views on the possibility of The Esplanade becoming traffic free permanently. Sustainable transport charity Sustrans has put together a survey asking people what they think of the changes made to help people adhere to social distancing guidelines. ‌ The Space to Move survey covers locations across the UK,including the towns of Clevedon, Nailsea and Portishead where a number of measures have been put in place. People across the UK are being invited to add their scheme and give feedback on it. North Somerset Council spokesman Nick Yates said: “Sustrans is running a survey to find out what people think about the changes we’ve made to allow for safer social distancing across North Somerset, including Portishead Esplanade. Article continues below “We will use this information to help inform future decision making.” People wanting to find out more about the survey and get involved can go [here](http://www.sustrans.org.uk/space-to-move.) ‌ * * *

'Bold' plans to close more than a dozen busy roads across Bristol revealed St Mark's Road, Dean Lane and Clifton Village have all been earmarked for closure to general traffic ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 18:45, 13 Aug 2020 Updated 18:47, 13 Aug 2020 'Bold' plans have been revealed to close at least 16 busy Bristol roads to motorists. ‌ [Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council)leaders have launched a consultation into proposals to shut the routes - many of which are popular walking areas. ‌ They hope the move will help reduce our city's dangerous levels of air pollution. ‌ READ MORE: [Bristol City Council prosecuted carer who claimed payments for person who had died](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-city-council-prosecuted-carer-4422906)READ MORE: ['What is wrong with people?': Opinion split after Russell Howard cuts Bristol gig short](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/music-nightlife/russell-howard-cuts-bristol-gig-4422632) From St Mark's Road, in [Easton](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/easton), St Werburgh's Mina Road, Dean Lane in [Southville](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/southville) and roads in[Clifton](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/clifton)Village, the council has picked some of the city's most popular locations. Many of the proposed closures have been suggested by residents, the council says. Earlier this month, general traffic was[banned from using Bristol Bridge](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-bridge-ban-traffic-seemingly-4406424) in the city centre. ‌ And now the council plans to plough forward with its 'second wave' of transport schemes, designed to make it easier to walk, cycle and use public transport. ### What the mayor says Mayor Marvin Rees said: “We are taking bold action to create a better, more connected future for everyone and to help Bristol emerge from this crisis in a more inclusive and sustainable way. “By diverting traffic away from our community hubs, we will protect public health and unlock barriers to inclusive economic growth with cleaner air, safer and better public transport, and improved walking and cycling routes for everyone. ‌ READ MORE: [Police hunt for witnesses to Chinese takeaway burglary](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/police-hunt-witnesses-chinese-takeaway-4422344) “These major transport improvements were already in the pipeline, but the [coronavirus](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/coronavirus)means we needed to accelerate the plans to support social distancing. “The pandemic has had huge impacts on our usual travel habits and, despite its challenges, we saw air pollution levels drop by almost half during the months of lockdown with big increases in walking and cycling. ‌ "We want to capture those benefits and protect the long-term public health of the city as well as the viability of our public transport services that provide real value to our communities. “This next phase will strengthen the new schemes and we will be talking to communities across the city to determine the next steps for creating more liveable neighbourhoods that are free from traffic congestion and pollution.” ### Here's a list of all the roads being considered for closure ‌ * St Mark's Road, Easton * Clifton Village (_Bristol Live_ has asked which roads this would see closed) * Beaufort Road/Victoria Avenue, Redfield * Mina Road, St Werburghs * Cotham Hill * Greville Road/Upton Road, Southville * Langton Court Bridge, St Anne’s * Rosemary Lane, Eastville * Redcliffe Mead/Prewett Street, Redcliffe * Overton Road, Bishopston * Picton Street, Montpelier * Dean Lane, Southville * Woodland Road, Clifton The proposals would retain access to the roads but prevent through traffic using them by closing one end. It's hoped this will provide safer walking and cycling routes. READ MORE: [Mum pens hilarious sweary rant about husband's shopping fail](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/whats-on-news/mum-pens-hilarious-sweary-rant-4422271) How is it being funded? ----------------------- Bristol City Council, in partnership with the West of England Combined Authority, has now applied for further government funding to extend the temporary work already done. ‌ The long-term ambition is to make these changes permanent as part of the transformation of Bristol’s transport network. READ MORE: [Woman told to 'pull T-shirt down' over her shorts in Sainsbury's after complaint](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/shopping/woman-told-pull-shirt-down-4421965) Other work ---------- * Old City pedestrianisation * Lewins Mead bike lane * Upper Maudlin Street, Park Row, Marlborough Street and Colston Street bike lanes (including changes to St Michael’s Hill junction to ban the left turn onto St Michael’s Hill from Perry Road and to ban the right turn out of St Michael’s Hill onto Perry Road) * Clifton Triangle bike lane (including a bus stop bypass to better integrate Queen's Road bus stops) New cycling improvements: Article continues below * Nelson Street – new protected bike lane and improvements to pedestrian crossing facilities * New high quality, on-street, secure cycle shelters across the city for residents in flat or terraced apartments. Residents can comment on the plans, which could be put in place as early as this winter, [here.](http://www.bristol.gov.uk/covidtransport.)

Hundreds of residents hit back at campaign to stop Bristol high street being pedestrianised "St Marks Road is a good high street with a good diversity of shops and it’s really well-loved, but that doesn’t mean it’s perfect" ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 15:38, 20 Aug 2020 Updated 20:01, 20 Aug 2020 Hundreds of people have signed a counter-petition calling for the pedestrianisation of an Easton shopping street. ‌ Bristol City Council [revealed proposals](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bold-plans-close-more-dozen-4423474) on August 13 for part of St Marks Road – the stretch between Henrietta Street and Berwick Road – to close to general traffic, along with 15 other Bristol routes. ‌ Some 1,166 people signed a [petition](https://www.change.org/p/marvin-rees-save-st-marks-road-easton-bristol) against the scheme after two long-running shops, Pak Butchers and Bristol Sweet Mart, said [it would hurt trade and force them to leave the street](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/shopping/two-much-loved-shops-would-4437056). ‌ But now Easton resident and transport planner Rob Bryher has launched a [counter-petition](https://www.change.org/p/bristol-city-council-create-a-liveable-neighbourhood-in-st-marks-road-easton-bristol-to-save-our-high-street?recruiter=8587208&utm_source=share_petition&utm_medium=copylink&utm_campaign=share_petition), which has seen 251 people sign in support of the plans. Mr Bryher, 36, said: “I live 100 yards from the road, and it’s an area dominated by motor vehicles. “It’s a very densely packed area. St Marks Road is a good high street with a good diversity of shops and it’s really well-loved, but that doesn’t mean it’s perfect. ‌ “There are cars littered all along it. People can barely walk on the pavements because of all the parked cars. They have to walk on the road. “Pushing my nine-month-old daughter in a buggy down St Marks Road is almost impossible. There needs to be less emphasis on vehicle movements.” ‌ Pak Butchers co-owner Abdul Malik says the business – which opened its St Marks Road branch in 1995 and has more than 18 staff – is “on the brink of collapse” following the coronavirus crisis. He fears pedestrianisation will drive away customers who are reliant on cars, but Mr Bryher disagrees. components.molecules.ReadMore: [Woman's horror at Bristol Travelodge hotel after stripping duvet to see 'skin-crawling' stain](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/whats-on-news/womans-horror-bristol-travelodge-hotel-4441947)components.molecules.ReadMore: [Man attacked women outside store after massive shoplifting spree](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/man-attacked-women-outside-store-4440990) Citing a [2016 TFL study](http://content.tfl.gov.uk/town-centres-report-2014-15.pdf), Mr Bryher said: “Shoppers walking and cycling visit high streets more frequently and spend more money compared to those in cars.” ‌ Asked if the businesses are better-placed to judge the impact given their experience trading in the area, the planner said: “They’re going to have an understanding. “I absolutely concur that people visit them from all over the country, but we’re talking about an area of 60m being closed, not the whole road. “I understand where they’re coming from. They’re in a position of great vulnerability because it’s been a terrible few months. ‌ “They don’t think this is good timing, but I think it’s perfect timing from a different perspective. Bristol has just got the money from central Government so that we can finally fund schemes like this.” Mr Bryher also responded to concerns pedestrianisation could worsen congestion in surrounding streets. ‌ He said: “I have a Master's in planning. There is really good evidence on disappearing traffic. The idea is that whenever traffic restrictions are put in, traffic nearly always lessens. “You’ve taken out space that could be used for cars, and the effect is people usually don’t make the same car journeys. **For news tailored to your local area****, powered by [In Your Area](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/):** ‌ **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** “Travel behaviour isn’t just influenced by saying people should all walk and cycle more. It’s also influenced by the built environment. “Nobody is asking to stop Broadmead or Cabot Circus from being pedestrianised. There is a benefit from those being places where people can sit down and spend time with friends, and we could see the same benefit here.” ‌ The prospect of fewer car journeys to the area has left Pak Butchers concerned it will lose out on its many customers who travel from afar. Mr Malik has suggested a new car park in the area could mitigate the impact of pedestrianisation, but Mr Bryher says he would object to this. ‌ The planner said: “Where would they put a car park? The roads are so constricted in this area. “The businesses need to think about how they can get people from bigger car parks in the area, like IKEA’s, to their shops. “It’s not a sustainable solution to build more car parks. Businesses in this area need to think outside the box.” ‌ He added: “This scheme would mean a massive improvement to air quality for our community. We have polluted high streets.” Both Bristol Sweet Mart – the biggest supplier of ethnic foods and spices in the South West – and Pak Butchers rely heavily on deliveries. ‌ Mr Bryher believes it does not “make sense” for the businesses to say the proposals would hamper their system for deliveries. He says vehicles would “simply require a turning circle” for vehicles at the junction of Henrietta Street and St Marks Road for existing delivery arrangements to continue. “The priorities of either side of the proposed section of road would obviously need to be changed to allow for this, with two-way and one-way priorities being instituted as required,” he said. ‌ Bristol Association of Restaurants, Bars and Independent Establishments (BARBIE) launched the campaign against the plans, which it argues “would be the end of St Marks Road”. It was crowned the best street in the UK at the 2020 Urbanism Awards and draws thousands to its Grand Iftar street party each year. ‌ Responding to the counter-petition, Mr Malik said: “We should not be trying to fix something that is not broken. ‌ “In essence we should be sharing our street and its characteristics as a shining example for others to follow – not following, but leading.” Asked if he agrees that deliveries could continue as normal, he said the narrow streets around St Marks Road “would not be able to cope with lorries and vans and the added diversion route of traffic”. ‌ He added: “There is a need to look at the area in practical terms, not on paper. “People who have spent their lives in the area and who own property and businesses in the area will have far greater knowledge of the challenges that a potential scheme would pose on the surrounding area. “I do not agree that the side streets would provide any solutions to the problems traders face, and I am certain local residents will not be happy if we propose solutions which will congest or create more traffic for their neighbourhoods.” ‌ Mayor of Bristol, Marvin Rees, said in a Bristol City Council meeting on Wednesday (August 19) the pedestrianisation of St Marks Road is not certain to go ahead. He revealed the Government gave councils two weeks to apply for funding to “bring forward green transport offers” like pedestrianisation. There was not enough time to hold a public consultation before making the bid, so the council indicated how it would like to spend the money, according to Mr Rees. He added: “Worst case scenario is that through the consultation we find out it absolutely will not work and we don’t spend the money, and we talk to the Government about what we do with that. “But we had to get ourselves in the game, otherwise we would have missed the opportunity.” Article continues below A Bristol City Council spokeswoman said: “The next phase of transport changes in the city will see community conversations take place to find ways to create more liveable neighbourhoods that are free from congestion and pollution. “We will shortly start engaging with the local community, businesses and residents regarding the proposed road closure for St Marks Road in Easton.”

Keynsham High Street: How businesses have reacted to closing it off to traffic But critics say very few pedestrians actually walk in the road - and those that do risk colliding with a cyclist ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 10:46, 25 Aug 2020 Businesses say closing [Keynsham](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/keynsham) High Street to traffic has hit trade by up to 20 per cent. ‌ Pedestrianisation was brought in under emergency powers so shoppers can keep a safe social distance without worrying about stepping into the street. ‌ But critics say very few pedestrians actually walk in the road - and those that do risk colliding with a cyclist. ‌ Town council chair Andy Wait said there were plenty of supporters and there would be a full consultation if the trial was to be made permanent. David Quick, the manager of greengrocers WF Buss, said footfall in his shop was down 20 per cent since the scheme was introduced, while Nigel Church said his newsagents, Church’s, was quieter than it had been in months. “The council has been trying to close the road for years,” said Mr Church. “All of a sudden they managed to get their way. ‌ components.molecules.ReadMore: [Extinction Rebellion protest: Police issue statement as XR plan to block Bristol traffic for days](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/extinction-rebellion-protest-police-issue-4453553)components.molecules.ReadMore: [Ice cream van stranded on beach - rescue crews called](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/local-news/ice-cream-van-stranded-beach-4454351) “They want to create a café culture but the demographic of Keynsham is too old for that. “A lot of customers think it’s a waste of time. I’m definitely not in favour. I’m losing passing trade every day. “I hope it goes back to the way it was. The council don’t listen. I feel they’ve already made their minds up.” ‌ Mr Quick added: “I don’t know if people are staying away because they think they’ll face traffic chaos - there’s been a lot of that in Keynsham. The council say it’s only temporary, but then the one-way system was meant to be as well. “They forced the one-way system through and will probably force this through. I don’t think it’s going to help traders. “People are so used to the pavements - it’s alien walking down the middle of the road.” ‌ Tattoo artist Kelly Yeates, who owns Savannah Studio, said: “We get the feeling they’re trying to make it permanent. It’s a concern for the independents. It will affect footfall. “I sat in all the council meetings when the road went one-way. It directly affected footfall. ‌ “The councillors just said they were keeping it. They weren’t interested in hearing from traders, so I don’t bother any more.” Helen Godfrey, the owner of Conscience Foods and Lifestyle, said she was initially in favour of pedestrianisation but it left her business “quieter than ever”. She said the hours were too restrictive for a small town that struggles for footfall, and had left her unable to access a car park she pays rent on. ‌ “They still allow cyclists down. I’ve almost been knocked down twice. On Saturdays you have young people doing wheelies - how intimidating is that?” **For news tailored to your local area****, powered by [In Your Area](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/):** **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** ‌ One trader who did support the scheme did not give his name. He said: “I have no problem with it. I think it works. “Normally the buses fill the shop with fumes. If it’s all pedestrianised it’s better. It makes a better shopping experience. “Covid was quite lucky for the council to put this in motion.” ‌ Councillor Hal MacFie, a Liberal Democrat, said shoppers were “almost universally positive” about being able to shop in a car-free environment, but he was concerned that shops were losing out on trade. Measures to improve opportunities for walking and cycling were high in the Lib Dem manifesto promises but many opposition councillors are not convinced about the scheme in Keynsham. Conservative councillor Lisa O’Brien said it had caused issues for residents with mobility problems and was “ill thought out and not necessary”. ‌ “I have fought this closure from the start and continue to do so,” she said. “It is causing traffic problems, illegal parking and congestion. It is also not helping the retailers in the High street.” ‌ Cllr Brian Simmons said using informal consultations to make far-reaching decisions was “unethical, undemocratic and discourteous”, adding that some elderly disabled people could not access the shops and were going to Longwell Green instead. Cllr Alan Hale said the “biggest nonsense” of the scheme was retaining the cycle lane rather than sending cyclists an extra 100 metres, warning that they are a potential danger in the High Street. He added: “Cllr Wait has never made any secret of his wish to see the High Street fully pedestrianised. The administration has a significant majority to enable them to do whatever they want to do.” ‌ Defending the scheme, Lib Dem Cllr Wait, also who sits on B&NES Council, said: “I am fully in favour of this development and have plenty of evidence from residents and businesses to support this view. This is a temporary trial and if it were to be made permanent there would be full consultation. “As regards the times when the High Street is closed, this is a trial and there may be an argument that this could be reduced.” ‌ He accepted that a “small minority” of cyclists were a problem but said signs now clearly indicate how they should behave. Transport cabinet member Joanna Wright thanked the 250 people who had responded to the consultation so far. Article continues below She said: “The measures were put in place to allow people to social distance safely following the Government directive, but we are taking the opportunity to find out whether there is support for restrictions to be retained in some form. “We will be assessing the feedback to explore the best options for Keynsham going forward. “We continue to welcome people’s views, which can be given through the Sustrans Space to Move [website](https://www.sustrans.org.uk/space-to-move/)."
