7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4472428.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_prince-street-bridge.jpg) View Image Pedestrians using the full width of Prince Street Bridge during the XR protest this weekend(Image: Harry Jordan/ Extinction Rebellion Bristol) Activists who have spent days occupying part of Bristol's harbourside hope their protest will result in permanent change. ‌ Prince Street Bridge has been closed to motorists since Friday morning, when [Extinction Rebellion](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/extinction-rebellion) (XR) launched a four-day protest at key sites in the city. ‌ The cycle lane has still been accessible and pedestrians have been able to use the entire width of the bridge, strolling along the side of the road where cars usually cross. Article continues below Today (August 31) marks the end of XR's occupation, but they hope it will not be the last time that [vehicles](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/traffic-travel)are banned from the bridge. Pete Hughes, Extinction Rebellion's Bristol coordinator, said: "We are hopeful that the [[Bristol City](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council)] council will continue to reserve Prince Street Bridge for use just by cyclists and pedestrians. "With 10 times the number of individuals on foot or bicycle crossing the bridge compared to motorised vehicles, it is senseless that we revert to a 50/50 split." ‌ Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. You can check out at any time. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice) [Join us on WhatsApp](https://chat.whatsapp.com/JwmceTjpWjYACrvdGPRfyJ) The council[closed Bristol Bridge](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-bridge-close-traffic-what-4336285) at the start of August, partly to improve air quality, and some people want to see this approach rolled out. Rebels were due to decamp from Prince Street and Wapping Wharf this afternoon [Monday], taking their action to Cardiff and then to London. Article continues below Their disruption this time around, which saw a[life-sized elephant installed](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/extinction-rebellion-spraying-elephant-footprints-4470153) in the city centre, was designed to raise awareness of the [Climate and Ecological Emergency (CEE) Bill.](https://xrbristol.org.uk/climate-and-ecological-emergency-bill/) Bristolians were encouraged to take photos in the street and at home, with placards asking their MPs to back the bill. READ MORE: [The best pictures from Extinction Rebellion's protest at Bristol Airport](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/gallery/) Pete said: “When people ask why XR are taking this kind of action, we say it’s to get those in power to listen to the people. ‌ “Mayor[Marvin Rees](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/marvin-rees)has said that XR is pushing at the wrong doors, that our actions are focused in Labour-held cities. In fact this is happening nationally and it’s not just about which political party has seats. "Across the country we are asking all MPs and city mayors to put their weight behind this bill without delay." The CEE Bill focuses on citizens' assemblies as a mode of decision-making to tackle the climate crisis. ‌ Bristol XR coordinator Pete added: "This has worked incredibly effectively in countries like Ireland, Poland and the Netherlands. “It will allow the people of the UK to find real, radical and democratic solutions to the environmental crises facing the UK and internationally. "This is the hard graft, behind-the-scenes legislative work that needs to be done." ‌ Among the action protesters took today was a socially-distanced samba workshop outside the Arnolfini, which saw members of XR Families bang pots and pans to make their message heard. A branch of XR called the Aged Agitators also reached out to members of the public to explain what the CEE Bill is and why they think it should be passed. READ MORE: [Traveller camp pitches up on Eastville Park with 10 vehicles](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/traveller-camp-pitches-up-eastville-4470432)READ MORE: [21 things you only really notice when you leave Bristol](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/21-things-you-only-really-4467210) Aged Agitator Sue Kilroe, 70, from Kingsdown, said: “It’s often quite simple to change where your money goes. If you have a pension, you have the right to insist it's ethically invested. “Pressure for change works. Over 70 financial organisations have recently signed up to a framework tackling the climate emergency. “This is still not enough, and in the current pandemic we need the Climate and Ecological Emergency Bill more than ever. “We are urging members of the public to lobby their MP to support the CEE Bill.” Article continues below Protesters were due to pack up at 2pm to head for Cardiff. Covid-19 pandemic has accelerated plans to cut traffic from the city centre and give priority to pedestrians and [cyclists](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cycling) across Bristol. Article continues below What began as temporary measures to help social distancing have become a once-in-a-generation opportunity to change the way we travel, with many of the schemes set to become permanent fixtures. Article continues below But the city council isn't simply creating pop-up cycle lanes, sitting back and saying: “Build it, and they will come.” Article continues below 138205441690 Better by Bike, the official cycling website for the region’s local authorities, funded by Bristol city, North Somerset, South Gloucestershire and Bath & North East Somerset councils, has been relaunched to help everyone from experienced cyclists to those getting back on the saddle for the first time in years. You can plan a safe route, find cycle maps and rides suitable for all abilities, and access a wealth of help and information to build confidence on two wheels. The West of England Combined Authority (Weca), meanwhile, has just launched a campaign called Joy in the Journey to get people walking and cycling as an alternative to the car. [![Image 8: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Put your skills to the test. Whether you love word games, tricky cryptic crosswords, Sudoku, or our other brain teasers, you'll find a new favourite today! Play Now](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games/) And the authorities seem to be pushing at an open door, with the number of people using active travel during lockdown reaching record levels. Eleven per cent of residents are cycling more now than before March, a third are walking more and 62 per cent are willing to do more of both to reduce their contribution to climate change. Article continues below 138205439175 Even before the pandemic, 94 per cent of people in Weca’s Local Cycling & Walking Infrastructure Plan survey said the region would be a better place if more people walked or cycled. More than half of the 500 firms who took part in Business West’s latest survey said they were putting in plans to increase the uptake of cycling among employees, with a further 34 per cent investing in supporting infrastructure to help store bikes securely. components.molecules.ReadMore: [Calls for another Bristol bridge to permanently close to traffic](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/calls-another-bristol-bridge-permanently-4472491)components.molecules.ReadMore: [The region's 14 most controversial planning applications that were thrown out](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/regions-14-most-controversial-planning-4469660) A Bristol City Council spokesperson said: “We are making significant changes to our transport system to improve air quality and make it easier and safer for people travelling by foot, by bike or on public transport in the city. Article continues below “Our focus recently has been on widening pavements to help with social distancing, the pedestrianisation of the Old City, the closure of Bristol Bridge to general traffic and new city centre bike lanes to add to our already extensive network. “Priority has been given to set up bike lanes that are protected from traffic and routes on roads with low levels of traffic and shared paths, to ensure people feel safe and more confident on the roads, and encourage people to make the switch from car to bike. “We understand that cycling on well-used roads can be daunting, particularly for first time cyclists. Article continues below components.molecules.ReadMore: [This is why McDonald's tell their customers the ice cream machine is broken](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/food-drink/mcdonalds-tell-customers-ice-cream-4471366)components.molecules.ReadMore: ['Physical activity is good for everyone' Experts say exercise is low risk for people with heart disease](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/physical-activity-good-everyone-experts-4467406) “The newly relaunched Better by Bike website offers a range of support to people who have never cycled before and those looking to gain confidence. “This includes advice on how to start cycling, cycle maps, leisure rides, bike loans and personal travel planning to look at safe routes for regular journeys. “Through Better by Bike, we’re also reaching out to community groups and leaders to offer accessible routes into cycling, such as free 1:1 adult cycle training, and highlighting the low-cost, traffic-free cycle skills courses through the Bristol Family Cycling Centre (BFCC). Article continues below “BFCC has a variety of courses on offer for people of all ages and abilities, and a full range of adapted cycles for those with disabilities or those who find two wheels difficult.” West of England mayor Tim Bowles said of Weca’s Joy in the Journey campaign: “During lockdown many people have taken advantage of quieter roads to walk or cycle more regularly. “As more people begin to return to school, college and work we have a real opportunity to capture the positive changes we have seen to improve the physical and mental health of residents, improve air quality and ease congestion across the West of England. Article continues below “That’s why I’m encouraging more people to find joy in the journey by swapping a short car journey for walking or cycling whether commuting to work, taking the kids to school or popping to the shops. “Not only will walking or cycling boost your mood but it will also help us on the road to a greener future for the region.” **Sign up to our daily newsletter using the box at the top of this article, read all about what's involved [here](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-live-latest-news-email-2049191), or click [here](https://communicatoremail.com/F/gqxNwa0hZubC9_IKKGjv78/) to see all of our newsletters** Article continues below Sustrans head of partnerships Jon Usher said: “Our research shows that even before the Covid pandemic, a majority of residents in the West of England supported measures to improve walking and cycling on high streets and the restriction of traffic outside schools and on residential streets. “As schools and workplaces reopen in September we need to take this opportunity to make active travel the obvious choice for all ages and abilities. “It’s great to see the measures that Weca and councils in the region have already taken and we fully support the vision for the future.” Article continues below More information is at [Travelwest](https://travelwest.info/) website’s 'joyinthejourney' page or [Better by Bike](https://betterbybike.info/). Hundreds sign petition to demand Bristol Bridge traffic closure is reversed "The decision to close off Bristol Bridge, Baldwin street and some of the access to the city centre is beyond a joke" --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 12:08, 03 Sep 2020 Updated 12:22, 03 Sep 2020 Hundreds of people have signed an online petition asking the Mayor of Bristol to reverse the traffic measures introduced in the city centre a month ago. ‌ Almost 700 people signed the online petition set up by Ben Thomas in the past week, with numbers rising every day. ‌ The petition calls for the roads into the Old City part of Bristol to be reopened to private vehicles, and says the decision to close off Bristol Bridge, Baldwin Street and other parts of the city is 'beyond a joke'. ‌ Access across Bristol Bridge, through Baldwin Street, around Castle Park and at the bottom of Union Street is still free and open for people walking and cycling, riding motorbikes or driving taxis and buses, but people driving private vehicles face a £100 fine. components.molecules.ReadMore: [NHS worker who was victim of racist attack says 'the streets aren't safe until they are caught'](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/nhs-worker-who-victim-racist-4479185) The measure was brought in on August 1 and is running as an 18-month trial, which will either be scrapped, extended or made permanent on January 31, 2022. The council is holding a six-month consultation period on the idea - which also began on the same day they brought in the restrictions. ‌ Mayor Marvin Rees and other council chiefs said the measure was needed to cut vehicle access to the medieval Old City of Bristol, help the wider plan to increase air quality in the city centre, and make the increased pedestrianisation of areas around King Street, Corn Street and St Nick's Market easier to do. But the plan has seen something of a backlash - people living in south Bristol say the closure has blocked up their easiest route to drive across the city, and some business owners in Victoria Street, Redcliffe - the main approach to Bristol Bridge from the south - have [said the closure has hit their trade harder](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-bridge-closure-worse-business-4423131) than the coronavirus pandemic lockdown did. ‌ Mr Thomas said in [his petition](https://www.change.org/p/the-mayor-of-bristol-marvin-rees-reverse-the-decision-to-close-bristol-bridge-baldwin-st-access-to-the-city-centre) the diversions 'make everyone's journeys longer, therefore spending more time in the vehicles, creating more pollution'. "The reasons stated for doing so are to help with pollution and social distancing which are ludicrous to say the least!" he said. "The diversions make everyone's journey's longer therefore spending more time in the vehicles, creating MORE pollution. ‌ **For news tailored to your local area****, powered by [In Your Area](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/):** "Local businesses have suffered enough over the past six months and this will be the final nail in the coffin for some. ‌ "Marvin Rees and Bristol City Council have a lot to answer for and we, the residents of Bristol shouldn't accept these changes. "They have made a big enough mess of the traffic situation over the years in our great city," he added. ‌ [Earlier this month](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-bridge-baldwin-street-closures-4477760), the council’s strategic city transport service manager Adam Crowther described how some of the fast-track measures - like the closure of Bristol Bridge to private vehicles - have already had an immediate impact on air quality. Speaking to scrutiny councillors in late August, Mr Crowther said the closure of Bristol Bridge and Baldwin St had “effectively removed all the through-traffic from the centre of town”. ‌ “That change, I think we can certainly argue as a city, has made a significant improvement to air quality in the whole central part of the city, well in advance of what we would have expected through implementing a clean air zone. “Baldwin Street was one of our worst streets [for air pollution]; it will now be one of our best streets. “So we’ve made an immediate impact that wouldn’t have happened until 2023," he added. Bristol is in the midst of a major transformation and how it will eventually look is still undecided as planning permission is continually granted for a vast range of new projects. ‌ The Broad Plain area in particular is [changing dramatically as more and more cranes dominate the skyline](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/you-can-see-many-cranes-3318014) - a sign that building work is underway and in some cases near completion. ‌ Located close to Temple Meads Station, Temple Quarter and the city centre, the area in and around Broad Plain is undergoing rapid social and economic change. ‌ The part of the city between [Temple Meads](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/temple-meads) and Old Market has been earmarked for development for a while, but it’s only recently that the change has really begun to take place. But in the next year or so Broad Plain is set to be surrounded by high-rise tower blocks to the south and the west. Projects include the transformation of the old [Gardiner Haskins' building and build an aprt-hotel, office space and 160 homes in a 20-storey tower block](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/images-show-how-gardiner-haskins-3963000), as well as the new mixed-use development Glassfields which is under construction on the corner of Temple way and Avon Street. ‌ Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. It has launched a consultation on a draft public realm strategy for the area which includes plans to revamp the entrances to the Temple Way underpass by removing the staircases on either side and widening the approach to the subway by St Philip and St Jacob Church. ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article3963060.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_KW_BRI_180320Soapworksdevelopment_02.jpg) View 3 Images A CGI of how the Soapworks development could look(Image: Woods Bagot/First Base) ‌ There are also plans to reduce traffic in the area and the council is looking at two options. These are: 1. Retain vehicular access from Temple Way but reduce through traffic on Broad Plain and Unity Street by making it one way eastbound only 2. No entry into Unity Street from Temple Way. All traffic to enter from Midland Road and turn around in Broad Plain. Vehicle numbers would be reduced to servicing only so no dedicated cycle provision is needed on Unity Street ‌ ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4154413.ece/ALTERNATES/s1168v/0_newsletter-image.jpg) ### Want Bristol news straight to your inbox? Sign up to our daily newsletter using the box at the top of this article, or by clicking [here](https://communicatoremail.com/F/gqxNwa0hZubC9_IKKGjv78/) to see all of our newsletters The proposals follow feedback to an initial public engagement in September 2019 designed to understand issues and opportunities in the area and support the community’s vision for an attractive central neighbourhood. The consultation will be open for six weeks, closing on Sunday, October 18. ‌ Nicola Beech, cabinet member for strategic design and city planning, said: “These proposals can help make Broad Plain a cleaner, greener and more social, attractive neighbourhood and we look forward to hearing what people think about them. “Improved pedestrian and cycle routes, along with more prominent signage, will make travelling in and around Broad Plain a better experience for residents and people moving through the area. ![Image 10](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4193760.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_ML_BRI200603construction-337JPG.jpg) View 3 Images Temple Way offices in June 2020(Image: Michael Lloyd Photography) ‌ “These changes will particularly help connect the adjacent neighbourhoods of St Judes and the Dings with the city centre and with each other, in a way that is accessible for all members of the community. “Broad Plain will become the missing piece of the puzzle that will help pull together this important area at the heart of the city whilst retaining its own character; becoming a flourishing, healthy neighbourhood in its own right.” The proposals also have the support of the Old Market Community Association. ‌ Director of the association Paul Bradburn said: “The OMCA are very pleased to be involved with the planned transformation of this small but very important part of Old Market. “With all the changes happening to the area placing so much pressure upon the public space it is reassuring to know that the council’s team have made real efforts to involve the local stakeholders, paying special attention to all the work already done within our Neighbourhood Development Plan. the spotlight last month with calls to [pedestrianise Cotham Hill to help businesses](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/calls-cotham-hill-pedestrianised-help-4399476) during the [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster), should look like. Article continues below This comes after ["bold plans" to close at least 16 busy Bristol roads](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bold-plans-close-more-dozen-4423474) to motorists were revealed earlier this month, with [council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council)leaders launching a consultation into proposals to shut the routes - many of which are popular walking areas. ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4461754.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_6-greville-road-permanent_bunting.jpg) View 3 Images (Image: Smith Maloney) A spokesman for the group said: "During the lockdown, people in Bristol experienced low traffic and clean air where they live. ‌ [![Image 9: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? "Liveable Neighbourhoods, the streets are for locals, not through-traffic." Article continues below The Liveable Neighbourhoods for Bristol campaign is already supported by over 20 groups, including Playing Out, Bristol Older People’s Forum, Bristol Cycling Campaign and the Bristol Walking Alliance. "Residents and local businesses still have full access and can get deliveries, but the only way to pass from one main road to another is on foot or by bike." ‌ To help launch the campaign, local resident Sandy Murray, of Smith Maloney Architects, has published some images to get people talking about how North Street could look if a Liveable Neighbourhood was implemented in [Southville](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/Southville). ![Image 14](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4461778.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_11-gathorne-road-temporary.jpg) View 3 Images Mr Murray said: “Our hope at Smith Maloney is that the catastrophic impact of the global pandemic can be used as a catalyst to transform the urban streetscape, allowing local communities and businesses to thrive whilst maintaining social distancing guidelines, whilst also promoting cleaner air and greener spaces. ‌ "We believe that roads like North Street could be a benchmark for the sustainable city streets of the future.” ![Image 15](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4154413.ece/ALTERNATES/s1168v/0_newsletter-image.jpg) ### Want Bristol news straight to your inbox? 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4437104.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_Pak-3.jpg) View 4 Images The staff of Pak Butchers fear for the area The pedestrianisation of an Easton shopping street could be put to a public vote if a new application is approved. ‌ Last month Bristol City Council [revealed proposals](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bold-plans-close-more-dozen-4423474) for the stretch of St Marks Road between Henrietta Street and Berwick Road to close to general traffic. ‌ But 3,604 people have signed a [petition](https://www.change.org/p/marvin-rees-save-st-marks-road-easton-bristol) against the scheme after two long-running shops, Pak Butchers and Bristol Sweet Mart, said [it would hurt trade and force them to leave the street](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/shopping/two-much-loved-shops-would-4437056). Article continues below Now Pak Butchers co-owner Abdul Malik has revealed a plan for people living and working in the area to decide the future of the street. He and 21 other locals want to be recognised as an Easton ‘neighbourhood forum’ – which under the Localism Act 2011 would allow them to design a neighbourhood plan. The ‘Easton Energiser’ plan would be adopted if it is backed by at least half the voters in a local referendum, and if it fits with planning policy and local strategy. ‌ Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. That’s the whole point.” He described the council’s pedestrianisation proposal as “a typical example” of Easton residents not feeling like their voices are being heard. “It has prompted the organisation of a forum due to opposition at such a mass scale,” he said. ‌ READ MORE: [Bokman gets top food hygiene rating after zero-star score cost restaurant £15k](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/food-drink/bokman-gets-top-food-hygiene-4524597)READ MORE: [Superfan who tattooed Percy Pig on his leg now gets huge cuddly pig toy](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-man-percy-pig-tattoo-4522504) There is also a [petition](https://www.change.org/p/bristol-city-council-create-a-liveable-neighbourhood-in-st-marks-road-easton-bristol-to-save-our-high-street?recruiter=8587208&utm_source=share_petition&utm_medium=copylink&utm_campaign=share_petition) with 355 signatures which [calls on the council to press ahead with pedestrianisation](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/hundreds-residents-hit-back-campaign-4443064), in a bid to cut pollution and improve the walking, cycling and shopping experience. Mr Malik believes more data needs to be collected on the merits of the scheme before a decision is made. He says the Saaf Hava air quality monitoring project will provide open-source data from its 20 sites across Easton. ‌ The Easton Energiser plan is only an outline at the moment, but it sets out an intention to “build on the initial 21 people who live or work in the area who have established the initial steering group”. ![Image 10](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4443673.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_ML_BRI200820pedestrian-005JPG.jpg) View 4 Images (Image: Michael Lloyd Photography) Mr Malik hopes the group will come to include everyone who lives and works in the designated area. The document also proposes an effort to tackle pollution on residential main roads in Easton, such as Easton Way. It comes after the Bristol Association of Restaurants, Bars and Independent Establishments (BARBIE) claimed pedestrianisation “would be the end of St Marks Road”. The street was crowned the best in the UK at the 2020 Urbanism Awards and draws thousands to its Grand Iftar street party each year. **For news tailored to your local area****, powered by [In Your Area](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/):** **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** Campaign group Love St Marks Road, which was behind the petition supporting pedestrianisation, has worries about the neighbourhood forum proposal. Its spokesman said: “It is always encouraging when people attempt to make positive change in their neighbourhoods. “However, we have concerns that the formation and make-up of this group is heavily geared towards closing down the ongoing open discussions about the need to move to more healthy, low-traffic neighbourhoods. “We would hope that at least half of the group moving forward would be made up of local residents and be inclusive of those who are in favour of traffic reduction on St Marks Road. ![Image 11](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4437103.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Pak-2.jpg) View 4 Images Staff at Pak Butchers “At present, this move looks like it is aimed at stopping dead any kind of discussion of restricting through traffic in Easton. “Easton deserves a rounded debate on the best approach to take, so we will be aiming to put forward our own proposals for a neighbourhood plan that prioritises the needs of people, health, sustainability, community, schools and local businesses above motorised traffic." The group said it would support a “well-trusted community organisation like Eastside Community Trust” being involved in any neighbourhood plan. Last month Mayor of Bristol, Marvin Rees, said the pedestrianisation of St Marks Road is not certain to go ahead. Councillor Kye Dudd, cabinet member for transport said: "Like many cities and urban areas across the UK, we’ve embraced the opportunity to dramatically improve the way we travel in Bristol. "This is not just about social distancing. It’s about transforming our communities and creating more liveable environments that are free from heavy traffic and pollution, while better managing through traffic. "We’re not imposing these changes on residents in these areas, but we’re reacting to feedback we’ve received from them about how we could improve walking and cycling. Back in early June we invited comments from people about transport changes they would like to see in their area. “St Marks Road was voted the UK’s best street last year. It’s extremely busy with cyclists and pedestrians before lockdown happened and for a number of years we’ve been in discussion with residents and businesses about making these movements easier. "We’re now looking to build on that by speaking with the community to get their views before we make any decisions or draw up any detailed proposals. Article continues below "We are talking to local people about adjustments we could put in place that work for St Marks Road and everyone who lives, works and visits this area. More Bristol streets to become pedestrian-only zones due to 'urgent need' to provide space for social distancing Huge inflatable octopus arms hanging above Old City will mark the changes which are necessary to help tackle the spread of coronavirus. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 06:17, 08 Oct 2020 Updated 10:24, 08 Oct 2020 More streets in the centre of Bristol will become pedestrian-only zones due to an 'urgent need' to provide more space for social distancing. ‌ Bristol City Council said from next week, the new times road closures will move to roads being shut all day from early next year. ‌ St Stephen Street and St Nicholas Streets will join Clare and Corn Streets in all-day closures, with the exception of a morning loading window for businesses, from Monday, October 12. ‌ The council has also commissioned huge inflatable octopus arms which will hang above the Old City streets to mark the major changes to the area. READ MORE: [Bristol University coronavirus outbreak: More than 100 students test positive for Covid-19](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-university-coronavirus-outbreak-more-4584970) A [council spokesperson](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) said: "The Old City road changes have been brought forward temporarily due to the urgent need to provide space for social distancing. ‌ "But the aspiration is to make the changes permanent in early 2021, to reduce air pollution in the area in the long term. "There will be public consultation before anything is made permanent." ‌ Lilly Drakoulakou, 32, is the owner of the Playground Coffee House in St Nicholas Street. She said pedestrianisation had been a fantastic, positive outcome for them. The coffee shop owner said their venue is only small and their concept was based on the idea of an adult playground, with people sitting next to strangers and playing a game with them. ‌ "This was not feasible anymore [because of coronavirus] and my entire structure was based around that," she continued. "I have five tables so I could have been running at full capacity with five people. "I now have six tables outside which has allowed me to double the capacity. "It has saved my business." ‌ Ms Drakoulakou said she didn't think she would have made the decision to reopen, for the time being at least, had it not been for the pedestrianisation. "It is fantastic to see our council reacting so quickly to our needs because we are all in this together," she continued. ‌ Ben Edgerley, of Brozen Bar, also in St Nicholas Street, said pedestrianisation had counteracted some of the effects of coronavirus, adding it had brought some people back in. "It has made the street nicer and it feels more upmarket," he said. The business owner - who runs the bar with his brother Joe - said cars used to go down the street quite fast while it is now a lot quieter. ‌ He would like to see more green in the area, maybe a tree planted there, Mr Edgerley added. Because of coronavirus, they had to operate at half of their capacity but their outdoor seating areas means they are only down by 10/20%. "I think it should be done more widely in Bristol because it changes the feel of the street," he added. "It has been a positive change for us." 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4514045.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/1_JMP_SWA_140920kingswood_Bristol_001_JPG.jpg) View Image Regent Street, Kingswood(Image: John Myers) Kingswood town centre is set to undergo major changes in a £12.5million scheme. ‌ [South Gloucestershire](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/kingswood-bradley-stoke-yate-shopping-3973913) Council announced it has secured the Government funding for a project proposing the pedestrianisation of [Regent Street](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/kingswood). ‌ The plans could see Park Road's derelict former church, the Grade-I listed Whitfield Tabernacle, restored as a "performance arts centre and cultural cinema". Article continues below They also include "the creation of a new public open space, ushering opportunities for markets, performance arts and cultural events". [Map shows where in Bristol snow is forecast as 'arctic blast' hits this week](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/where-will-snow-fall-bristol-10650459?int_source=nba) [Huge fly-tip dumped under a mile away from council tip](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/gallery/huge-fly-tip-dumped-under-10650882?int_source=nba) The council expects there to be new green space from a redevelopment of the Grade-II listed Masters Church. Masters Church and Chapel House, also Grade-II listed, are part of the Whitfield Tabernacle Conservation Area, which is planned to be accessible from Regent Street. ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) ****To get the latest news to your inbox, [click here](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/newsletter-preference-centre/)****. The council says the funding will allow traffic to be rerouted from Regent Street, while promoting walking and cycling, though specific details on the changes are yet to be released. It believes pedestrianisation will bring "a quality public space for activity and strengthen the links between Kings Chase Shopping Centre, Regent Street, the Tabernacle, and Kingswood Park". Article continues below Banning traffic from Regent Street was supported by 67 per cent of people in a survey this year, the council added. It hopes the Tabernacle revamp will see "an exciting new offer in family and evening entertainment for Kingswood". The [council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/south-gloucestershire-council) says it will release more information "in due course" for a public consultation. It did not give a time-frame. ‌ Council leader, Councillor Toby Savage, praised the "unprecedented scale of investment" in Kingswood town centre. He said: “It is timely in so many ways as we do everything we possibly can to support our town centres face the extreme challenges of declining high street retail, internet shopping boom and the Covid-19 pandemic. ‌ “I have been delighted to see urgent stabilisation works already happening to the Tabernacle alongside the Masters Church redevelopment and I am extremely excited about the opportunities we have to lead regeneration by acquiring empty and underused properties at a time where the private sector is not in a place to do so. "I hope we can extend and apply our success in securing this scale of funding and this approach to masterplanning to support our other town centres.” Kingswood MP Chris Skidmore says he helped secure the funding, alongside the council and West of England Combined Authority. Article continues below He said: “With so much local ambition for a positive future of Kingswood town centre that respects our proud heritage, I am focused on ensuring there is enough resource to ensure they come to fruition and pledge to continue campaigning for further investment and support for our area.” Follow Bristol Live: * [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/bristol.live) * [X pedestrianisation of part of Regent Street in Kingswood](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4861255.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/1_Kingswood-traffic-diversions.png) View 2 Images Proposed traffic diversions to allow pedestrianisation of part of Regent Street in Kingswood(Image: South Gloucestershire Council 2020 Future High Streets Fund engagement survey) Traffic could be diverted around Kingswood town centre if plans to pedestrianise part of it go ahead. ‌ [South Gloucestershire Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/south-gloucestershire-council) says it remains “fully committed” to the pedestrianisation of Regent Street as it prepares to launch a formal public consultation on its masterplan to rejuvenate the town’s High Street. ‌ Pedestrianisation, a new public space for events like markets, and the transformation of the derelict Whitfield Tabernacle into a “performance arts centre and cultural cinema” were among the [plans that won the council £12.5million from the government’s Future High Streets Fund](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/town-centre-set-transformed-cinema-4837994) last year. Article continues below The council says it is “urgently” revising the business case options at the request of the government and is exploring alternative sources for match-funding to pay for the proposed changes. “We are urgently considering these options in January and are preparing to launch a formal consultation in respect of the masterplan,” a spokesman said. You can check out at any time. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice) [Join us on WhatsApp](https://chat.whatsapp.com/JwmceTjpWjYACrvdGPRfyJ) * a significant commercial investment (which is subject to commercial confidentiality and formal cabinet decision) * the pedestrianisation of Regent Street and investment in public realm * the restoration of the Whitfield Tabernacle to provide a cultural and community venue.” Residents were presented with two options for the diversion of traffic around part of Regent Street in a survey about the proposals last year. ![Image 8: Proposed traffic diversions to allow pedestrianisation of part of Regent Street in Kingswood](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4861255.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_Kingswood-traffic-diversions.png) View 2 Images Proposed traffic diversions to allow pedestrianisation of part of Regent Street in Kingswood(Image: South Gloucestershire Council 2020 Future High Streets Fund engagement survey) Article continues below In the first, eastbound traffic was diverted to the north via Kimberley Road, Gilbert Road and Park Road. In the second, eastbound traffic was diverted south via Blackhorse Road and Cecil Road. Overall, 67 per cent of the nearly 600 residents who responded to the survey supported the idea of pedestrianising part of Regent Street, according to a council report on the findings. ‌ But residents did not express a strong preference for either route for diverting traffic, with half saying both options were equally acceptable or that they didn’t know which they preferred. Each route was preferred by 16 per cent of respondents. Those who preferred the northern diversion said it would prevent traffic becoming even worse. ‌ Those in favour of the southern diversion said the roads were more suitable and the area was less residential. Residents were also asked whether they thought buses should still go through the pedestrianised part of Regent Street or be diverted south through Morovian Road, with a priority bus lane along Cecil Road. ‌ Some 28 per cent said they preferred buses to be diverted versus 20 per cent who wanted them to go through Regent Street. For the council’s part, it saw the southern diversion route as bringing more challenges, such as a need for “significant road widening and junction improvements”. The council told the Local Democracy Reporting Service yesterday (January 5) it could not provide a timeline for the [Kingswood](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/kingswood) High Street project because of the funding issues. Article continues below However, a spokesperson said works were about to start to stabilise and provide a new roof for the Grade I-listed Tabernacle, and that it should be safe enough to reopen to the public by November. “The funding considerations we need to explore over the coming weeks and months alongside this significant injection from the Government will impact on the timetables of each project and we cannot therefore provide clarity at this stage, except to say that we expect phase one of the commercial investment to be complete within six months and the Tabernacle is poised to see first phase works commence very shortly,” the spokesperson said. 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4901861.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_JMP_SWA_170121_St_Marks_Road__011_JPG.jpg) View 2 Images Abdul Malik, right, and Thomas Dowdeswell are opposed to pedestrianisation of St Marks Road. Behind them, the shuttered kiosk set up in the hope of helping the community engage with a consultation on the plans(Image: John Myers) An Easton community group has considered legal action over plans to pedestrianise a shopping street. ‌ Bristol City Council [revealed proposals](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bold-plans-close-more-dozen-4423474) in August for the stretch of St Marks Road between Henrietta Street and Berwick Road to close to general traffic. ‌ More than 4,000 people signed a petition against the scheme after two long-running shops, Pak Butchers and Bristol Sweet Mart, said [it would hurt trade and force them to leave the street](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/shopping/two-much-loved-shops-would-4437056). Article continues below The council ran a consultation from December 7 to January 17 – but St Marks Road Community Group believes some people are being left out of the democratic process. [Map shows where in Bristol snow is forecast as 'arctic blast' hits this week](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/where-will-snow-fall-bristol-10650459?int_source=nba) [Huge fly-tip dumped under a mile away from council tip](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/gallery/huge-fly-tip-dumped-under-10650882?int_source=nba) It has written to the council: “The council has failed in its legal duty toward its citizens, and we will be seeking legal advice on challenging the continued ignorance in this regard.” The letter adds: “The country is in full lockdown to slow the spread of Covid-19. Many people in Easton are not able to leave their homes. Some may be isolating or shielding. ‌ [![Image 8: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Put your skills to the test. Whether you love word games, tricky cryptic crosswords, Sudoku, or our other brain teasers, you'll find a new favourite today! Play Now](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games/) “The South Asian community is more at risk from Covid-19 than most. IT or language support is critical for many if they are to complete the survey.” The group set up a St Marks Road kiosk on December 29 to help the community respond to the consultation, but it had to close when the Government announced the third lockdown on January 4. “We have not been able to assist the community in completing the survey,” added the group, which is calling on the council to postpone consultation until lockdown ends. Article continues below The street was crowned the best in the UK at the 2020 Urbanism Awards and draws thousands to its Grand Iftar street party each year. Home to the famous Easton Jamia Masjid mosque, St Marks Road is celebrated for its diversity. Its community group believes ethnic minorities would be disproportionately affected by the mooted changes. _\_**Get the biggest stories from across Bristol [straight to your inbox](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/newsletter-preference-centre/).**\__ ‌ The complaint – backed by the mosque and St Mark's Baptist Church – accuses the council of failing in its Equalities Act obligations and excluding sections of the community. One member of the group, Pak Butchers co-owner Abdul Malik, said: “We don’t understand what the panic is at the moment. I don’t know why it is being rushed through. “It hurts me really. All my life I’ve advocated bridge-building. I’ve always thought of the council as being a friend of the local community, but this has really disturbed me. ‌ “This shouldn’t be a priority at the moment. The priority should be keeping people safe. Leave people in peace. “A couple of local residents have broken down in front of me because of how the council has treated them. In all honesty, I have cried myself.” The businessman, who opened Pak Butchers’ St Marks Road branch in 1995, says the consultation has come at the worst time of his and other local traders’ careers. ‌ Mr Malik, who is also chairman of Easton Jamia Masjid, added: “The shops are performing at 50 per cent of what they were before lockdown. “We’ve got so many things to think about – how we continue to employ staff, how suppliers are going to supply us. ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4901862.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_JMP_SWA_170121_St_Marks_Road__006_JPG.jpg) View 2 Images Bristol Sweet Mart on St Marks Road(Image: John Myers) “And still we are sending emails for this consultation process, making sure the community are happy. People have lost their minds over this. “Things are changing rapidly and many members of my community don’t understand it.” Mr Malik fears banning traffic would drive away customers who are reliant on cars and hamper deliveries. There is also a petition with 385 signatures which [calls on the council to press ahead with pedestrianisation](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/hundreds-residents-hit-back-campaign-4443064), in a bid to cut pollution and improve the walking, cycling and shopping experience. Mr Malik said: “In a council meeting before lockdown, we were assured by Bristol Mayor Marvin Rees that we don’t need to worry. “He told us, ‘Regardless of what the survey says, we will come back to you.’ I think that is wrong. “You can’t go to a community and raise expectations, then say the traders don’t agree to it. Then the traders become villains. The consultation has to be done right. “At the start of the current lockdown, we asked the council for a postponement of the deadline. We haven’t had any response.” As well as running an online consultation, the council has posted surveys on the proposals to between 5,000 and 8,000 households, according to an estimate from St Marks Road Community Group. Mr Malik said: “We estimate it has cost £50,000 or £60,000. That’s money which the council could have easily spent on St Marks Road to make it better.” **Story continues below** The group has not suggested a new deadline for the consultation because of the uncertainty over coronavirus, but says there needs to be further opportunity for the community to engage. Mr Malik has campaigned for the council to work with locals on [the ‘Easton Energiser’ neighbourhood forum on an alternative plan](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/pedestrianisation-shopping-street-could-put-4525575) for St Marks Road, but says there has been no response from the council. Councillor Kye Dudd, cabinet member for transport, said: “St Marks Road was voted the UK’s best street in 2019 and is a popular, vibrant community hub. It is busy with cyclists and pedestrians and we’ve been in discussion with residents and businesses about making these movements easier. Article continues below “Once we have studied all the responses from the engagement period we will come back to local traders and groups to start a co-design process on a possible improvement scheme. “We are not committed to any one idea and we are keen for any change to benefit the community as a whole. "Bristol can emerge from this crisis in a more sustainable way if we protect public health and unlock barriers to inclusive economic growth with cleaner air and safe and reliable sustainable transport Handout) A mum is campaigning to get cars banned outside a Bristol school at drop-off and pick-up times. ‌ Last year, [cars were banned outside two schools in the city](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/cars-banned-outside-two-bristol-3815045) as part of the council's 'School Sreets' scheme which aims to [improve air quality across Bristol.](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/roads-outside-schools-could-closed-3001742) ‌ At present, Wansdyke Primary School in [Hartcliffe](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/hartcliffe) and St Peter's C of E Primary School in [Bishopsworth](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bishopsworth) are the two schools piloting the scheme - but a Greenbank mum would like to see the scheme expanded. Article continues below [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) has said [COVID-19](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/coronavirus) and school closures has meant that their plans to expand the scheme across the city had been delayed. [Map shows where in Bristol snow is forecast as 'arctic blast' hits this week](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/where-will-snow-fall-bristol-10650459?int_source=nba) [Huge fly-tip dumped under a mile away from council tip](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/gallery/huge-fly-tip-dumped-under-10650882?int_source=nba) Zoe Trinder-Widdess said the pandemic had accentuated the need for School Streets as the pavements are taken up with families queuing. The mum-of-one said that at present drop-offs and pick-ups at Whitehall Primary School, where her daughter goes to, are hectic and a mess. ‌ [![Image 8: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Put your skills to the test. Whether you love word games, tricky cryptic crosswords, Sudoku, or our other brain teasers, you'll find a new favourite today! Play Now](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games/) "They have done a pilot in two schools but the progress from the council is incredibly slow," she continued. "We want the council to pick up the pace and implement more School Streets. "Now it is the time to do it as it is really needed. "It feels like we would not get one for years if we didn't keep the pressure up. Article continues below "We would love to see more people to talking to their schools about it." ********_Stay up to date: get the biggest stories from across Bristol [straight to your inbox](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/newsletter-preference-centre/)._******** The campaign would mean vehicles would not be allowed to use the roads by the primary school - Johnsons Road and Johnsons Lane - at pick up and drop off times, with exemptions granted to residents and blue badge holders. ‌ Ms Trinder-Widdess said one of the main problems at present was cars driving down Johnsons Road - which back onto the Bristol and Bath Railway Path - and doing three point turns at the bottom of the cul-de-sac while families, cyclists and pedestrians are also trying to use the space. Another issue is inconsiderate parking, she said, particularly in the area with the widened pavement by the nursery. ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4913544.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_EFR_BRI_210121_safeschool_03.jpg) View 2 Images (Image: Handout) ‌ Ms Trinder-Widdess said the school was aware of the problem and wrote to parents last November asking them not to drive down the cul-de-sac leading to the school gates, adding they support the idea for a School Street. "The idea behind School Streets is to make it safer and make the air cleaner around the school," she added. "There will be some people who have to drive because they have to work, but hopefully it would encourage some people to walk. "I work in health research so I know how damaging poor quality air is, especially for children as their lungs are still developing. ‌ "I think it is really important for us to change how we use our urban spaces, to change the balance of how we see streets - not as a space for cars but a space for people to live. "[School Streets] should make the space around the school much more pleasant and would show us how streets could be used in different ways, rather just as a space for driving and storing cars." The Greenbank resident said that her nine-year-old daughter Greta was now able to go to and from school on her own, but that she was worried because of people's erratic driving. **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** ### What the council says Councillor Kye Dudd, cabinet member for transport, said: “Last year we were excited to introduce our first two school streets to Bristol, welcoming the idea of safer, healthier and more pleasant journeys to school for children and their families. “Unfortunately, COVID-19 and school closures has meant that our plans to expand the scheme across the city have been delayed. “We are aware of the growing interest in school streets in Bristol and across the country, and are on track to increase this offer to more schools over the coming years, with two new school streets expected to launch this March and April. Article continues below "As part of wider plans to encourage walking and cycling, we have been making changes to roads across the city following a rise in people choosing to walk and cycle during the pandemic, including pavement widening, pedestrianisation and temporary cycle lanes. "Areas where a school streets scheme may not be the best suited option can still seek out a range of other options via the council to support schools in encouraging safer, healthier, more active travel; including park and stride zones, road safety training and bike security.” Follow Bristol Live: * [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/bristol.live) * [X (Twitter)](https://x.com/bristollive) * Last chance for people to voice opinion on closure of Bristol Bridge The council has said the closure has led to reduced congestion and improved bus reliability ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 09:57, 28 Jan 2021 Bristolians have until Monday to give their views on the closure of Bristol Bridge to general traffic. ‌ In August last year, [priority was given to buses, taxis, cyclists](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-bridge-close-traffic-what-4336285) and pedestrians travelling through the city centre, with new camera-monitored bus gates installed on Bristol Bridge, Baldwin Street and Union Street. ‌ [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) has said as a result of the closure there has been reduced congestion and improved bus reliability in the central area. ‌ In a statement, the council said: "Motorised vehicles can still access Baldwin Street and Union Street using other routes but they can no longer use these streets to cut through the city. "Traffic on the roads where the bus gates have been introduced has dropped, on average, by around half as a result of the move, with First West of England taking advantage of the change by doubling the number of route 2 buses that cross Bristol Bridge." The scheme is part of a package of [transport](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/traffic-travel)improvements to ease congestion and pollution across the city. ‌ The council said these plans were already in the pipeline, but were accelerated to help residents safely navigate the city during the [COVID-19](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/coronavirus) pandemic. [Marvin Rees](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/marvin-rees), mayor of Bristol, said: “We are taking bold action to create a better, more connected future for everyone in and around Bristol. "Restricting through-traffic from the [city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre) is one way we will help to protect public health and unlock barriers to inclusive economic growth with cleaner air, safer and better public transport, and improved walking and cycling routes for everyone. ‌ “We want to capture the benefits that lockdown brought to our air quality wherever possible, and protect the long-term health of the city as well as the viability of our bus services that are crucial for our communities.” The scheme had been implemented temporarily as a trial, with the intention to make it permanent if it’s successful. ********_Stay up to date: get the biggest stories from across Bristol [straight to your inbox](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/newsletter-preference-centre/)._******** ‌ Anyone who uses Bristol Bridge, particularly local businesses, is invited to have their say in the formal consultation period, which ends at midnight on Monday (February 1). The council will consider the feedback from the consultation before deciding whether to make the scheme permanent, with a decision expected in the summer, depending on the ongoing impacts of the pandemic. ‌ Councillor Kye Dudd, cabinet member for transport, said: “We appreciate this has been a big change for the city’s transport network and that there will be a period of adjustment as we all get used to the new road layouts. "We have been monitoring the impacts of the trial closely and we’re really keen for local residents, businesses and groups to take part in the consultation and give us their views on how it has gone. “Before the current lockdown, Bristol’s air pollution was rising again and it is vital that we do everything we can to bring levels down to within legally compliant levels in the shortest time possible. ‌ "While it cannot deliver clean air for Bristol by itself and we need to continue exploring [clean air zone](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/clean-air-zone) options, there are positive indications that this change will improve air quality and bus reliability on some of the city’s previously most congested roads without impacting negatively on others." Cllr Dudd said that so far they had not seen significant problems elsewhere on the network as a result, even during times when traffic reached pre-COVID-19 levels. ‌ Chris Hanson, operations director First West of England, said moves such as the pedestrianisation of parts of the city centre and improving access for buses had enabled them to provide more efficient transport links for customers travelling into this part of the city, with over 25 routes serving the centre. He said: "We took immediate advantage of this by increasing the number of route 2 buses that cross Bristol Bridge with the introduction of a new 2a route from [Stockwood](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/stockwood) to [Southmead](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/southmead), which runs parallels to the number 2 for most of its route. “We have seen bus punctuality improve as a result of the change in access and have had some great feedback from our customers who travel on these routes." Article continues below To give your views on the scheme visit the Consultation Hub by Monday, February 1. For more information, visit: www.bristol.gov.uk/bristolbridgeinfo

A general view of Cotham Hill, Bristol. A Bristol street filled with independent businesses will be shut to drivers next month to give shops and restaurants extra space when they reopen. ‌ From April 12, [hospitality venues will be permitted to reopen](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/key-dates-four-stages-lifting-5032391) using outdoor seating areas. ‌ [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council)says a road closure on Cotham Hill will allow for a larger capacity of seating and will give businesses adequate space for loading and deliveries. ‌ Two parts of the road will be closed to traffic - between Whiteladies Gate and Hampton Lane, and between Hampton Park and Abbotsford Road. [Map shows where in Bristol snow is forecast as 'arctic blast' hits this week](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/where-will-snow-fall-bristol-10650459?int_source=nba) [Huge fly-tip dumped under a mile away from council tip](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/gallery/huge-fly-tip-dumped-under-10650882?int_source=nba) The closure will be implemented using temporary barriers that will provide space for businesses to trade outdoors on both sides of the road, with a shared space for pedestrians and cyclists in the middle. Barriers and signs will be in place to ensure reduced cycle speeds in the shared space. Dan Williams, owner of Coffee and Beer, and Kieran and Imogen Waite, Bravas owners, said the move could save businesses from closing permanently. ‌ [![Image 3: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Without it we would have to remain closed and, after an incredibly difficult year, this could be the difference between our businesses surviving or not. "It will help to cement Cotham Hill as an independent, destination high street where people can come for a stroll to browse and support the variety of great businesses. "The closure will give people more space to do this safely during the pandemic as well as create a more accessible, cleaner environment - whilst helping to address local concerns about safety and speeding traffic. ‌ "We are excited to see some new and old faces soon and hope this temporary closure will be a successful trial to help inform a more permanent strategy for the road.” The council says that although the closure to traffic is a temporary measure, it will monitor its impacts to help design a similar, long-term scheme. **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** ‌ Mayor Marvin Rees said: “Since last summer we have delivered a package of transport upgrades to make it easier for Bristolians to get around during the pandemic. "We have been flexible in our approach of using temporary materials to create more space for pedestrian and cyclists, and I am pleased that we are now able to do the same for [Cotham Hill.](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cotham) "It has been clear from speaking to traders and our recent engagement that some form of road closure is a key priority for local people, and we will be working with the community on plans for a longer-term scheme. Our aim is to deliver more liveable neighbourhoods right across the city that are free from traffic congestion and pollution.” ‌ Cllr Kye Dudd, Cabinet Member for Transport, said the council will be looking into how it can avoid negative impacts on nearby roads. “We are pleased we can provide this interim solution for businesses that will support them to reopen during the next stage of COVID-19 restrictions," he said. "Our next move will be to work with locals to design a scheme that takes a more holistic view at the area to avoid negative impacts on nearby roads. North Somerset - in a bid to promote cycling and walking. ‌ North Somerset Council has announced plans to make rural lanes between Clevedon, Yatton, Nailsea and Backwell traffic free. ‌ The move would see roads in areas including Backwell Bow, Moor Lane and Court Lane in Clevedon and Davis Lane in Kenn become vehicle free zones. Article continues below Council highways bosses say the move would help them in their aim to increase walking and cycling across the district by 200 per cent by 2030. Authority bosses have now applied for a traffic regulation order to prohibit vehicles - particularly HGVs - from the roads and a consultation on the plans runs until the end of April. There are also plans to look at introducing physical measures to block off the lanes to traffic, although this will be subject to further consultation. ‌ [![Image 3: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Put your skills to the test. Whether you love word games, tricky cryptic crosswords, Sudoku, or our other brain teasers, you'll find a new favourite today! Play Now](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games/) **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** The plans are included in the authority’s Active Travel Strategy with the vision to make ‘walking and cycling the natural choice for a cleaner, healthier and more active North Somerset.’ Essential motor vehicle access would still be allowed to homes and businesses in the affected areas. Article continues below A council spokesman said: “To support our strategy, our intention is to address rat running and inappropriate use, especially HGV use, of our rural lanes network while continuing to allow essential motor vehicle access to frontages and businesses. “The council is proposing to restrict access by motor vehicles to the lanes between Clevedon, Yatton, [Nailsea](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/changes-being-made-nailseas-rapid-5244743)and Backwell in order to promote and enable greater active travel, particularly walking and cycling. “For example, residents, landowners, businesses, pubs and hospitality venues will continue to have motor vehicle access for all their needs and those of visitors, clients, employees and suppliers and customers. ‌ “The resulting reduction in the traffic will create a more pleasant, inviting and safer environment for active travel while preserving the rural nature of the area and providing protection from increasing traffic growth resulting from further development pressures.” The lanes network is well used by local residents wanting to avoid main roads as a cut through between the towns and villages. READ MORE: [Weston-super-Mare carnival cancelled for second year in a row](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/local-news/weston-super-mare-carnival-cancelled-5245115)READ MORE: [Vandals trash bird watching hides at nature reserve near Bristol](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/vandals-trash-bird-watching-hides-5244410) They often get gridlocked when there are issues with the M5 and local roads get congested as a result. ‌ The plans - known as the Rural Lane Active Travel Enforcement Scheme - will be funded with money from the Department for Transport’s Active Travel Fund. The measures could also be supported by reducing speed limits, introducing ‘entrance gateways’, traffic calming and introducing physical measures to close roads to vehicles. Council bosses say the desire for[safer walking, cycling and horse riding routes](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/fitness-clubs-animal-shape-running-5226466)was highlighted as a result of the first national lockdown as a result of the coronavirus pandemic. ‌ The spokesman added: “This will build on the huge demand for cycling and walking routes that was demonstrated in the first covid lockdown. “By going through this process we expect to transform the feel of these lanes so that they become a viable option for many more local residents to travel actively between the communities connected by this rural network. “Most journey lengths within the area will be perfectly suited to cycling but the lanes will also be attractive to pedestrians and equestrians and improve access to the countryside. “This will build on the huge latent demand for cycling and walking that was [demonstrated in the first covid lockdown.](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/weston-super-mare-neighbourhood-no-5231437)” The authority said the move would also help it achieve its target of becoming carbon neutral by 2030. The consultation on the scheme runs until April 30 and people can find out more [here.](https://www.n-somerset.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2021-03/31%20Mar%201%20Apr%20highways%20and%20public%20rights%20of%20way%20notices.pdf) **The roads across North Somerset which could become traffic free** Backwell Bow, Backwell - its entire length. Cotham Hill traffic ban 'dangerous and unworkable' says community group They're worried the ban could pose a risk to life due to issues with public safety ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 05:00, 03 Apr 2021 Updated 17:39, 27 Apr 2021 A traffic ban on Cotham Hill, which will give hospitality venues extra trading space when they reopen, is ‘dangerous and unworkable’ say some residents and traders. Members of the Hampton Park and Cotham Hill Community Group (HPCHCG), that live and work along [the street to be partially shut to traffic](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/traffic-banned-destination-bristol-street-5212159) for three months, have expressed extreme concerns about the ban they say ‘hasn’t been thought through at all’. But [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) says it has had hundreds of comments in support of the pedestrianisation plan. It says it gave a survey to Cotham Hill locals asking for their feedback last year, and out of 2632 asked, 571 respondents made comments supporting pedestrianisation and a further 202 supported outdoor seating for traders. [BristolLive recently spoke to some hospitality venues who are welcoming the plan](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/food-drink/bristol-restaurant-owners-say-cotham-5223523), but members of the community group who oppose it say it’s so dangerous it could pose a risk to life. **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** According to the council’s plan, 6-16 and 30-44 Cotham Hill will be closed to traffic to allow vendors to accommodate outdoor seating for their customers, after being closed for months due to Covid-19. Members of the group say they welcome some form of pedestrianisation on the street, however the council has put ‘little thought’ into how it will work in practice and hasn’t considered the implications on other traders and residents living nearby. The main concerns of members of the group - as highlighted in a joint statement by the HPCHCG- are those of public safety, as a narrow lane, home to businesses, flats and student accommodation, is to become a drop off point for lorries. Some residents and business owners on the streets adjacent to Cotham Hill - Hampton Park and Hampton Lane - are worried they’ll have issues parking, that delivery lorries could block the main route out of their street, and that vehicles loading and unloading could make the area highly polluted. They’re also concerned that this is likely to see people congregating late at night and keeping people awake. Owners of Cotham Hill Fruit and Veg shop, as well as neighbouring café Rubicon Too, are worried the traffic ban will have a huge impact on their business as they are based on the corner of Hampton Park which meets Cotham Hill. This means they are likely to have lorries park outside of their shops to load and unload, as they sit in between the two stretches of road to be closed to traffic, meaning customers are less likely to want to sit outside and have a coffee. Ali Shams, the owner of the fruit and veg store, is also concerned the fumes from the lorries could affect his fresh produce which he sells outside of the shopfront. He said: “The ban is designed for a few businesses and not for the whole community. “Nobody’s going to sit out there because of the lorries and the fumes. “It will affect my business, and if I was a customer it would put me off.” Anand Shah, owner of Cotham Hill Pharmacy and Post Office, says that lots of people from across Bristol visit his pharmacy, which they’re unlikely to do if they can’t park nearby. “And where are post men going to park?” he said. Mr. Shah says he is concerned the council have rushed through the ban, and haven’t thought about the businesses on the street that will be operating as normal. “If [the council] is going to do this, then we need some kind of financial support as it will affect us. “I’m all for supporting local businesses but the council are only thinking short term.” And residents and traders on Cotham Hill say they weren’t properly consulted about the traffic ban. Dr. Penny Dobson, member of the HPCHCG, said: “On the 19th of March, Bristol City Council released a rushed and dangerous pedestrianisation plan to the public. “Despite assurances that they would be consulted, local residents’ requests for meetings were pushed off or cancelled at the last minute. “The Hampton Park and Cotham Hill Community Group finally received what they believed was a draft proposal on the evening of the 18th of March, only to discover days later that this was a fait accompli.” But Bristol City Council said: “We have been in close contact with traders for many months after they approached us last year requesting a road closure to enable them to trade outside. “Between 9 November and 17 January Bristol City Council conducted an early engagement survey on how to improve walking, cycling and the street environment for Cotham Hill. “This community survey was available online and paper copies were also distributed to around 3300 local properties on and around Cotham Hill. Officers also met virtually with local businesses and residential and community groups to hear feedback. “Letters have also be distributed to all businesses on Cotham Hill to update them on the upcoming temporary closure, and emails have been sent to key resident and community groups. Letters will also soon be with residents.” But Mr. Shah said he ‘wasn’t told’ and found out via social media. “I think the way it’s been handled is a bit unfair,” he said. And it’s not just traders who are against the ban. Cotham Hill resident Dean Barnes says it is a “terrible idea.” Mr. Barnes says he thinks a one-way system on Cotham Hill would work well, but not a complete traffic ban. “Make it one way and slow it all down by putting in planting areas. It’s dangerous to have a build up of lorries that can’t drive through - one knocked my scaffolding off the other day.” It’s something that will cause more noise pollution in an already student dense area. “People will congregate” he said, “and it will cause chaos.” Among a list of concerns are that the traffic ban will pose a risk to public safety. As part of the plan, Hampton Lane will become one of the nearest available zones for vehicles to load and unload. Traders say people will struggle to drive down the lane if it’s heavily built up, which traders say it inevitably will be, meaning they will be late for work and so will their deliveries. Another business owner on Hampton Lane says there’s likely to be more accidents with students walking out onto a road full of vehicles making their way down a narrow lane. There aren’t just businesses which trade out of Hampton Lane but also long term residents as well as students living in rented accommodation. Dudley Thomas accesses his garage via Hampton Lane, and says this will be very difficult for him if there is a build-up of traffic. “Brewery lorries often park here and sometimes block the road,” he said. “And the lane is narrow all the way and swamped with bumps, meaning it’s not particularly safe for traffic. “Even pedestrians will struggle getting down here.” “There’s also the issue of pollution,” says Mr. Thomas. “There is already a very noticeable diesel smell in our garden, which is the fumes from the lorries which sometimes leave their engines on. “This is going to be an absolute nightmare.” In response to the objections, a Bristol City Council spokesperson said: “We have had hundreds of comments in support of pedestrianisation of Cotham Hill and we are pleased to provide an interim solution that will allow businesses to trade outdoors, giving them a much-needed boost after a very challenging year. “This temporary scheme has been designed to remove through traffic from the street and create a nicer street environment for everyone. We will continue to engage with the community to monitor the scheme’s impacts and design a more long-term solution for the road. “We encourage people to get out, enjoy the outdoor shared space and support the local economy - when COVID-19 restrictions allow.” The council says it will monitor the temporary ban before designing a long-term scheme. “The road closure is a temporary arrangement to provide urgent support to businesses by allowing them to trade outdoors. “The council will monitor its impacts to help design a similar, more robust long-term scheme that takes a holistic view of the neighbourhood. “This will include monitoring traffic levels and flows on surrounding roads, including Hampton Park and Hampton Lane, to determine whether changes are needed elsewhere to make the road closure work." **More stories from Bristol:** **[Bristol finally has more lockdown loos as new toilet block installed at harbourside](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-finally-more-lockdown-loos-5259135)** Article continues below **[Driver attempts 30-mile journey with 'shed' perched on car roof](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/driver-attempts-30-mile-journey-5259915)**
