Grubb**](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/authors/sophie-grubb/) Content Editor 05:00, 22 Apr 2021 ![Image 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4654943.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_st-marks-road.jpg) View 4 Images St Marks Road in Easton is a central point of the community(Image: Bristol Live) A vibrant Bristol road recently crowned the best street in the UK will not be closed off to traffic. ‌ The proposal to pedestrianise St Marks Road in [Easton](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/easton) prompted controversy last year, with long-established businesses like Bristol Sweet Mart [fearing they would lose trade and have to close.](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/shopping/two-much-loved-shops-would-4437056) ‌ A petition was launched to oppose the idea but another group of campaigners came up with a counter-petition, stressing the need to stop cars from cluttering the narrow high street. Article continues below [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) then launched a survey generally asking what people liked and did not like about St Marks Road, and how it could be made better. [Map shows where in Bristol snow is forecast as 'arctic blast' hits this week](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/where-will-snow-fall-bristol-10650459?int_source=nba) [Huge fly-tip dumped under a mile away from council tip](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/gallery/huge-fly-tip-dumped-under-10650882?int_source=nba) It has now shared the community's feedback and has confirmed that the pedestrianisation idea, which had been suggested for the stretch between Henrietta Street and Berwick Road, has been shelved. An update shared on the council's consultation site confirms: "Pedestrianisation is not being considered. ‌ "The [alternative] options will be presented to a local community working group who will help co-design the options." Easton businessman Abdul Malik welcomed the decision, but said it came after "months and months of anxiety" for traders. The Pak Butchers founder said: "We had been quietly optimistic but we were very relieved when it came back. Article continues below "It's opened a huge can of worms about where we go from here, what they are going to do and if money [for improvements] is still going to be available. "We really want to enhance the road, it's the greatest street in the country and it needs to be put on the map." St Marks Road, which is lined with shops, restaurants and community facilities, was [named the best in the UK at the 2020 Urbanism Awards](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/st-marks-road-urbanism-award-3589658). ‌ It is home to the Easton Jamia Masjid and also hosts the annual Grand Iftar street party, uniting thousands of people to mark the end of Ramadan. ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4901861.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_JMP_SWA_170121_St_Marks_Road__011_JPG.jpg) View 4 Images Abdul Malik, right, and Thomas Dowdeswell are opposed to pedestrianisation of St Marks Road. Behind them, the shuttered kiosk set up in the hope of helping the community engage with a consultation on the plans(Image: John Myers) #### 'I don't think we would have survived' Abdul revealed that he was already arranging a survey with a view to selling his shop or lease if the plan had progressed, adding: "I don't think we would have survived in a pedestrianised street." ‌ While some people argued pedestrianisation improves footfall, traders had concerns about the impact on deliveries as well as deterring customers who travel from further afield to shop there. Sweet Mart in particular attracts people from all over the city and beyond, for its unique offer as the biggest supplier of ethnic foods and spices in the South West. The controversial proposal to close St Marks Road at one end and make it access-only came after the government made funding available to councils, specifically to improve active travel like walking and cycling. ‌ Bristol council issued a list of 12 streets being considered, and some of those proposals have already been implemented - Cotham Hill, for example, [has been closed to traffic since April 12](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/food-drink/bristol-restaurant-owners-say-cotham-5223523). **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** Adbul said that while pedestrianisation might work in other parts of the city, the approach must not be 'one size fits all', adding: "Knee jerk policies have the potential to damage communities. "You lose a couple of businesses in St Marks Road and it will all change, for the worse." He said as someone who cycles he is also keen to see improvements and work on "realistic" solutions with other representatives from the community. A working group is being arranged to help co-design alternative options with the council and come up with collaborative suggestions to benefit everyone. ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4901862.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_JMP_SWA_170121_St_Marks_Road__006_JPG.jpg) View 4 Images Bristol Sweet Mart on St Marks Road(Image: John Myers) Easton resident Rob Bryher, who co-founded the Love St Marks Road group to campaign for a lower-traffic street, said the creation of a "cohesive group" was a positive step. He said: "We didn't think they would pedestrianise the whole space and that's not what we were calling for - we were calling for timed closures for access at certain times. "It's not clear to me [from the council's statement] if that is off the table, but I agree with the traders that it's important we have a proper conversation. "We don't want conflict, we want to get into the room with other people and discuss it. There are lots of different options." ![Image 10](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article4443675.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_ML_BRI200820pedestrian-001JPGjp.jpg) View 4 Images Rob Bryher on St Marks Road in Easton(Image: Michael Lloyd Photography) #### 120 in support, 257 against The council received more than 1,115 responses to its survey about St Marks Road, having circulated more than 3,500 paper copies in different languages as well as online. About one half of respondents agreed that the street is busy with traffic, with more than 50 per cent saying they would highly prioritise measures to create cleaner air and make walking and cycling there a nicer and safer experience. More than 500 people commented specifically about the potential for pedestrianisation. Article continues below The council said of those, 120 expressed support but a further 257 objected, with the remainder making alternative suggestions such as partial closures. Local elections: Candidates clash over getting people to ditch cars Bristol Live hosted the transport and environment debate on Facebook Live ------------------------------------------------------------------------- 11:42, 23 Apr 2021 Seven local election candidates have clashed over how to get people out of cars and onto public transport, cycling and walking – and whether they even should. ‌ The [transport](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/transport)and [environment](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/environment)debate, hosted by [Bristol Live’s Facebook page](https://www.facebook.com/bristol.live), included [Labour’s](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/labour-party)Kye Dudd, who is running to be reelected city councillor for Central ward and is cabinet member for transport, energy and New Green Deal, Ed Plowden, [Green](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/green-party)candidate for Windmill Hill, and Mark Weston, [Conservative](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/conservative-party)group leader who is standing to be re-elected for [Henbury](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/henbury)& Brentry. ‌ Also taking part were [West of England metro mayoral](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/metro-mayor)[Lib Dem](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/liberal-democrats) hopeful [Stephen Williams](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/local-elections-who-stephen-williams-5325974) and three candidates for [mayor of Bristol](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-mayor) – [Tom Baldwin](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-mayoral-election-candidate-tom-5308657) from the Trade Unionist and Socialist Coalition, Reform UK’s [Robert Clarke](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-mayor-election-candidate-robert-5321243) and independent [John Langley](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-mayor-election-john-langley-5308389). Article continues below With voters going to the polls on Thursday, May 6, here’s what was said at the hustings on Wednesday, April 21. **Q: What is the biggest issue facing Bristol around transport and the environment and how would you address it?** Kye Dudd said: “Our policy has been prioritising public transport and active travel and we intend to carry on doing that. ‌ We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) “We’ve brought together a policy called the Bus Deal where we invest large amounts of money in the highways system into the city creating bus priority and more bus lanes at junctions, and in return, bus companies have promised to double the frequency of services. “Bristol needs a mass transit system that can transport thousands of people per hour.” Article continues below He said the intention was to make permanent the temporary cycle lanes installed in the city centre during lockdown. Stephen Williams said Bristol and the region suffered the “worst public transport system” in the country and had “stood still for two decades” while other areas had much better suburban rail and bus networks. “Hardly anything new has happened apart from [metrobus](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/metrobus)which runs along three routes, so we need a transport revolution in the region,” he said. ‌ “I want to take up the power of bus franchising, so we can say to any operator these are our terms and conditions if you want to operate in a highly profitable part of the country. “I will work with Network Rail to reopen railway stations around Bristol which have been talked about for a long time.” Mark Weston said: “There is no single solution to Bristol or the West of England's transport woes. ‌ “When we talk about a mass transit system we are not talking about a single delivery matter, we’re certainly not going to have any underground, the price tag for that means it’s never going to happen. “It needs to be multi-modal so people can access different forms of transport to different places. Rail has a lot of potential but only in certain areas. “We need to look at how rail connects to buses and how that connects to cycling so you have a seamless flow across public transport.” ‌ Robert Clarke said: “A lot of working-class people depend on their vehicles for work, not luxury. “A lot of people are going into corporate offices in luxury cars and there should be some penalisation for them but not for normal working-class people moving around the city in their vehicles doing all kinds of work Brisolians need. “The buses are a rip-off and should be subsidised far more. “There is a lot of virtue signalling but if it’s not practical, it’s not going to work. Do people really want to walk 365 days a year a couple of miles to work in the rain or cycle around Bristol’s hills?” Tom Baldwin said: “Our transport policy centres around public transport that is owned by the public, that is run for a service not a profit. “We would ensure the money comes back to the city and not to the shareholder, that we can democratically suggest routes, make it cheap and affordable and give people an alternative to driving that is viable rather than a congestion charge which will be a regressive tax. “There has to be an alternative to get people out of cars. “There is an existing rail network in Bristol and a lot more use can be made of it.” **Q: What would you do to tackle the city’s air quality crisis?** Ed Plowden said: “We have a massive air quality problem with 300 deaths a year and the Green Party absolutely supports a charging zone for dirty vehicles that come into the city centre. “We will introduce a workplace parking levy and put that into cheaper bus fares particularly for young people. “We will take control of bus services through franchising or partnership working so all investment goes back into Bristol.” John Langley said: “What does concern me is motorists being penalised for having a vehicle because they are soft targets. “Cycle lanes are the biggest waste of space. “There is one next to me built at huge expense and it’s used by about six people a day. “If you’re going to ban cars eventually, which is probably the idea, it’s a complete waste building cycle lanes.” **Q: What are your plans for transport and air quality in Bristol?** Kye Dudd said: “There are two separate issues here – the [Clean Air Zone](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/clean-air-zone) (CAZ) is a public health intervention, removing dirty vehicles where air quality is illegal; and a CO2 problem which is very damaging to the climate. “The biggest source of CO2 in the city is the need and demand for heat, and to transform the city’s energy system needs £4billion.” He said to meet climate targets meant decarbonising all vehicles and reducing traffic by 40 per cent. “The only way you do that is to introduce policies like better, cheaper, cleaner public transport, more cycling and walking, and freight consolidation centres, so it’s a multi-pronged approach.” Stephen Williams said: “I support CAZs in Bristol and Bath as a short-term measure but it is not a long-term solution because it is a daily cordon charge around the city centre, so as a tool it’s pretty blunt. “We need to move to road user pricing where every vehicle movement is charged according to what time of day it is, what road it is, what vehicle it is. That is how you will fine tune people’s behaviour. “I also want to speed up the transition of buses from diesel. The vast amount of buses in our region are still diesel and First does not intend changing them all over until 2035 which is far too late. “One advantage of bus franchising is to set quality standards for vehicles and put some capital on the table to get that transition from diesel to electric and hydrogen.” **Q: How would you make construction more environmentally friendly?** Ed Plowden said: “We will accelerate the City Leap programme, build more wind turbines in [Avonmouth](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/avonmouth), but it’s also about retrofitting homes. “So we would use an 80p weekly increase in council rents to retrofit all council housing which would pay back dividends massively more in people’s savings on fuel than the actual rent increase. “When we talk about electric cars we cannot produce enough electricity to move all these vehicles around, so we need a total change to our modes of transport to get us away from our dangerous addiction to cars.” John Langley said: “I would be very keen to see all the council housing stock fitted with solar panels.” Stephen Williams said: “As minister for housing and communities in the coalition government I introduced the Infrastructure Act 2015 which has a zero-carbon standard for new homes and obliges house builders to pay into funds to retrofit older homes. “That legislation was suspended by the Conservative government. The law is still there and could be used. “Regional mayors can ask central government for more devolved powers, so I would ask for that for the West of England, which would be very hard to resist given I was the author of the legislation. “If that power is devolved to the region we could have highest standards for new builds but also funds to retrofit older houses.” Kye Dudd said: “The energy service in the council has led on massive investment in projects including Redcliffe and Old Market district heating systems. “We are about to invest £7million into the biggest water-source heat pump in the country which will go into Castle Park, take water from Bristol harbour and transform it to heat thousands of homes across the city. “The problem is the gap between what we are doing and what needs to be done to deliver carbon neutrality. We are talking about £4billion. “We need to be on a wartime footing to transform the energy and transport systems.” Tom Baldwin said: “We have not just an environmental crisis but we will be going into a jobs crisis, and we have had a developing housing crisis. “You can address them through a programme of public works of employing people in insulating homes, conversion to clean energy production and the mass programme of building council housing by directly employed labour which means we get to set the quality standards rather than having to beg developers. “But we need the funding to do that. We have seen with the billions they have thrown correctly at dealing with coronavirus that the money is there to deal with a crisis. “We need a mayor to mobilise people to take on the government.” Robert Clarke said: “You might say you’re going to make sure people won’t drive their vehicles but that will be working-class people pushed to the side. “Motor vehicles are one of the biggest single liberating forces for working-class people. “You cannot force this stuff down people’s open mouths. People say to me they’re being forced out of vehicles and out of the centre of the city. “You are pushing all these vehicles out to other neighbourhoods where there is a larger population who are sucking up all this pollution.” **Q: What would you do to enhance the city's urban environment?** Mark Weston said: “We need to toughen sanctions when it comes to cutting trees down. “When it comes to tree preservation orders, the fine the person receives is not commensurate with the costs of replacing that beautiful tree. “It’s a slap on the wrist, but to a developer that is nothing, it’s the margin of building another house there. “We need to be planting semi-mature trees to get the benefit quicker. I’m a big supporter of the Forest of Avon, so let’s see if we can expand the tree cover.” Stephen Williams said: “Bristol City Council has been poor at enforcement of developers, whether it’s cutting down trees or sticking to the terms of planning permissions. “On trees, one of the major responsibilities with the next regional mayor will be to put together a land use plan for the region. “My manifesto has some principles for that plan, including that all new housing developments must come with a mix of native trees to support biodiversity. “I want green corridors connecting the two cities that are attractive and safe routes for people to walk from inner-city Bristol out into the countryside.” Ed Plowden said: “The Green Party will double the amount of tree cover in Bristol by 2040. “I like the idea of green corridors but I would make them dual use to cycle and walk into the centre for their commuting journeys as well as using them to get out to access the countryside. “We shouldn't just conceptualise cycling and walking as leisure activities but fundamental to our future transport system, particularly using e-bikes which have shown to be a massive opportunity.” John Langley said: “No one has mentioned the bee population. “We have so many rooftops in Bristol that can be used for bees and that is something we can just get on with.” **Closing comments** Kye Dudd said: “Our key priority is making public transport more reliable, efficient and clean. “We need to promote active travel, so we will provide liveable neighbourhoods, making streets safer. “On climate emergency we are committed to delivering investment into the city that is required. “We have set up a City Leap process to attract at least £1billion to decarbonise the city’s energy system.” Ed Plowden said: “The Green Party has a fully costed plan to revitalise our public transport, walking and cycling networks to rebalance our city away from its dangerous addiction to carbon and motor cars. “We need to think about the planning system to prevent the need to travel, so we believe in 15-minute neighbourhoods where you can access all your needs within a 15-minute round walk. “We want to reallocate all the money Weca is putting into new roads into using the roads we have got better to transport many more people by bus, cycling and walking. “We want to make sure the damage car drivers do to our city that they pay a fair share.” Tom Baldwin said: “My policy centres on public ownership, whether that is in housing and development, public transport or energy. “We need these things to be run for what are democratically decided needs for the city and not for private profit. “It is people with older cars who will fall foul of the charging. “People will be fighting for their jobs and incomes and we need a mayor who gives a voice to the working class and not the private developers, private bus firms and big business.” Stephen Williams said: “Sorting out our transport system is my number one priority. “If I take office I will immediately tell officers to stop work on new roads like the South Bristol Ring Road and instead put together a plan to franchise our buses so we take control of our bus network.” Robert Clarke said: “We need less pollution, we don’t want to penalise the people or force them to give up their cars. “There should be a referendum in Bristol on all the efforts to reduce pollution.” John Langley said: “Car drivers should not be over-penalised. “In terms of reducing pollution from commercial traffic it makes sense to introduce measures so deliveries are made from 8am to 8pm which would reduce a lot of traffic around the city centre. “In terms of bus travel, we should think about introducing free travel at weekends to get people into the city centre and spending their money to enable the economy.” Mark Weston said: “Bus franchising sounds good but you only have to look at what Bristol City Council has done with Bristol Energy to see the pitfalls of council ownership. “The solution with transport is about partnership – partnership with neighbouring authorities, between different modes of transport like bus and rail so we can ring the city with park and rides, and partnership with the public. Article continues below “We need to take them with us and show them a transport solution so they will want to stop using their cars. “We need to accept different areas of the city require different solutions and have different environments.” **Find out about the West of England Metro Mayor candidates: read profiles for Labour candidate [Dan Norris](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/local-elections-who-dan-norris-5325963), Green Party candidate [Jerome Thomas](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/local-elections-who-jerome-thomas-5325972), Conservative [Samuel Wiliams](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/local-elections-who-samuel-williams-5325901), and Liberal Democrat [Stephen Williams](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/local-elections-who-stephen-williams-5325974).**

Council to ban cars from streets outside two Bristol schools during peak times Any motorists caught ignoring the ban could be issued with a fine ----------------------------------------------------------------- 17:54, 05 May 2021 Updated 10:16, 06 May 2021 Traffic will be banned from streets outside two Bristol primary [schools](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/education)for two hours each weekday. ‌ Victoria Park Primary School in [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster) and Redfield Educate Together Primary Academy in [Redfield](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/whats-on-news/changing-face-church-road-how-4588632)will be next to try the School Streets scheme, after two other schools in the city trialled it last year. ‌ The national initiative is designed to reduce road danger and air pollution, prohibiting motorists from certain roads at peak drop-off and pick-up times, with only pedestrians and cyclists allowed through. ‌ [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) has announced that the changes will be in force from Wednesday, May 26 affecting the following roads: * Victoria Avenue, Redfield * Raymend Road, Bedminster * Atlas Road, Bedminster The above roads will be closed to vehicles during term time weekdays, between the hours of 8.15am-9.15am and 3pm-4pm. ‌ The direction of the one-way system on Raymend Road, between St John’s Lane and Stanbury Road, will be reversed to allow residents within the zone to exit (but not enter) their streets during those times. Signs and barriers will be put up to make the closures clear and any drivers caught breaking the rules face a fine. ‌ The expansion of the pilot scheme follows the ongoing[trial commenced by two schools last year](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/cars-banned-outside-two-bristol-3815045) - Wansdyke Primary School in [Hartcliffe](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/hartcliffe) and St Peter's C of E Primary School in [Bishopsworth](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bishopsworth). Theirs began in February 2020 for 18 months, but the council has not yet said how long this next phase of the trial will last for. ‌ If seen to be a success, the temporary measures could become permanent and more schools could follow in introducing traffic-free zones. In a letter to parents in March, Victoria Park's headteacher Nic Bailey said the school was among 40 to initially express interest in the scheme. #### 'Congestion and poor air quality' He wrote: "Our school, like many others in Bristol, suffers from congestion, road safety issues and poor air quality immediately outside the school gates. ‌ "School Streets has the potential to transform the roads directly adjacent to our school, making them safer for pupils and a more pleasant environment for residents and the wider school community." He said a 'park and stride point' would be identified at a car park near the school, offering a safe space from which parents and pupils can walk the final part of their journey if they have to drive in part. ‌ Residents living within the closures will be allowed to leave their road during the restricted times, for example to go out to work in the morning, but they will not be allowed access back into the street during the prohibited times. Exceptions will be made in some cases where access is necessary, the council said, as well as for emergency vehicles. Clare Reddington, chief executive of Watershed, tweeted in support of traffic calming measures but raised concerns about residents not being allowed to drive to their own homes during the restricted hours. ‌ * **_What are your thoughts on the closure? Email sophie.grubb@reachplc.com or let us know in the comments below_** She tweeted on Monday (May 3): "We hardly use our car and am pro clean air zones and limiting parent traffic BUT our road (unlike others) won’t get residents permits. "And no one has been asked about access requirements. So @BristolCouncil appears to be completely ableist in their planning." ‌ In response, the council said anyone who makes them aware of a "reasonable, valid reason for exemption" will be considered for access, for example Blue Badge holders. **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** Adam Crowther, head of city transport at Bristol City Council, said: "We are pleased to continue expanding Bristol School Streets with the two new schools in the pilot project, which is creating a safer and healthier environment for children outside of school gates. Article continues below "With public transport capacity still limited, it has never been more important for us to do all we can to encourage people to walk, cycle or scoot for short journeys wherever possible. "We hope that these new additions to the project will continue to deliver benefits to local people as we also look to roll it out to other schools in the city."

removed](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5442158.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/1_fe74dd1a-6826-4086-8cc8-003c19fa16bc.jpg) View 4 Images The Berkeley Road planter before it was removed An unauthorised planter in a Bishopston road was vandalised after dividing opinion — but the residents behind the feature hope to win over the neighbourhood. ‌ With its well-tended front yards and trees lining the street, Berkeley Road is in some ways a picture of urban serenity. Some residents, though, have concerns over its use as a rat run and antisocial pavement parking. ‌ A five-strong neighbourhood group, formed to address traffic problems, came up with an idea to deal with those issues and help "make the space owned by the community". Article continues below During the early May Bank Holiday, they planted some tall grasses in a wooden crate and placed it in the road, just next to the pavement. They put a second, smaller planter on the pavement on the other side of the road. [Map shows where in Bristol snow is forecast as 'arctic blast' hits this week](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/where-will-snow-fall-bristol-10650459?int_source=nba) [Huge fly-tip dumped under a mile away from council tip](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/gallery/huge-fly-tip-dumped-under-10650882?int_source=nba) The group did not expect the reaction which followed. A post about the planters, on social media platform Nextdoor, prompted more than 450 comments. Many were passionately supportive of the idea, but there was also some strong opposition. The first post read: "Seems like quite a selfish thing to do to me (and almost certainly not approved by the council), although of course I don't know what's happened in the past to cause them to take this action." ‌ Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice) [Join us on WhatsApp](https://chat.whatsapp.com/JwmceTjpWjYACrvdGPRfyJ) One reply said: "Sometimes you have to do something a little radical to help people to think of the local people... I take my hat off to these wonderful creative people and will be doing the same on my dropped curb." The scheme was called a "brilliant way to prevent antisocial pavement parking" in one comment, while another said: "Great idea! Why should motorists be allowed to park and not flowers?" Article continues below One local wrote: "These are illegal. The road and the pavement belong to and are managed by the council. You can’t just put things there. "If the residents are having issues with cars parking too close to their legally dropped kerb, then they should take photos and take it to the council." In a statement, Bristol City Council said it wants to deliver more liveable neighbourhoods, but in this case the planters will "need to be removed to allow for the correct processes to be followed.” ‌ But an unknown person, apparently not in favour of the idea, had already taken it upon themselves to remove the planter from the road, days after some of its slats were kicked in. The second planter remains on the pavement at the time of writing. ![Image 8: The remaining, smaller planter on Berkeley Road](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5442160.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_e39a2a48-c353-4f57-933b-1c7215014ba4.jpg) View 4 Images The remaining, smaller planter on Berkeley Road We visited the street this week and spoke to one of the members of the group behind the planters. Dr Philip Tattsbridge talked about why they were put in place, the community's mixed reaction, and his hopes to convince more people of their benefits. ‌ The 60-year-old psychiatrist, who has lived on the road for 20 years, outlined the group's vision for the street while he waxed some drawers for his kitchen cabinet. He said: "One of the concerns we have got is people parking on the pavement, and how that affects people who are walking down the street — particularly people who have disabilities. "It’s part of a broader issue of a sense of entitlement by some car owners, that the road is for them and not the people who live there." ‌ He added: "There are a lot of people who work on Gloucester Road who park up here." Showing us a picture of Berkeley Road on a Bank Holiday, almost free of cars, he said: "It’s shocking how empty it is there, compared to how it is now." The planter in the road was "not an anti-parking device", he says. The group had actually hoped the planter would protect parked cars from having their wing mirrors clipped. ![Image 9: The Berkeley Road planter when it was put in place on the early May Bank Holiday](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5442193.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Bank-H.jpg) View 4 Images The Berkeley Road planter when it was put in place on the early May Bank Holiday But Dr Tattsbridge would like to see more drivers — if they are able — "displaced" onto their bikes, public transport, scooters, their feet, and "larger through roads". "The underlying aim is to reclaim the street we live on for those who live on it, and to require those who are passing through our street to do so at 20mph," Dr Tattsbridge added. The group hope to introduce planters at a few points along the street, with a potential "chicane layout". They believe this would reduce speeding on Berkeley Road and make it less likely to be used as a rat run or filled with parked cars. They had also hoped the "trial" of the planters would simply make the street nicer to look at. "We bought what we thought was quite an attractive-looking crate from a greengrocers," Dr Tattsbridge said. "We planted some miscanthus and put it out. Then we were surprised to hear, after however many hours, it was exciting a lot of comments on a social media site. That kind of spiralled. "One person was of the opinion it was ugly and illegal and selfish. I think it had a reasonable balance of opinion, but there were some very strong-minded views from a small number of individuals expressing themselves in a very intemperate way – which is the story of social media, isn’t it?" Within a few days, some of the slats of the planter in the road had been kicked in. It had also been moved onto the pavement. Dr Tattsbridge described this as "an initial move of opposition". The group aimed for a compromise by putting the planter partially back onto the road, partially still on the pavement. ![Image 10: The "compromise" position of the planter after it was vandalised](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5442151.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_Partially-on.jpg) View 4 Images The "compromise" position of the planter after it was vandalised But this did not seem to allay the concerns of the disgruntled opponent. When Dr Tattsbridge looked at the spot on Monday, the planter was gone entirely, taken to an unknown location. The psychiatrist said the traffic issues group want to work with the neighbourhood, adding: "We have no objection to people driving. We're not saying we want to fully pedestrianise the street. "The chicane layout would be an ultimate objective. The planters could be at sections of the road where the problems of pavement parking and speeding traffic are most acute. "We are just outside the proposed [Clean Air Zone](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/clean-air-zone). There is a concern in the road that there will be a displacement of traffic, which will increase the amount of parking. **Get the biggest stories from across Bristol [straight to your inbox](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/newsletter-preference-centre/).** "This is about trying to make the space owned by the community, and a safe space. It should be for the residents." The group — who use a speed gun a few times a month to monitor traffic — also plans to get permission to close Berkeley Road to traffic on a few occasions each year, so street parties can be held. Dr Tattsbridge does not claim the five members of the group speak for the street as a whole, adding: "It’s our goal to get as much support as we can." He said getting council permission for planters along Berkeley Road is something the group are "actively considering". A council spokesman said: “Planters can be an effective and attractive traffic calming measure but their use does need to be carefully considered to ensure they are appropriate for the area, safe, and do not obstruct or damage the highway or footpaths. **_What is happening where you live? Thornbury High Street is set to become permanent - with one important change. ‌ The local authority’s [Conservative](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/conservative-party) administration is due to rubber-stamp a report locking in the changes from last summer on Monday (June 7). ‌ But it is adding drop-off and pick-up points for shoppers after they and traders complained they were cut off from the shops. Article continues below [South Gloucestershire Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/south-gloucestershire-council) used an emergency order to close the High Street to traffic in June last year to help people comply with social distancing. [Map shows where in Bristol snow is forecast as 'arctic blast' hits this week](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/where-will-snow-fall-bristol-10650459?int_source=nba) [Huge fly-tip dumped under a mile away from council tip](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/gallery/huge-fly-tip-dumped-under-10650882?int_source=nba) The following month it added a one-way system for delivery drivers and residential access, as well as a 20mph speed limit, under a new order allowing it to make experimental changes while holding a public consultation. But it was clear well before the six-month consultation closed in February that the scheme was unpopular with many residents and businesses. ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) More than 1,800 people signed a petition against the closure, and traders in [Thornbury](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/thornbury) said making the pedestrianisation permanent would [decimate trade](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/traffic-free-thornbury-high-street-4789889). **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** A year after the changes were first brought in, the High Street remains closed to through-traffic between The Close and Castle Court, with vehicles diverted via Midland Lane, Rock Street, Quaker Lane and on to The Plain. Article continues below As well as the one-way system and 20mph limit, the council has made other changes to address various concerns - including adding six disabled parking bays, kerb ramps, new cycle parking, and new seating - but these have not been enough to win over the majority in favour of the scheme. Of the nearly 2,900 who responded to the consultation survey, 65 per cent disagreed with making the pedestrian and cycle zone permanent, and 49 per cent disagreed with the one-way system completely. Just under a third of respondents agreed with the current one-way system, and nearly 60 per cent thought that buses should be allowed through it. ‌ A full 80 per cent of respondents wanted the 20mph speed limit made permanent, and many people wanted to see improved access for parking. The results are set out in a report due to be discussed by cabinet members, who will be asked to approve a permanent ban on through-traffic in the High Street, a one-way system for delivery vehicles, and pick-up and drop-off points for customers. “The preferred option seeks to balance the split view of the community,” the report says. ‌ “It would create space for motorised vehicle access to the High Street where that access is supporting the economic [sic] of a thriving High Street, through open access for deliveries, improved loading and unloading provisions, drop off and pick up points and access for residents. “However, motorised through traffic would remain prohibited. “A review of disabled parking will ensure that parking options are maximised.” ‌ ![Image 8: Future Thornbury High Street concept image](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5492126.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Future-Thornbury-High-Street-concept-image.jpg) View 2 Images How Thornbury High Street could look in future(Image: South Gloucestershire Council) The report also recommends a set of interim changes while the vision for the future of the High Street is fully developed, including measures to slow traffic on the High Street. If cabinet members agree to all the recommendations, the following interim changes will be introduced this month: * create a clear vehicle lane using textured paint (through traffic is still banned) * extend the temporary ramps on the kerbs * create clear and well signed parallel loading and unloading bays and drop off and pick up points * install extra street furniture, such as benches and adapted cycle parking * remove some planters, secure those that are left, and make sure the planting fits in with Thornbury In Bloom displays * review entrance and exits to slow traffic on the High Street * review signage to ensure appropriate access from Bristol Road and Midland Way roundabout. Councillor Steve Reade, cabinet member for regeneration, environment and strategic infrastructure, said: “The future High Street vision supports the regeneration of the town centre and puts the High Street at the heart of a thriving community supporting the town’s recovery from the pandemic. We all want to see a space that meets the needs of all residents and visitors both in safety, access and experience. “Thank you to the many residents, businesses and groups that gave us their feedback. As a result, vehicles will still be able to access to the High Street in one direction, but only in support of the businesses there. This future vision will embrace and encourage active travel, through safe cycling and walking routes to the High Street, enabling all to enjoy the reduction in traffic and noise when using the High Street. “Longer term, we want to make sure as a priority that the centre of Thornbury is accessible for those using public transport and we will review bus service provision to make sure those needs are met. “We also want to play our part in delivering a digitally enabled High Street, with fast and strong connectivity for businesses and visitors alike, maximising the opportunity for online retail through click and collect, making use of shared space for skills and training, and recognising the demand for more remote working with residents staying local and working from home.” ### Download the Bristol Live app See our best content via our dedicated smartphone apps and keep up to date on all our breaking news stories - including the latest on crime, business, travel and weather. It has been given another £60,000 to develop a permanent scheme and is expecting to get around £6million more from the West of England Combined Authority once the scheme is approved at the end of the year. Separately, the council is considering a traffic speed reduction scheme for the south end of the High Street, which is experiencing issues of inappropriate access especially by heavy goods vehicles, speeding traffic and parking. 12:50, 08 Jun 2021 Updated 15:50, 08 Jun 2021 There was a minor, 'polite' confrontation during a protest in Clifton Village this morning. Article continues below Around a hundred people marched in the area earlier today to[protest against pedestrianisation plans](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/clifton-protesters-against-pedestrianisation-block-5501515). ‌ Green Councillor Paula O'Rourke has confirmed a section of [Princess Victoria Street](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/clifton) in Clifton Village will close to general traffic in an 18-month experimental traffic order. She hopes the trial will be able to start in July. Article continues below More than 500 people have objected to [the pedestrianisation, which will stretch from The Quadrant to Miles Morgan Travel](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/shopping/popular-shopping-street-pedestrianised-hundreds-5500210) — and a protest took place today. He added: "Can I ask, very politely, would you mind asking these people if they could move out of their way so I can continue my job? "Thank you very much." ‌ The crowd then made room for the car to go past, but it briefly stopped as it was doing so. A woman then told the driver: “Stop messing about and go on.” ‌ Critics of the plans fear the impact on shoppers' access and deliveries to businesses, and congestion in the village. Send your videos to [video@trinitymirror.com](mailto:video@trinitymirror.com) Hundreds are expected to march today against pedestrianisation plans, according to protest organisers. Green Councillor Paula O'Rourke has confirmed a section of [Princess Victoria Street](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/clifton) in Clifton Village will close to general traffic in an 18-month experimental traffic order. She hopes the trial will be able to start in July. More than 500 people have objected to [the pedestrianisation, which will stretch from The Quadrant to Miles Morgan Travel](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/shopping/popular-shopping-street-pedestrianised-hundreds-5500210) — and a protest is scheduled for 11am today (June 8). We will have updates on the demonstration in this live blog. **Scroll down for the latest updates**. One of the organisers said people will block Princess Victoria Street from 11am "for as long as they want to stand and have a voice". He expects hundreds to join a march around the village. Critics of the plans fear the impact on shoppers' access and deliveries to businesses, and congestion in the village. They claim there has been a lack of consultation. **Get the biggest stories [straight to your inbox](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/newsletter-preference-centre/).** Ms O'Rourke insisted there was a full consultation including 2,000 letters to residents. A survey was live for six weeks in December and January. **You can read our [full report on the scheme here](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/shopping/popular-shopping-street-pedestrianised-hundreds-5500210). Cork**](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/authors/tristan-cork/) Chief Reporter 15:00, 06 Jul 2021 Updated 15:01, 06 Jul 2021 A nine-year-old boy is so concerned about going to school next to one of Bristol’s busiest road junctions that he has started a fundraising campaign to do something about it. Article continues below 138205441702 Jakub Kozlowski goes to Parson Street Primary School in Bedminster, which sits on the corner of the Parson Street gyratory - one of the key road interchanges in South Bristol. Article continues below He said he was inspired to act after reading about the case of another nine-year-old child, who also lived and went to school on a busy and very polluted main road. Article continues below 138205441837 **READ MORE:**[Clean Air Zone is delayed for another year](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristols-clean-air-zone-delayed-5601638) Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, who lived near the South Circular Road in Lewisham, south-east London, died in 2013, and recently a coroner [ruled that her death from asthma was directly related to the amount of pollution](https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/uk-news/breaking-pollution-recorded-cause-death-23176121) caused by drivers on the congested road near her home and school. So Jakob decided to act - despite being only nine, he’s running 2km every school day for two weeks to[raise money](https://www.justgiving.com/crowdfunding/jakub-kozlowski)for two things. [![Image 7: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Put your skills to the test. Whether you love word games, tricky cryptic crosswords, Sudoku, or our other brain teasers, you'll find a new favourite today! Play Now](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games/) The first is to buy banners for the school to put up outside on the busy junction, asking drivers to turn off their engines while they wait at the lights. And if there’s money left over, he said he would buy air purifiers for each classroom, so the children at his school can at least get cleaner air when they are trying to learn. “He was horrified to find out about Ella, the little girl from London who suffered from asthma and whose death was traced to air pollution,” said his dad Rob. Article continues below “He began to worry about his own health and that of his friends and fellow pupils since the playground in Parsons Street Primary School is only metres away from the busy crossroads that surround the school,” he added. Outside on Monday, Jakub watched as lorries, buses, vans and cars stopped at the lights right on the corner of his school. It’s the crossroads of Bedminster Road and Parson Street, better known to drivers and their sat navs as the A38 and the A4174. Article continues below The South Bristol Link Road, which opened in January 2017, was supposed to cut some of the traffic past his school, and it did for a while, but at any point in the rotation of the crossroads’ traffic light system, there is always a line of cars, lorries, vans and buses waiting a long time at a red light. ![Image 8: Jakub Kozlowski, 9, a pupil at Parson Street School in Bedminster](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5616290.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_TCR_BRI_060721JakubBRIjpeg.jpg) View 2 Images Jakub Kozlowski, 9, a pupil at Parson Street School in Bedminster(Image: Bristol Live) “I recently learned about the bad quality of the air around school,” Jakub told Bristol Live. “It is one of the most affected places in Bristol and I think more should be done about that. Article continues below “My friend has asthma but it affects all of us. It’s very frustrating and annoying when I see all the cars and lorries with their engines running. The air pollution just sits there and it’s not nice. The banners will just ask people to turn their engines off,” he added. School leaders are backing Jakub’s campaign - at Parson Street they have long complained about air quality and other issues from traffic congestion around the school. Recently, the school’s ‘Green Team’ held a silent protest outside the school highlighting the poor air quality, and in previous years, the school has campaigned in vain for a 20mph speed limit. Article continues below Ironically, it seems the school’s location on a busy junction is both the cause for the air pollution problems and also the main reason why little or nothing has been done. ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5616383.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_TCR_BRI_060721ParsonStreetBRIJPG.jpg) View 2 Images Pupils and staff at Parson Street School prepare for their 'silent protest' against traffic and air pollution outside(Image: Parson Street School) Bristol City Council introduced a pilot scheme creating ‘anti-idling’ zones outside schools in 2019, pledging then to expand that across the city, but it hasn’t reached Parson Street yet. Article continues below In February 2020, the council[launched a pilot scheme to create ‘School Streets’](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/18-month-ban-cars-outside-3879806) at four locations around the city. The ‘School Streets’ initiative effectively discourages through traffic by turning the roads into pedestrian and cyclist priority zones directly before and after the school day. When they were launched, the council said the scheme was in response to the Mayor of Bristol’s Clean Air Day speech in 2020, which set out the council’s commitment to encourage more active travel and achieve cleaner air. Article continues below **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** “School Streets has the potential to transform the school run for children and their families, creating a safer space for more pupils to enjoy a less stressful, healthier journey by walking, cycling or scooting,” said the Mayor Marvin Rees at the time of the launch. “We have already received encouraging feedback from schools, parents and pupils, and will continue to involve local residents and the wider community in developing this scheme. Article continues below “Removing cars and other motorists from the immediate area outside of schools is also a step in the right direction for addressing the wider issues of congestion and poor air quality outside of the school gates,” he added. However, because Parson Street is located at the junction of two busy A-roads, the School Streets initiative cannot be implemented there. Article continues below There is an air quality monitor at Parson Street school, which feeds in data on nitrogen dioxide and other harmful particulates. In 2018, it was the fourth worst school site in Bristol, and by the start of 2020 was showing NO2 levels higher than legal limits on a twice-daily basis. Publicly available data from the monitoring station at the school showed a familiar pattern, with nitrogen dioxide levels reaching a peak around 9-10am, with a second peak around 5pm-6pm, and during weekdays those two peaks were regularly over legal limits. * You can [find out more about Jakub's fundraising activities here.](https://www.justgiving.com/crowdfunding/jakub-kozlowski) Article continues below ****Want our best stories with fewer ads and alerts when the biggest news stories drop? 11:51, 07 Jul 2021 ![Image 7: Bristol Bridge closed to general traffic](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5620120.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_Bristol-Bridge.png) View Image Bristol Bridge The closure of Bristol Bridge and some nearby routes to general traffic will be made permanent. Article continues below 138205439166 Bristol City Council's experimental traffic order — announced in August last year as an 18-month trial — will become permanent on Saturday, July 17. Article continues below The order restricts general traffic on: Article continues below 138205441690 * Bristol Bridge * Baldwin Street, between St Augustine’s Parade and Marsh Street * Baldwin Street to High Street * Union Street's left turn onto Rupert Street **READ NEXT**: [City centre unit still empty a year after getting alcohol licence](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/food-drink/city-centre-unit-still-empty-5618012) Buses, solo motorcycles, taxis and cycles are given priority under the order. Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. You can check out at any time. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice) [Join us on WhatsApp](https://chat.whatsapp.com/JwmceTjpWjYACrvdGPRfyJ) Making the announcement during a press briefing this morning (July 7), Bristol Mayor Marvin Rees said: "This intervention was one of the activities we have taken to intervene in the way traffic flows around the city to improve our air quality. "It has proven successful. "It is also part of the commitment we have made to delivering rapid bus routes around the city, which is contributing to the business case for the mass transit system that we are doing the work on." Article continues below Describing the move as a very positive intervention for the city, the Mayor said air quality had improved on Victoria Street on almost all monthly readings since the scheme was introduced. In the weeks after the trial came into force, 3,574 people signed a [petition](https://www.change.org/p/the-mayor-of-bristol-marvin-rees-reverse-the-decision-to-close-bristol-bridge-baldwin-st-access-to-the-city-centre) calling for the scheme to be reversed, citing the impact on local businesses. This triggered a [counter-petition](https://www.change.org/p/b-keep-bristol-bridge-closed-to-car-traffic-and-support-a-car-free-healthy-city-centre) signed by 1,425 supporters of a "car-free healthy city centre". Hamid Parast, who owned Centre Cafe Lounge on Baldwin Street, claimed the scheme caused difficulties for deliveries, citing this as [one of the reasons for the cafe's closure](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/food-drink/complete-disaster-causes-bristol-cafe-5604539) in February. Article continues below But there has also been praise from Baldwin Street businesses. Brewdog bar, Oowee takeaway and Five Grains cafe spoke last week about how the trial had [created a more enjoyable environment for customers](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/shopping/businesses-baffled-bristol-area-ranked-5602350) and made it easier for cyclists to deliver food from the street's businesses. "In making this decision I considered that the scheme would achieve elements of the wider transport policy aspirations of the city council’s overall transport strategy, as set out in the Joint Local Transport Plan 2020 to 2036." Brown**](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/authors/shashana-brown/) Multimedia Journalist 05:00, 14 Jul 2021 It has been four months since [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council)announced [Cotham Hill](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cotham) will be temporarily closed to motorists to support businesses during the pandemic. Article continues below But just how much has this impacted traders and visitors in the area, three months after barricades and closed signs were implemented? ‌ The word ‘continental’ is used by many who are either sipping lattes in seated areas in the middle of the road or buying an array of enticing fruits and vegetables on the corner. Article continues below **Read more:**['Freedom Day' rule changes prompt cautious message from Bristol leaders](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/freedom-day-rule-changes-prompt-5644214) Though it's a stark contrast from the roaring sounds of vehicles passing on Whiteladies road, the casual stroller can simply go about their day while only taking notice of vehicles unloading goods on a side street. Business owner Oren Adani has welcomed the measures which he says allow traders to thrive. ‌ Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. You can check out at any time. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice) [Join us on WhatsApp](https://chat.whatsapp.com/JwmceTjpWjYACrvdGPRfyJ) Having operated Falefel King on Cotham Hill for 12 years, he is well versed on life before the pandemic. "Now it's very continental and it's really nice to see people sitting on the streets and enjoying what the street has to offer - especially within the food scene," he said. ![Image 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5644201.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_BRI_130721Cothamhill_.jpg) View 4 Images Cotham Hill fruit and vegetable store(Image: Shashana Brown/Bristol Live) ‌ Like many of the food businesses between Whiteladies Gate and Hampton Lane, he had to spend a lot of money building outdoor seating structures to make the most of the current restrictions. "During the lockdown when we were only allowed to see people outside, having the outdoor seating benefited us hugely," he added. "A lot of people would come to us as a takeaway but there were many that would come to us on their lunch break that would need a place to sit down." ‌ However, the 32-year-old is a little sceptical as to how the short- term road measures will impact traders in the near future. "It hasn't been here long enough for us to really see the benefit compared to pre-lockdown but I would definitely like to keep it. "It just wouldn't make sense to get rid of it so quickly, ''he added. ‌ Mr Adani believes that if [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council)does not decide to implement a permanent scheme, then an extension of the current methods would be ideal. Though the local authority has responded to the calls from traders to provide outdoor capacity on [Cotham Hill](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cotham), many still feel that not enough has been done. Some say that the street looks 'uglier' and 'less attractive', citing that it looks more like a building site than a shopping area. ‌ Mr Adani said it has been down to the traders to create stylish outdoor structures and seating areas. He said the council had promised to install planters in place of the white and red cones and barricades as well as bins, but sadly those promises have so far amounted to nothing. ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5644202.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_BRI_130721Cothamhill__03.jpg) View 4 Images Outdoor seating area installed in front of Falefel King (Image: Shashana Brown/Bristol Live) Because of this, he said the street is often covered with litter and it's down to the traders to make it look more presentable. He believes the street would attract more visitors to the area if it looked more appealing. [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) said the scheme had been 'overwhelmingly welcomed' and they continue to work with businesses during the transition. Harry, current manager of Brandon Trust charity shop situated at the entrance of Cotham Hill, said life on the street is vibrant and has a continental vibe. “There is definitely a lot of trade passing through and people are spending more time in this area because of the cafes and coffee shops,” he said. For him, business has been ‘amazing’ with plenty of visitors coming to shop. ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5644190.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_BRI_130721Cothamhill__04.jpg) View 4 Images Harry - current manager of Brandon Trust in Cotham Hill(Image: Shashana Brown/Bristol Live) As a very student prone area, he said a lot of expensive items are often donated as they begin to move out. “I think the road closure has made a really nice atmosphere - it feels cosy,” he added. Mayor Marvin Rees said: “Since last summer we have delivered a package of transport upgrades to make it easier for Bristolians to get around during the pandemic. "We have been flexible in our approach of using temporary materials to create more space for pedestrians and cyclists, and I am pleased that we are now able to do the same for [Cotham Hill](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cotham). "It has been clear from speaking to traders and our recent engagement that some form of road closure is a key priority for local people, and we will be working with the community on plans for a longer-term scheme. ![Image 10](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5644199.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_BRI_130721Cothamhill__06.jpg) View 4 Images Business owners say the road signs and barricades make the roads look like a 'building site'(Image: Shashana Brown/Bristol Live) "Our aim is to deliver more[liveable neighbourhoods](https://news.bristol.gov.uk/news/cotham-hill-to-close-to-motorists-to-support-businesses-during-pandemic) right across the city that are free from traffic congestion and pollution.” Even though the Cotham Hill closure is only temporary, a statement on Bristol City Council's website, said: “Whilst this is an urgent measure to support business we are working on a more permanent scheme which will be subject to further engagement with the community. “This will take a look at a more holistic approach at the area and could incorporate changes to the wider area.” A Bristol City Council spokesperson hailed the pedestrianisation scheme as 'one of the leading examples of making significant changes to Bristol’s roads and streets to create more liveable neighbourhoods'. They said: “We are continuing to engage with the community and local businesses to monitor the scheme’s impacts, using feedback to identify improvements and are designing a permanent solution for the road which we will seek views on later in the year. “These changes have been overwhelmingly welcomed with hundreds of responses supporting the moves to give businesses and citizens more space and improving walking and cycling journeys in the area. “Following the trial period, and this feedback, we will install new planters to replace the temporary red and white barriers in the next few weeks. New signs and road markings to advise people to cycle slowly through the shared area will also be delivered.’’ ###### **Are there still plans to pedestrianised other roads in Bristol?** There are 10 remaining roads under review to improve walking and cycling journeys, however the council has provided feedback for both Cotham Hill and[St Marks Road.](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/easton) It concluded that[pedestrianisation is not being considere](https://bristol.citizenspace.com/sustainable-transport/st-marks-road-engagement-survey/)d for St Marks Road however, feedback from surveys and engagement with local businesses, community groups and local stakeholders will be used to produce some design options for the street. 2](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5657131.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_JK_BR_040820bus-gate-bridge-014JPG.jpg) View Image Bristol Bridge pictured last August when the closure was first in place(Image: jon Kent/Bristol Live) The number of fines that have been issued as a result of the Bristol Bridge closure has been revealed by the council for the first time. ‌ Last week, [Bristol City Council announced](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-bridge-traffic-ban-made-5619870) the trial closure of the bridge and some nearby routes to most [traffic](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/traffic-travel) will be made permanent this weekend on Saturday, July 17. ‌ And the authority has now revealed the scheme has raised £1.6m after 81,000 fines have been issued since enforcement started in November last year. ‌ **READ MORE: [Street View images show how Bristol has changed in 10 years](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/gallery/street-view-images-show-how-5651693)** A [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) spokesperson said: “There are six cameras involved in the Bristol Bridge scheme spread across the approaches to the bridge, St Augustine’s Parade, Baldwin Street and Union Street. "Since enforcement started in November last year, there have been 81,000 fines issued. It varies between 3,800 and 23,000 total fines issued from the individual cameras ‌ “On Bristol Bridge itself, we have issued 33,582 fines since November. "The total value of fines issued during this period is £1.6m which is money that is directed straight back into covering the costs of enforcement with any surplus used to benefit the transport network.” **_What do you think about this story? Let us know in the comments below._** ‌ The closure has banned general traffic from Bristol Bridge; Baldwin Street between St Augustine’s Parade and Marsh Street; Baldwin Street to High Street; and Union Street's left turn onto Rupert Street. Buses, solo motorcycles, taxis and cycles are given priority under the order. **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** ‌ Making the announcement during a press briefing last week, Bristol Mayor [Marvin Rees](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/marvin-rees) said: "This intervention was one of the activities we have taken to intervene in the way traffic flows around the city to improve our air quality. "It has proven successful. "It is also part of the commitment we have made to delivering rapid bus routes around the city, which is contributing to the business case for the mass transit system that we are doing the work on." ‌ Describing the move as a very positive intervention for the city, the Mayor said air quality had improved on Victoria Street on almost all monthly readings since the scheme was introduced. Last week, _Bristol Live_ revealed the data [from the council's "decision report",](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-bridge-traffic-ban-most-5633862) which showed 61 per cent of the 865 responses were in opposition to the scheme. In the weeks after the trial came into force, 3,574 people signed a [petition](https://www.change.org/p/the-mayor-of-bristol-marvin-rees-reverse-the-decision-to-close-bristol-bridge-baldwin-st-access-to-the-city-centre) calling for the scheme to be reversed, citing the impact on local businesses. This triggered a [counter-petition](https://www.change.org/p/b-keep-bristol-bridge-closed-to-car-traffic-and-support-a-car-free-healthy-city-centre) signed by 1,425 supporters of a "car-free healthy city centre". ‌ Hamid Parast, who owned Centre Cafe Lounge on Baldwin Street, claimed the scheme caused difficulties for deliveries, citing this as [one of the reasons for the cafe's closure](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/food-drink/complete-disaster-causes-bristol-cafe-5604539) in February. But there has also been praise from Baldwin Street businesses. Article continues below Brewdog bar, Oowee takeaway and Five Grains cafe spoke about how the trial had [created a more enjoyable environment for customers](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/shopping/businesses-baffled-bristol-area-ranked-5602350) and made it easier for cyclists to deliver food from the street's businesses. **Get the best stories about the things you love most curated by us and delivered to your inbox every day. recent years and were hard hit by the pandemic(Image: BristolLive) The [city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre)and nine high streets will be the first to benefit from a £4.7m cash injection to restore life to the heart of Bristol's communities. ‌ Local high streets have been suffering for years under pressure from online traders, large supermarkets and retail parks, and the pandemic has only hastened their decline. ‌ [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) announced in March it was launching a £4.725 million recovery package for the regeneration and recovery of the city centre and 47 high streets. Article continues below **READ MORE: [Live updates as 'Freedom Day' arrives in Bristol](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/freedom-day-bristol-live-updates-5668538)** Last week the city’s ruling [Labour](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/labour-party) cabinet gave its approval to spend the funding, with the city centre and nine high streets across Bristol first in line for recovery and renewal. The nine high streets are: ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. The majority of the funding, £2.725m, has been allocated by the [West of England Combined Authority](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/west-of-england-combined-authority) (Weca) from its Love Our High Streets fund. Addressing cabinet members on Tuesday (July 13), city mayor [Marvin Rees](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/marvin-rees) said: “This cash boost will help to spearhead the regeneration and recovery of the city centre and 47 high streets across Bristol. Article continues below “In total, £2m of funding has been earmarked from my capital recovery fund and £2.7m from Weca’s Love Our High Streets fund which has been ring-fenced for Bristol. “Nine high streets will be the focus of initial support. The money will be used to improve the street scene, reduce the number of vacant premises by providing financial support to open new businesses including hospitality and creative spaces. “This investment will see us working with businesses, residents, community groups, the creative and events sector and other stakeholders to design public realm and street scene improvements reflecting the needs and aspirations of each area concerned.” ‌ **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** East Street in [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster) has already started along the path of regeneration with some local businesses making use of grants of up to £10,000 that are still available to regenerate underused shops, cafes, artists studios and offices. The money was allocated by Weca in 2018 after East Street was [chosen along with two other streets](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/north-bristol-high-streets-need-2304549) in the region to receive Love our High Street pilot project funding. ‌ ![Image 8: An illustration of East Street as part of the 'East Street Vision' from Bedminster BID](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5406812.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_TCR_BRI_120521EastStreetBRI.jpg) View 2 Images An illustration of East Street as part of the 'East Street Vision' from Bedminster BID(Image: Bedminster BID) An [ambitious £10m plan](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/businesses-unveil-10-million-plan-5406557) to invigorate East Street has also been launched by Bedminster’s business community, after they spent more than a year talking to local residents, people from across South Bristol who visit there already, and traders in East Street. [Southville](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/southville) councillor Tony Dyer told cabinet members: “We are very keen to get investment into the East Street vision.” ‌ A cabinet report about the £4.7 million investment programme said: “This programme aims to support existing high streets business from non-essential retail, hospitality, culture and events sectors which have been severely impacted by Covid restrictions and lockdown measures, but also diversify and re-animate high streets, increasing footfall and encouraging visitors into the local economy. “Within the city centre, which is a key economic and cultural focus for the region, activity will focus on safe reopening, a diverse and inclusive co-ordinated cultural and experiential events programme, support for the hospitality sector, meanwhile/pop-up uses and greening. ### Download the Bristol Live app See our best content via our dedicated smartphone apps and keep up to date on all our breaking news stories - including the latest on crime, business, travel and weather. planters(Image: Councillor Carla Denyer) Planters have been installed on [Cotham Hill](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cotham) to make the temporary pedestrianised look good again. ‌ Last Friday (July 16), dozens of planters were beautifully arranged outside businesses in place of road signs and barricades. ‌ This comes months after [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) closed the street to motorists to [support businesses during the pandemic](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/what-life-like-bristols-cotham-5644105). "In late 2020, the Council ran a survey which received 2,632 responses. Over 80 per cent said that more space for pedestrians was a high priority. ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. "I and my fellow councillor Tom Hathway have been working closely with council staff, locals and businesses to make improvements. Although there are still a few issues to be resolved, today (July 16) is a big milestone in that process. Article continues below "The red and white plastic barriers have been replaced with attractive planters, and better signage has been added to the road, reminding all users to use the space carefully and considerately. "I think it looks much better, and hopefully we will see it working better for everybody too. ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5669890.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_BRI_190721CothamHill__05.jpg) View 3 Images Traders welcome the changes to Cotham Hill Road (Image: Councillor Carla Denyer) ‌ “Later this summer, the Council will start a new consultation, asking residents and businesses whether they would like to see these or other changes made permanent. "I would encourage everyone who lives or works near Cotham Hill to take part.” Traders have welcomed the changes to [Cotham Hill](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cotham) and[told Bristol Live last week](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/what-life-like-bristols-cotham-5644105)that even though the measures are temporary, they hope it will be extended. ‌ #### Long-term future Bristol City Council said the Cotham Hill pedestrianisation has been "one of the leading examples" of creating "liveable neighbourhoods" to reduce traffic while supporting high streets. It confirmed that it is now drawing up a more permanent plan for the street, which it will seek feedback on later this year. ‌ A spokesperson added: "We are continuing to engage with the community and local businesses to monitor the scheme’s impacts, using feedback to identify improvements and are designing a permanent solution for the road which we will seek views on later in the year. "These changes have been overwhelmingly welcomed with hundreds of responses supporting the moves to give businesses and citizens more space and improving walking and cycling journeys in the area. "New planters have been installed in line with the plan we have for this area to create more liveable neighbourhoods - areas free from traffic and congestion.
