2017](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5809243.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_Brunel-Ford-site.jpg) View 2 Images The former Brunel Ford dealership in Muller Road before it was fenced off in 2017 A community of people living in vans on an empty old car dealership site in Bristol are to be evicted next week - so the council can build 32 new homes. ‌ [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) has announced it intends to move the [people living in vans and caravans](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/hardworking-middle-aged-unique-study-2672885) on the old Brunel Ford dealership site on Muller Road off the site, saying they are unlawfully occupying land that is intended to be developed. ‌ And the council has issued a notice warning local residents and commuters that they will have to close Muller Road, the main route between Horfield and the M32 junction at Eastville, to do it. Article continues below READ MORE: [Huge operation to evict Bristol's largest van-dweller site](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/huge-operation-evict-bristols-largest-5439859) The road closure notice comes into effect at 6am next Wednesday, August 25, and the council said depending on how long it takes to physically move them on, it could be closed all day. The council was supposed to start work building the 32 new homes for local people back in June, but work was put on hold when a large number of people living in vans arrived and set up home there. ‌ [![Image 8: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Put your skills to the test. Whether you love word games, tricky cryptic crosswords, Sudoku, or our other brain teasers, you'll find a new favourite today! Play Now](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games/) In May this year, a similar eviction just down the road on a site owned by Wales and West Utilities, saw a [huge operation involving hundreds of police officers and bailiffs.](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/huge-operation-evict-bristols-largest-5439859) Then, around 40 vans and caravans and all the people living in them, were moved off the site in Glenfrome Road, near Ikea in Eastville, in an operation that lasted all day and included allegations the [bailiffs had been heavy-handed](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/huge-operation-evict-bristols-largest-5439859) with the people being evicted. It is unknown how many people are living on the site of the old Brunel Ford dealership and garage, but it is thought some came from that Glenfrome Road site in May, just weeks before work on the development was supposed to start. Article continues below The car dealership closed down about nine years ago, and by 2013 was reduced to wasteland, and fenced off. It was included in a plan to build a new Lidl store, but that ended up only on the former Royal Mail sorting office next door. Since 2017, it’s been surrounded by a huge fence and left completely empty. ![Image 9: The former Brunel Ford dealership in Muller Road has been fenced off for four years](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5809242.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/2_Brunel-Ford-site-2.jpg) View 2 Images The former Brunel Ford dealership in Muller Road has been fenced off for four years Last year, council planners approved a council scheme to build 32 affordable homes on it. Housing chiefs said the majority would be homes for social rent - effectively new council homes - and some would be offered for shared ownership to make the scheme financially viable. ‌ Council housing chiefs now want to start work on that development, and have asked the van dwellers to leave. If, between now and dawn next Wednesday, the van dwellers do move off, then the road closure won’t be needed, but a section of Muller Road between the junctions with Brent Road and Ralph Road in Horfield will be closed, if a forced eviction is to take place. “The road will be reopened as soon as possible, but it may remain closed all day,” said a spokesperson for Bristol City Council. ‌ “The council has worked with the vehicle dwellers to establish any welfare needs, and to find suitable alternative accommodation, offering them alternative pitches at other sites. **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** “Legal action is always a last resort, but we were due to start building 32 council homes on the site in June, which will become available for a social rent for families on our waiting list. This has already been delayed due to the occupation of the land. Building affordable housing for Bristol is one of our top priorities, and we do not want any further delays with this development to make homes being available for Bristol families. ‌ “We acknowledge that this road closure is likely to have a major impact on local traffic, and may cause local people some inconvenience, but would like to reassure you that we will do all that we can to have the road reopened as soon as possible. “We appreciate that people living in vehicles do so for a variety of reasons and our focus is on finding solutions that are sustainable,” he added. **Want our best stories with fewer ads and alerts when the biggest news stories drop? **Jack Donoghue** 05:00, 24 Aug 2021 Updated 12:24, 25 Aug 2021 ![Image 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5822605.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_Picture1.jpg) View 3 Images Mark Smith, a business manager at Titcombe Bespoke Jewellery, works on Princess Victoria Street Pedestrianisation along Princess Victoria Street has divided opinion during the first few days of the scheme's trial. ‌ The changes in [Clifton](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/clifton)Village, which could last up to 18 months, will see the road between Waterloo Road and Regent Street closed to motorists from 11am to 5pm every day, including at weekends. ‌ Supporters of the[Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) trial hope that it will lead to cleaner air and less pollution, as well as making it more suitable for [cyclists](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cycling)and pedestrians. Article continues below **READ MORE: [What life is like on Cotham Hill since it closed to cars](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/what-life-like-bristols-cotham-5644105)** The [road was closed last week](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/cliftons-princess-victoria-street-pedestrianised-5784507) (August 16) so adjustments could be made, and the trial officially began on Saturday (August 21). While there was positive feedback on social media, some business owners who trade on the street have voiced their opposition. ‌ [![Image 8: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Play Now](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games/) In many shop windows along the road, flyers have been posted to show opposition to the scheme, and[there have been protests](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/shopping/popular-shopping-street-pedestrianised-hundreds-5500210)on the road in recent months. **Would you like to see pedestrianisation in your area? We want to hear your thoughts on this story, so please log in and leave your comment below.** Mark Smith, a business manager at Titcombe Bespoke Jewellery, is one of those with concerns about the impact of pedestrianisation. Article continues below He[told Bristol Live](https://www.facebook.com/bristol.live/videos/923885418012532) that the scheme has been "all stick and no carrot" so far. "I’m not anti-pedestrianisation, I think it's definitely the way forward," said Mark. ![Image 9: Princess Victoria Street in Clifton](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5500309.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_WhatsApp-Image-2021-06-07-at-141100-1jpeg.jpg) View 3 Images Princess Victoria Street, Clifton "But the changes to the road layout and the movement of traffic that is going to be done will cause problems in the future for the residents of Clifton Village. ‌ "I know there’s been a lot of talk that a lot of the residents are for this, but that’s not necessarily been borne out by my experiences of what the locals have said to us." Mark said that he would like to see different measures to protect the environment in Clifton Village, such as more public transport routes and more charging points for electric vehicles. **Get the best stories about the things you love most curated by us and delivered to your inbox every day. He explained: "Pedestrianisation of Clifton Village isn’t in itself a bad thing, I think it’s a very good thing. "We do need to be less reliant on cars, but the closure of the main access road into Clifton Village is only going to divert traffic through residential streets and move the pollution that is here from cars to peoples’ front gardens, to where people live." ‌ Several other business owners have also expressed concern about the area losing some of its appeal to tourists. **_What is happening where you live? And he also thinks that, given the financial difficulties that Covid-19 has brought, now is not the time to be experimenting with pedestrianisation. Bristol mayor [Marvin Rees](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/marvin-rees) has also expressed his support, saying the city needs "bold action" to cut congestion and pollution. He said pedestrianisation schemes on Cotham Hill, King Street and in the Old City have "proved to be very popular". Consultation will run for the first six months of the trial, and Cllr O'Rourke said that 2,000 consultation letters were posted in the area before the pedestrianisation began. More than 70 women marry dozens of trees to oppose Bristol building plans * [](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/) * [News](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/) * [Bristol News](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/) * [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) The ceremony was aimed to highlight plans which could see trees felled and the building of 166 new flats -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 15:31, 07 Sep 2021 More than 70 women have married dozens of trees in a ceremony opposing plans which could see the trees removed from a prospective building site. ‌ The event took place in Bristol where organisers are worried about the threat to trees posed by proposals to build 166 apartments. ‌ The ceremony was aimed to highlight plans which could see trees felled and [the building of 166 new flats](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/new-harbourside-homes-coming-baltic-4565024) by the city council-owned Goram Homes. ‌ **Read more: [IKEA stock shortage in Bristol explained as pictures show empty shelves](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/ikea-stock-shortage-bristol-explained-5879169)** The brides wore wedding dresses from different global cultures, with event creator Siobhan Kierans saying that she hoped the event showed that “trees are our partners for life.” The group were inspired by women in India who threw their arms around trees to protect forests from being destroyed. ‌ One of the “brides”, Suzan Hackett, [told the BBC](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-bristol-58423302) : “To get married to a tree is an absolute privilege. It’s not just a sentimental gesture, it is highly significant and symbolic. “Trees are pure examples of unconditional love, which fits in so beautifully with the whole idea of marriage. Marriage is for life, breathing is for life. ‌ “Bristol needs mature trees more than it does luxury private housing.” The planning application on the site between the docks and Cumberland Road is from Goram Homes and Essex-based developers Hill, with the Baltic Wharf Homes website promising “a fantastic opportunity (on) an underutilised and prime harbourside location.” ‌ Plans for the £55m project incorporate one, two and three-bedroom flats – including exclusive waterfront penthouses and 66 affordable homes – as well as ground floor commercial space. [Baltic Wharf Caravan Club Site](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/caravan-site-forced-out-baltic-4603495), where the 74 trees are located, advise customers on their website that they are welcoming arrivals up to and including September 19, departing no later than midday on September 20. The club has been operating the campsite for several years on a renewable, short term lease and in 2017 purchased a new location near Ashton Court for a potential new site. Thornbury Chamber of Commerce said if pedestrianisation remains in place it would be [the death knell for the town centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/traffic-free-thornbury-high-street-4789889), alleging it has led to footfall plummeting due to people not being able to park outside the shops. Article continues below 138205441681 A meeting was called last week by residents against the changes - and so many people turned up that some had to be turned away, [reports the Gazette](https://www.gazetteseries.co.uk/news/19585858.residents-voice-opposition-thornbury-high-street-plans/). **Get the biggest stories from across Bristol**[straight to your inbox](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/newsletter-preference-centre/) Jackie Riddiford, of fruit and veg shop L.E Riddiford, told _BristolLive_ the pedestrianisation of the street has “certainly affected trade” with a “30 per cent drop in footfall after the initial closure". Article continues below 138205441681 Jackie said some people find it difficult to access the high street, with the bus stop which serves it having moved to a different spot following the initial pedestrianisation. But it’s those in favour of the street who have claimed their views "are often not listened to". “Customers love it, and people can get out and about freely now,” another business owner said during _Bristol Live's_ visit. Article continues below 138205439169 “It’s a more relaxed atmosphere, and we’ve had far more trade since the pedestrianisation. “It’s a shame I can’t express how I feel. I don’t want to go to the meeting as I am afraid of what will happen when I share my thoughts." ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5930774.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_6253c32d-35a9-4dd0-8a3d-695d19f1cabcjfif.jpg) View 2 Images Thornbury High Street Article continues below 138205439169 ##### What has the council said? South Gloucestershire Council's cabinet member for communities and local place, councillor Rachael Hunt, said: “Thornbury High Street is at the heart of the town and our vision is to help that heart beat more easily, to maintain access for traders and those with mobility issues of course. "But [we want] to encourage more people to walk and cycle there and to spend more time enjoying the unique surroundings of the town centre. “Many business owners and visitors have told us that reducing traffic has made the area much more pleasant to spend time in, but we want to hear from local people now about the best way to make the changes permanent, so we can all see the high street come back from the disruption of the pandemic in a strong way that will ensure it thrives into the future." Plans to close Park Street to private cars and introduce free buses announced by mayor Radical new plans for the city's transport have been revealed this evening -------------------------------------------------------------------------- 20:36, 20 Oct 2021 Closing Park Street to cars and offering free bus tickets and free electric bike loans are among radical proposals for the future of Bristol’s transport system, Marvin Rees has announced. ‌ In his annual State of the City address on Wednesday evening (October 20), the mayor reaffirmed his commitment to a £4billion mass transit system including an underground, as he outlined the scale of the challenges facing the city. ‌ Mr Rees said the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic would be with us for generations while the poorest and most marginalised residents would be hit hardest again if we don’t face up to the urgent need to tackle climate change. ‌ **READ MORE: [Bristol nightclub boycott planned amid injection spiking reports](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-nightclub-boycott-planned-amid-6089720)** The bulk of his speech at the Wills Memorial Building highlighted achievements to date and how the city is becoming fairer and more inclusive under his leadership, but on transport he revealed a number of new policies. The mayor said: “On transport, our flagship policy remains the mass transit system including the underground. ‌ “All routes have been identified linking the north, east, south, and airport to the city centre. “It will integrate buses and trains and include new stations, to form a transformative, low-carbon transport system. “We are about to launch a consultation on the introduction of bus prioritisation for the Wells Road, to the city centre, over the Downs and the whole length of the A4018. ‌ “We will ask you to comment on proposals to remove parking that causes congestion on key routes and the closure of Park Street to private cars. “This has the potential to reinvent public realm up to the Triangle and remove rat-runs from the Downs.” Mr Rees said [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council)had submitted the full business case for the Clean Air Zone, which would come into force next year, and was negotiating a package of support with the Government. ‌ This included £2million for clean buses, £720,000 for a new cycle scheme through Old Market, free electric bike loans and cycle training, free bus tickets, discounts on car club membership, support to buy electric cars and financial support for businesses and residents to upgrade polluting vehicles. “We estimate the CAZ will reduce traffic travelling into the city centre by approximately 2,000 vehicles per day, while delivering protections for lower paid workers, hospital patients and visitors, and blue badge holders,” he said. ‌ “Over half a century ago, Bristol lost its trams and, 20 years ago, lost out on an opportunity for ‘supertrams’. “This was down to poor leadership, impenetrable council structures, and regional squabbles. “We have the opportunity today to get beyond these historical failures and deliver something transformative. ‌ “We need government funding and we must ensure the West of England Combined Authority unlocks the investment Bristol and the city region needs. We need substance, not soundbites.” Mr Rees said the local authority faced a massive £42million shortfall on social care. He said: "We’ve been tackling the crisis that is local government finance. ‌ "The real costs of Covid and over a decade of austerity mean that the city again faces the challenge of an under-funded council budget. "We are working through the numbers but, as of today, we have a potential shortfall of £42million, that may lead to more difficult decisions for the city." The mayor said the coronavirus pandemic had “humbled us and warned us – **i** t has given us a taste of a natural world reasserting its authority”. ‌ He said: “In the modern era we have believed that we have the ability to control things, that whatever the crisis, ‘someone somewhere’ could solve it. “But we have tasted living in a world in which no one, nowhere could make a decision to end the crisis. “We now need to apply that experience of loss of control to the climate emergency. 2](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5221331.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_View-of-Park-Street-buildings.jpg) View 2 Images Park Street in the city centre (Image: Getty Images) The city mayor has compared plans to close Park Street to the controversy around Colston's statue, predicting a mixed reaction. ‌ In [his annual State of the City address](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/plans-close-park-street-private-6090807) on Wednesday evening (October 20), Bristol's mayor announced plans to close Park Street to cars as well as offering free bus tickets and free electric bike loans, among other measures to encourage more sustainable travel. ‌ Speaking during an interview with _BristolLive_ this morning, [Marvin Rees](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/marvin-rees) said he expects the proposals will receive a range of responses. ‌ **READ MORE: [Bristol mayor's stark climate warning](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/if-pass-tipping-point-therell-6090646)** He said: "Some people will be surprised, some people will be elated and some people will be really concerned. "We will have the same kind of range of perspectives in the same way as people reacted to the [Colston statue](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/edward-colston), for example. ‌ "Bristol is a diverse city with people experiencing the city in very different ways, having different lifestyles, and when any announcement is made the response will depend on that. "Our job is to try and help the diverse city navigate its way through a really complex set of opportunities and challenges - different people will react differently." Mr Rees said a public consultation on the proposals - which would see Park Street closed to private cars but accessible to public transport, taxis, deliveries and exempt vehicles - will be at some point over the coming months. ‌ **Get the biggest stories from across Bristol**[**straight to your inbox**](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/newsletter-preference-centre/) ![Image 3: Marvin Rees](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article6090803.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/3_Marvin-Mayor-at-State-of-the-City-2021.jpg) View 2 Images Marvin at the annual State of the City event The mayor said the plans also fit in with the urgency to redesign cities to minimise their impact on the planet and tackle the[climate emergency.](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/climate-change) ‌ "As we have approached all of these challenges and opportunities in how we rethink the way Bristol works, we have always taken into it the realisation that good things can have negative consequences for some people," he continued. "We are very aware of the fact for some people it will be absolutely fantastic, but we also think what does it mean for care workers? What does it mean for accessing the hospital and for tradespeople going around the city? "All of these things will be thought through and people will be engaged with. ‌ "It is not a solid plan - what we have said is that we would take the proposals to the city to have a conversation about this." Mr Rees described the proposals as a contributing intervention, with no single intervention offering a 'golden bullet' solution on system change. ‌ He added that they are part of a number of ideas being looked at to encourage people to use public transport, and continued: "We need to proactively think of the changing nature of the city - we are going to have a lot more residential [areas] in the middle of Bristol, mixed in with employment and retail. "We need to be ahead of that, to plan for it ahead rather than just happening by accident and us not having any control." The mayor said there are other changes coming to the city centre including the [Clean Air Zone](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/clean-air-zone) which, designed to curb traffic air pollution, will see older, more polluting vehicles charged £9 a day to enter a small area in the city centre. ‌ The council had been ordered by the Government to implement the CAZ by October this year, but [that has now been put back to the summer of 2022](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristols-clean-air-zone-delayed-5601638). Earlier this year, Mr Rees said t[he delay to the introduction of Bristol’s CAZ will “absolutely” not](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/delay-bristol-clean-air-zone-5622947) affect how soon residents get to breathe clean air. ‌ In his annual State of the City address yesterday evening, the mayor also [reaffirmed his commitment to a £4billion mass transit system](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/marvin-rees-full-speech-tonights-6090637) including an underground, as he outlined the scale of the challenges facing the city. Mr Rees said the impact of the [Covid-19](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/coronavirus) pandemic will be with us for generations and the poorest and most marginalised residents would be hit hardest again, if we don’t face up to the urgent need to tackle climate change. The bulk of his speech at the Wills Memorial Building highlighted achievements to date and how the city is becoming fairer and more inclusive under his leadership. What Park Street traders think about plans to close the street to cars Opinion was divided among the business owners we spoke to --------------------------------------------------------- 05:00, 26 Oct 2021 Park Street traders are split as to whether closing the street to cars would be the right thing to do or not. ‌ The business owners shared a range of views after the city mayor Marvin Rees announced plans to close Park Street to cars in [his annual State of the City address](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/plans-close-park-street-private-6090807) last week. ‌ The proposals would be one of the measures to be introduced to encourage more sustainable travel, but the mayor predicted a mixed reaction and [compared it to the controversy around Colston's statue](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/marvin-rees-compares-park-street-6091693). ‌ **READ MORE: [Shoppers in 'disbelief' at plans to close Broadmead store](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/ms-bristol-shoppers-disbelief-plans-6053241)** A public consultation on the proposals - which would see Park Street closed to private cars but accessible to public transport, taxis, deliveries and exempt vehicles - will be at some point over the coming months, the mayor said last week. Hannah Dymond, manager of Bird & Blend, which has been on Park Street for five years, said she liked the idea. ‌ Ms Dymond said, at the moment, people drive too fast and it is very noisy, adding closing the road to private cars would create a more peaceful environment. "I think it is likely it would make it more people friendly," she continued. "I do not think it would put people off as you can not really park on Park Street anyway. "I think people come here on foot and cars drive past here to go somewhere else." ‌ Ms Dymond said Park Street [shoppers](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/shopping-in-bristol) tend to park on the multi-storey Trenchard Street car park or the one along Jacob's Wells Road, adding that she would close Park Street from Park Row to the junction with St George's Road. Quite a lot of shoppers already walk or cycle as they are [environmentally conscious](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/environment), she continued. ‌ "I think that it would enhance rather than impact negatively," she added. "It is constant traffic and I would welcome its reduction, and particularly the improvement to air quality that comes with it. "Sometimes we are trying to talk to people and literally you can't hear them, especially if wearing a mask, and you have to wait until the traffic has gone past. "A lot of vehicles drive fast up here and you see a lot of near misses happening all the time." ‌ But Karen Purnell, manager of the Sue Ryder charity shop, would like things to stay as they are. The store manager said shoppers already struggle with parking and its cost, and that they would just go elsewhere if the street closes to private cars. ‌ "There are lots of people that just pop into Park Street for the hour," she continued. "To be able to get as close as you can is a good thing. "I would not support it at all and I worry it would damage trade. "I would support keeping things as they are." ‌ **********_What do you think about this story? Sign in and let us know in the comments_********** Ms Purnell said another concern for her would be people finding it hard to get donations to them, adding access to the [city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre) is already limited and described buses as ridiculous and hopeless. ‌ It is not an easy time for businesses, she continued, and her worry is that the proposed changes could make things worse. Michael Territo, one of the owners of Territo Tailoring, said he would like to know more about the exemptions and, for instance, what happens with blue badge holders. He said they have a large catchment area of people that go to their shop, including quite a lot of elderly customers. ‌ It is necessary to slow cars down, he continued, and crossing islands would be a good idea. The business owner suggested having Park Street as a one-way street and said he would be in favour of closing the street to private cars on Friday and Saturday evening from 7pm, to encourage people to eat in the area. ‌ "There are big steps in between having the road closed and open, like the one way," he continued. "I am in two minds about it. "This street needs to be a place where people can cross from one side to the other and it is very easy. "I think they could do a step in between. ‌ "There are lots of things to consider, I am not against it - I just hope all the things are considered." The shop owner continued: "It would offer people a peaceful shopping environment. "It is a pretty area as it is and this would make it nicer and quieter. ‌ "I think it would take time for people to get used it and maybe initially it would put people off, especially as they would need to walk up the hill. "Initially it may have a negative impact but I think people would get used to it. "It is necessary to have a discussion with all the shop owners to make sure it would not damage the area." ‌ Mr Gurung said that the [pandemic](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/coronavirus) has been really hard and that things hadn't gone back to normal for them yet. He added that, if the proposals go ahead, shop owners and their staff should be allowed to do their own deliveries, adding that a lot of the small businesses along the street like themselves do their own deliveries. ‌ He suggested starting initiatives such as offering free parking for electric cars or free electric car charging. Amia Watling, manager of Sobeys, said she had not heard about the plans, but that she would welcome the reduction in congestion as the street gets very busy. "My initial worry would be whether it would stop people coming to this part of Bristol as it would make it harder for them to get here," she continued. Article continues below The road is only open to pedestrians and cyclists from 11am to 5pm every day, which local councillors say reduces pollution from vehicles and makes the street safer for residents. Article continues below 138205441690 **READ MORE:**['Nightmare' as lorry 'crashes into car' on pedestrianised street in Clifton](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/nightmare-lorry-crashes-car-pedestrianised-5916809) But traders say that their income is being significantly impacted, and as consultation runs for the first six months, they are urging people to object to the scheme. We are desperate to work with you, the residents, and the authorities to achieve this, but need to be trading profitably." Article continues below One trader on the street, JP van Hoeve, says the scheme has been a "kick in the teeth". JP, who is the co-owner of About Face, thinks he is making about 20 per cent less money in his shop than he was in 2019. Article continues below He told _Bristol Live_ that business owners feel "very downbeat" and said that he knows "several traders who are really down on their takings”. ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5502716.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_JMP_SWA_080621_Princess_Victoria_Street__001_JPG.jpg) View Image Angry protesters carried a coffin through Clifton to oppose the plans earlier this year(Image: John Myers) He said that because the scheme has reduced the number of parking spaces on the street, fewer people come there to shop. Article continues below He estimates that footfall has decreased by about 50 per cent, as people used to park for half an hour and pop into a few shops, but they no longer can. He said the problem is particularly bad when the weather is poor. "When it rains, everything stops," he said. "Where in the old days you used to have cars coming in and dashing out even if it rained, for a quick this or that, that just doesn’t happen now." Article continues below And he said that he no longer sees regular customers who live in North Somerset, as they can't drive to the road and park up there. Cllr Paula O’Rourke and and Cllr Katy Grant, Clifton ward members, [said in August](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/cliftons-princess-victoria-street-pedestrianised-5784507): “[This] will give residents and visitors the space to shop at leisure. When the street is car-free, it will be a cleaner and safer place for community use. This change will make Clifton even more vibrant and exciting. "As it is being done as an experiment, we can continue to consult with the community and monitor if traffic is displaced and amend if needed." Article continues below Bristol mayor [Marvin Rees](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/marvin-rees) has also expressed his support, saying the city needs "bold action" to cut congestion and pollution. He said other pedestrianisation schemes on Cotham Hill, King Street and in the Old City have "proved to be very popular". ### The letter in full The letter from traders to residents says: "Clifton Village is a real treasure; a vibrant high street composed of independent traders that have survived the disaster of lockdowns. "These regular visitors support the shops that you, as residents love. Apart from the food and drink outlets in PV street which appear to be buzzing, the rest of the village is much quieter. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) In his speech last month, Mr Rees unexpectedly announced Park Street had been earmarked for closure to through traffic and that the public would be asked for their views on this idea and wider measures along the Number 2 bus route. He said: "We are about to launch a consultation on the introduction of bus prioritisation for the Wells Road, to the city centre, over the Downs and the whole length of the A4018. “We will ask you to comment on proposals to remove parking that causes congestion on key routes and the closure of Park Street to private cars. Article continues below 138205441828 “This has the potential to reinvent public realm up to the Triangle and remove rat-runs from the Downs.” Speaking on Monday, November 8, Cllr Weston said: “Sadly, the radical transport proposals outlined by the mayor in his recent annual address filled me with foreboding. “The idea of closing off Park Street to private vehicles not only removes passing trade from dependent businesses along that route, it further harms Broadmead. Article continues below 138205439166 ![Image 9: Cllr Mark Weston clashed with senior officers over City Leap at a meeting of Bristol's overview and management scrutiny board (OSMB) on Monday, July 12, 2021.](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5653134.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_weston-osm.png) View 3 Images Tory group leader Cllr Mark Weston at a council meeting at City Hall this summer(Image: Bristol City Council Live / YouTube) “In addition, as things stand, this change would disproportionately impact upon or disadvantage the elderly, infirm and disabled who often cannot use public transport. “Similarly, whilst well-intentioned, the planned bus prioritisation schemes along the A4018 are likely to act as a strong disincentive for many people to travel into Bristol for shopping when they have the convenience of plenty of free parking and an attractive retail offering at The Mall.” Article continues below 138205439166 Mr Rees’s unexpected Park Street announcement comes as other north Bristol Tory councillors are opposing transport plans by the West of England Combined Authority to install a bus gate at the entrance to North View from the A4018 and also close part of Queens Road to general traffic. Cllr Weston said his colleagues had been getting a “very angry response” from residents concerned that restrictions could stop them accessing local shops. He said: “These plans come at a particularly bad time for traders who are already struggling to rebuild following the economic shock brought about by the Covid lockdown. Article continues below 138205441681 “Consequently, I shall be urging the mayor to genuinely try to modify his reimagining of the public realm in the wake of the public consultation responses this generates.” The Conservative group leader’s motion has been submitted to a full council meeting of Bristol City Council on Tuesday evening (November 9) but is unlikely to be heard because of time constraints. It says: “Council is disappointed by the way the mayor is choosing to unveil controversial and potentially damaging transport proposals. Article continues below 138205441690 “The current administration seems intent on provoking a hostile political reaction rather than seeking to engage constructively with opposition parties to achieve consensus and positive change. ![Image 10: Marvin Rees](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article6090803.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/3_Marvin-Mayor-at-State-of-the-City-2021.jpg) View 3 Images Marvin delivering the annual State of the City address in October “Council is particularly concerned at the radical plan to close off Park Street (a major thoroughfare) to private vehicles, Queens Road (at the Victoria Rooms) and North View (at White Tree roundabout). Article continues below 138205439166 “Such a move would inevitably harm the various remaining businesses on each of those roads. “Making access to the city centre and North View much more difficult for shoppers will continue to reduce the attractiveness of Broadmead as a retail destination and thereby accelerate its continuing economic decline and will also jeopardise the businesses in Westbury Park. “Council fully understands that changes need to be made to improve air quality and reduce carbon emissions but following a unilaterally determined policy that puts many more jobs at risk without proper consideration of alternative strategies is not acceptable. Article continues below 138205439175 “Accordingly, Council asks for the mayor to give a commitment that there will be a genuine chance of changing any finalised scheme when the formal public consultation is launched. “Of course, this flexibility in design must also apply to his promised opportunity ‘to comment on proposals’ in relation to the planned bus prioritisation measures along the entire length of the A4018 and the No 2 bus route. “For consultation to be meaningful, the mayor and his transport planners should be prepared to take notice of the public’s views and act on them.” Article continues below **Get the best stories about the things you love most curated by us and delivered to your inbox every day. "I would not use public transport because I am always in a hurry and it takes too much time," she continued. "There is very little parking anywhere near Park Street anyway. "[If they closed Park Street to cars], it would stop people shopping here. Article continues below 138205441690 "It is a bad idea. I think you would see lots of places closing as there are lots of people like me who drive here. "I think people would just go elsewhere." Article continues below 138205441837 However, South Bristol resident Manuela said she liked the idea of Park Street being closed to cars. "But it would cause lots of trouble for lots of people," she said. "I do not drive but this road is used a lot. "The traffic in Bristol is already bad and if they keep closing roads it will be a nightmare. Article continues below 138205439133 "However, I wish it would be pedestrians only." Manuela - who has lived in Bristol for a year and a half - said that she walks up Park Street every day to get to work and that it is always busy with people and cars. ************_What do you think about this story? Mr Holland said that, if it would just lead to more traffic in nearby roads, it might not work. Article continues below 138205439133 He added: "There would be no point in having the extra pollution on other roads. "It depends on how they do it - you would need to see the plans. Article continues below 138205439133 "I think it would be quite a good idea to slow down and green up," he said. "We do not have to have all the money and traffic in certain areas, but could distribute it more across the city. "It would be an experiment, you can only try. "It [closing Park Street to cars] would be a bit of a high-profile case because it is next to College Green so it would get a lot of attention." Article continues below 138205441642 Mr Richards said he worries about air pollution, adding that modelling would give projections on traffic. He said that he would be affected by the changes, but that he would probably just walk instead. After the announcement was made, [Park Street traders were split](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/what-park-street-traders-think-6110495) as to whether closing the street to cars would be the right thing to do or not, with business owners also sharing a range of views on the proposals. Article continues below 138205439133 [Henbury](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/henbury)and Brentry ward Cllr Weston said restricting vehicle access to the [city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centrehttps-wwwbristolpostcouk-all-about-bristol-city-centre) would harm both passing trade and [Broadmead](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/broadmead)shopping centre. Clifton BID to come 'down off the fence' on controversial pedestrianisation trial Business leaders have hired a consultant to report to the council ----------------------------------------------------------------- 05:00, 15 Nov 2021 Business leaders in Clifton Village have pledged to come down off the fence as the debate about the controversial pedestrianisation of a key shopping street intensifies. ‌ The new chair of the Clifton BID - Business Improvement District - has promised to end the organisation’s impartiality over the trial which has seen one end of Princess Victoria Street closed to cars and transformed into a cafe culture friendly, pedestrianised street. ‌ The Clifton BID team, which is funded through a tax scheme that sees local businesses pay extra on their rates, has also announced it is hiring an independent consultant to conduct a study on the impact of the pedestrianisation on Princess Victoria Street and the wider area. ‌ **READ MORE**: [More than 100 'downbeat' Bristol businesses sign anti-pedestrianisation letter](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/more-100-downbeat-bristol-businesses-6167371) The pedestrianisation scheme was controversial even before it began, with local business owners and other residents staging mock funeral protests predicting the move to stop vehicles from driving down a 100-yard section of Princess Victoria Street would kill off many local businesses. The trial scheme [began in the middle of August](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/pedestrianisation-cliftons-princess-victoria-street-5821337), will be reviewed in six months but could last for 18 months before council chiefs decide whether to make the arrangement permanent or reopen the road to motorised vehicles. ‌ Many shopkeepers have said that in the three months since the start of the trial, footfall and business in their stores is down, blaming a lack of parking and customers choosing to shop elsewhere because they can’t drive close to the shops. Last week, [Bristol Live reported that more than 100](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/more-100-downbeat-bristol-businesses-6167371) had signed an open letter objecting to the trial and saying it is causing them to suffer a downturn in trade. But other businesses in the area say the pedestrianised area, which has picnic tables, benches and greenery installed there, has brought more people to the area and boosted business for them. During the debate before the introduction of the scheme, the Clifton BID organisation said it had to remain impartial. ‌ But now, with a new chair - Louise Dark - the organisation said it will support businesses on the issue more. Ms Dark is one half of the couple who have run Otomi, a Mexican products business on nearby Boyce’s Avenue for the past 14 years. The BID annual general meeting saw members voting to hire an independent consultant to gather evidence and information on the effects of the pedestrianisation ban. ‌ The BID team have hired a company called The Assembly Line, and in a message to BID members, Louise Dark said the review of the impact has to be completed soon, within the six month deadline in mid-February when the council will take a first look at the scheme. “The team will be visiting the village soon and come highly recommended,” said Ms Dark, in a message to BID members seen by Bristol Live. “This review needs to be presented to BCC before their 6-month review has been completed. “It has been brought to our attention that Clifton BID has (been) seen to be sitting on the fence when it comes to pedestrianisation. Article continues below “Initially Clifton BID had to be impartial as there were different points of view from the businesses. This has changed as time has gone on. We have agreed to contribute financial assistance to the production of the open letter and are happy to offer support wherever it is needed. We will keep the conversation going and try to apply pressure on the council as they will not engage with businesses and individuals,” she added. ****Get the best stories about the things you love most curated by us and delivered to your inbox every day. Experiment will pay people to leave their cars and live car-free for four weeks All the costs of the alternatives will be met as part of the project -------------------------------------------------------------------- 14:05, 07 Dec 2021 Updated 14:05, 07 Dec 2021 An experiment which will see people paid to not use their cars in Bristol for four weeks is looking for volunteers. ‌ The project is inviting people to sign up and take part, with organisers pledging to pay whatever the costs are for every journey that isn’t taken in the city by private car - including taxi and Uber bills, e-scooter rental, car club hire and bus fares. ‌ Those taking part will also get a fee for participating, as long as they promise to log every journey they make, how they made it and whether or not they would have gone in the car to make it. ‌ **READ MORE**: [Bristol should listen to people who HAVE to drive and what they SHOULD be saying](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/opinion-people-who-drive-bristol-18018) The project is being organised by climate action charity Possible, which is challenging people who would normally drive regularly in Bristol to see if it’s possible to not use their car at all between January 10 and February 6. Those taking part in the experiment will be asked to try to live ‘car-free’ for three of those weeks. ‌ “You’ll receive a participation fee and all non-car travel costs will be paid for, including cycle hire, car club and e-scooter credits,” Bristol’s Possible co-ordinator Rob Bryher said. “We’re particularly interested in hearing from people of colour, disabled people, carers and parents of pre-school or school-aged children,” he added. Mr Bryher said the experiment was about seeing whether it was possible - and to what extent it is possible - to get around Bristol as normal, but not in your own private car. He said many people do need their cars, but many people manage without one at all. The experiment was about seeing the kind of journeys that people struggle to manage without their own car, which will better inform future planning of public transport policies. ‌ Every time someone taking part in the experiment makes a journey, doesn’t use their own car, and there’s a cost involved - be that e-scooter rental or an Uber charge - they will be paid that by the Possible charity. “At Possible, we want to see a zero carbon society, built by and for everyone, and we want to see this fast,” a spokesperson said. “Our Car Free Bristol campaign brings to life a positive case for fewer cars on our city’s streets. ‌ **What do you think? Sign in and join the conversations in the comments below** “We are working with communities currently blighted by traffic and air pollution to co-design changes to local streets, taking space away from cars and giving it back to people and nature. “We recognise that there are many people, including disabled people, who cannot get around without a car. Our aim of fewer cars on the road means more space for those who need to drive - and a better Bristol for everyone. ‌ “At the same time, we will encourage and inspire local decision makers to raise ambitions and accelerate change at the city level,” he added. “There’s every chance that participants will need to use their car - we’re not taking cars off people or denying them access,” said Mr Bryher. “It’s going to be interesting to see how easy or hard it is for different kinds of people,” he added. facilities they would like to see in the redeveloped Vassall Centre. ‌ Bristol Charities purchased [the Vassall Centre in Fishponds last year](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/new-owners-vassall-centre-bristol-6183438) and has been working with Bristol architects AWW to develop ideas to deliver affordable, high-quality homes for the elderly and families, along with accessible, contemporary workspace for businesses and charities and a range of new community facilities. ‌ The new owner's aim is to create a "balanced new neighbourhood centre for multigenerational living and working". Article continues below **READ MORE: [New name for Broadwalk Shopping Centre as fresh development plans drawn up](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/new-name-broadwalk-shopping-centre-6505527)** Having completed an initial round of consultation, Bristol Charities is now looking for ideas for the publicly accessible parts of the project which include the potential community uses and activities that could be in the new building, as well as how to make these as welcoming as possible. The charity said: "Suggestions so far include a café, nursery, spaces for meetings and events, a small library and outside space to meet and relax. ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) "The project team is also looking for ideas to commemorate and celebrate the centre's historic role and legacy within the designs, such as an exhibition or art installation. ![Image 8: The Vassall Centre in Fishponds](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article6183493.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_091121vassallcentre.jpg) View 2 Images The Vassall Centre in Fishponds(Image: Spirit PR) "Starting life as a hospital facility for American soldiers in 1945, the Vassall Centre later became a medical limb replacement facility and currently offers affordable, accessible workspace and conference facilities for businesses, charities and not-for-profit organisations." Article continues below Bristol Charities said it also committed to increasing biodiversity, with new trees, planting and space for wildlife, and is appointing a landscape ecologist to help with this aspect of the proposals. Anne Anketell, chief executive officer at Bristol Charities said: "We are really interested in finding out what community facilities would work for local people and ensure the new neighbourhood centre benefits residents in Fishponds, so we'd urge people to take part in our survey, which will only take a few minutes to complete. "The existing buildings are now more than 75 years old, offer very low levels of energy efficiency and sustainability and have reached the end of their practical lifespan. ‌ "Upgrading them would be prohibitively costly and would not enable much-needed new homes for older people and families to be created in the area. "The views of local people are very important to us. We have listened carefully to the concerns of adjacent neighbours and are taking their issues into account as we further develop our proposals. Article continues below "People will get another opportunity to see the revised plans and comment on them in the next round of consultation in the next few weeks before we submit a planning application." _**Get the best stories about the things you love most curated by us and delivered to your inbox every day. 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article6541086.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_College-Green-screenshotJPG.jpg) View 4 Images Cars could be banned from College Green (Picture: Google Maps) College Green could be closed to cars to prioritise public transport, cycling and walking in the area. ‌ Back in October, city mayor [Marvin Rees](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/marvin-rees) announced plans to close Park Street to cars in [his annual State of the City address](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/plans-close-park-street-private-6090807). ‌ And, according to documents published as part of a consultation into [transport changes](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/traffic-travel) along [the number 2 bus route](https://travelwest.info/projects/a37-a4018-transport-corridor), it appears the traffic ban could be extended to College Green. Article continues below **READ MORE: [Park users feel 'penalised' as parking charges at beauty spots set to start](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/park-users-feel-penalised-parking-6527924)** The consultation states that buses, taxis, motorcycles, bikes and HGVs would still able to access the [city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre) area. As part of the changes, the left-turn from Canons Road to College Green would be removed so the pedestrian crossing island could be widened. ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) Consultation material states: "The bus gate at the top of Park Street would remove through traffic and prioritise public transport, cycling and walking. "Less traffic would allow us to expand the public space available on Park Street and help increase its status as a destination within the city. "The College Green/Canons Road/St Augustines Parade junction would be remodelled to account for the left turn from Canons Road being removed. Article continues below "Responses to the previous engagement asked us to improve pedestrian facilities by reallocating road space at this junction. "We are proposing an improved crossing and waiting area as the numbers of pedestrians and cyclists is extremely high." ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article6540761.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_College-Green-changesJPG.jpg) View 4 Images College Green changes ‌ A bus gate would be created at the top of Park Street and Berkeley Avenue would close to general traffic, with proposed new bus stops being installed at the top of Jacob Wells Road as well. The consultation states: "We were also asked to consider removing car traffic from Park Street to make it easier for buses and to reduce pollution and enable cyclists and pedestrians to have a more pleasant journey. "The bus gate at the top of Park Street would give priority to public transport, giving buses faster and more reliable access from and to the central area." ‌ ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article6540605.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_TriangleJPG.jpg) View 4 Images Proposed changes in the Triangle area The consultation states that Park Street Avenue could be closed at both ends to stop rat running between Park Row and Park Street and to provide the opportunity for public space. A widened footway on the east side of Park Street would be made, it continues, and parking moved to the west side of the street to make conditions safer for cyclists travelling down Park Street. ‌ It continues: "The closure of Park Street and College Green to through traffic would result in less traffic, whilst still allowing full access by alternative routes. "Less traffic would allow for the narrowing of the road and the widening of the eastern footway to create additional space for pedestrians, planting, and seating areas. "The movement of traffic would be made one way in a clockwise direction to reduce collisions at the junctions, on Great George Street and Charlotte Street with Park Street. "Footpaths would be widened at specific crossings on Park Street to make it safer and easier to cross the road." However, as Park Street is seen as a "pivotal section" of the number 2 bus route, a few alternative options are being proposed including installing a bus gate only restricting traffic inbound from the north or from the south. Looking at the proposed changes for the Triangle area, parking would be removed along Queens Road to allow for a segregated cycle lane to be created. The cycle lane would continue from Queens Road and join the junction of Triangle West/Queens Road to allow cyclists to reach the new cycle lane on the west side of Queens Road at the top of Park Street. Big changes around the Queens Road area are also being proposed. ![Image 10](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article6540524.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Queens-RoadJPG.jpg) View 4 Images An artist impression of what Queens Road could look like These include closing Richmond Hill and Park Place to traffic at the junction with Queens Road to allow for more public space and landscaped areas. A new cycle lane along Queens Road from St Paul’s Road, past Queen’s Avenue, would be added, with that stretch of Queens Road becoming one-way on each direction. A new cycle lane would be installed over the Bristol Bridge, together with a cycle lane, continuous and new widened footways, with loading bays and disabled bays along the west side of Victoria Street. The consultation states that the possible closure of Parrys Lane on the Downs would be considered in the future, but would be subject to detailed modelling moving forward. Also on the Downs, parking along Roman Road could be removed and the road be converted to a walking and cycling route. The consultation says: "Proposed new 24 hour outbound bus lane on Whiteladies Road between Wellington Park and York Street. "The new bus lane would allow buses to bypass queuing traffic on the approach to the Blackboy Hill junction, reducing delays to services and improving reliability. "It is proposed to remove through traffic and parking from Roman Road and convert it to a cycling and walking route." Looking at the Three Lamps junction in the south of the city, the Bellevue Road junction could be removed to reduce rat running through Totterdown onto the Wells Road. A new cycle route would be created through Redcatch Park to Broadwalk Shopping Centre. **_What is happening where you live? Find out by adding your postcode or [visit InYourArea](https://www.inyourarea.co.uk/)_** Changes would also be introduced in the Bayham Road area - with a number of streets becoming one ways and no entry - to stop general traffic from using the area to bypass Wells Road. A new bus lane could be installed along Southmead Road by the fire station as well. Also along Southmead Road, the dual-way carriageway stretch from Glenwood Road to Lake Road could be taken down to one lane in each direction. A three-metre segregated two-way cycle lane could also be added to the eastern side of Henleaze Road, with a footway added to the western side to improve access to Old Quarry Park. _You can express your views on the proposed changes on the TravelWest website [here](https://travelwest.info/projects/a37-a4018-transport-corridor). 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article6548752.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_Colleg-GreenJPG.jpg) View Image College Green in Bristol city centre (Image: Google Maps Street View) A charity that promotes walking and cycling has welcomed plans to ban cars on College Green and Park Street. ‌ Back in October, city mayor [Marvin Rees](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/marvin-rees) announced plans to close Park Street to cars in [his annual State of the City address](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/plans-close-park-street-private-6090807). ‌ And, according to documents published as part of a consultation into [transport changes](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/traffic-travel) along [the number 2 bus route](https://travelwest.info/projects/a37-a4018-transport-corridor), it appears [the traffic ban could be extended to College Green](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/plans-close-college-green-cars-6540314). Article continues below **READ MORE: [Park users feel 'penalised' as parking charges at beauty spots set to start](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/park-users-feel-penalised-parking-6527924)** The consultation states that buses, taxis, motorcycles, bikes and HGVs would still able to access the [city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre) area. Zoe Banks Gross, head of partnerships and public affairs for the south of England at Sustrans, has now spoken out in support of the changes. ‌ Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. You can check out at any time. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice) [Join us on WhatsApp](https://chat.whatsapp.com/JwmceTjpWjYACrvdGPRfyJ) She said: “Sustrans supports the proposed changes to College Green and Park Street in the consultation on changes to the Number 2 bus route. "The re-allocation of road space with improvements for pedestrians will make the space easier and more enjoyable for walking and cycling. This will improve safety as well as air quality in the area and help Bristol meet its goal to be carbon neutral by 2030. "Creating a space which allows for public transport as well as flows of people travelling actively will enhance this high street. This vital economic corridor could also see more footfall as a result of these changes.” Article continues below As part of the changes, the left-turn from Canons Road to College Green would be removed so the pedestrian crossing island could be widened. A bus gate would be created at the top of Park Street and Berkeley Avenue would close to general traffic, with proposed new bus stops being installed at the top of Jacob Wells Road as well. ‌ The consultation states that Park Street Avenue could be closed at both ends to stop rat running between Park Row and Park Street and to provide the opportunity for public space. A widened footway on the east side of Park Street would be made, it continues, and parking moved to the west side of the street to make conditions safer for cyclists travelling down Park Street. ‌ However, as Park Street is seen as a "pivotal section" of the number 2 bus route, a few alternative options are being proposed including installing a bus gate only restricting traffic inbound from the north or from the south. _You can express your views on the proposed changes on the TravelWest website [here](https://travelwest.info/projects/a37-a4018-transport-corridor). The consultation closes on Friday (January 28)._ **To keep up to date with latest Bristol news, and discuss thoughts with other residents, join our Bristol City Centre community group on Facebook [here](https://www.facebook.com/groups/420188526226115). Kent/Bristol Live) More than 140,000 fines have been issued in the space of 14 months as a result of the Bristol Bridge closure. ‌ Figures obtained by _BristolLive_ via a Freedom of Information request show that 141,045 fines have been issued since enforcement of the bus gate started in November 2020. ‌ This means that, on average, more than 10,000 fines are being handed out a month as a result of the scheme - more than 300 a day. Article continues below **READ MORE: [Driver's Bristol Bus Gate fine quashed because warning signs 'inadequate'](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/drivers-bristol-bus-gate-fine-5742169)** The [trial closure of the bridge and some nearby routes](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-bridge-traffic-ban-made-5619870) to most [traffic](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/traffic-travel) was made permanent last July, with [£1.6m raised in the nine months to July after 81,000 fines](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/exclusive-bristol-bridge-closure-results-5656948) were handed out. The latest figures - released this week by [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council)- show that a total of 141,045 fines have now been issued, taking its total value to £3.4m. ‌ Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. You can check out at any time. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice) [Join us on WhatsApp](https://chat.whatsapp.com/JwmceTjpWjYACrvdGPRfyJ) This is the total value for PCN issued in the period, irrespective of whether they have been paid, appealed or not paid. **_What do you think about this story? Let us know in the comments below._** The closure has banned general traffic from Bristol Bridge; Baldwin Street between St Augustine’s Parade and Marsh Street; Baldwin Street to High Street; and Union Street's left turn onto Rupert Street. Article continues below Buses, solo motorcycles, taxis and cycles are given priority under the order. The camera on Victoria Street is the one to have issued the most penalty charge notices (PCNs), with 47,656 fines issued. It is followed by the one on Baldwin Street with the High Street junction, which has handed out 41,892 PCNs. ‌ The one on Baldwin Street with the Marsh Street junction has issued 26,268, while the one on Baldwin Street with Broad Quay has handed out 18,087. On the other hand, the camera on Union Street to The Haymarket has issued the lowest number of fines (7,142). ‌ The figures also show that, on average, more fines are now being issued per month than at the start of the bus gate enforcement, when the average was 9,000 fines a month. Bristol City Council said in a statement: “Giving permanent priority to buses, cyclists and pedestrians over Bristol Bridge has reduced traffic in the central area of the city and improved bus punctuality and journey times, without causing significant problems elsewhere on the network. "The changes are helping to improve air quality and making it easier for people to catch the bus, walk and cycle in the city centre. ‌ “The scheme has been well publicised, and we have even installed larger signs in the area to make it even clearer for motorists that the bridge is closed to private vehicles. "An initial period of soft enforcement, where we issued warnings rather than fines, was also designed to give motorists time to get used to the new restrictions. Fines are issued to vehicles that don’t comply with this. “We continue to monitor the measures and will consider additional physical changes to help emphasise the new road layout, such as red road surfacing in the bus lanes.” Last August, a woman who was given a ticket for driving through the new city centre bus gate [had her fine quashed because the signs warning her](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/drivers-bristol-bus-gate-fine-5742169) about it weren’t good enough. Following the adjudication by a fines tribunal, Bristol City Council painted more warnings on the road and created lanes telling drivers that they were not allowed to go through the Baldwin Street junction at the side of Bristol Bridge. The measures were brought in at the start of August 2020, and were warned about with a mixture of semi-permanent and temporary signs, because it was a trial period. The Penalty Charge for a bus lane contravention is £60, discounted by 50 per cent to £30 if paid within 14 days of issue. Last July, _BristolLive_ revealed the data [from the council's "decision report",](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-bridge-traffic-ban-most-5633862) which showed 61 per cent of the 865 responses were in opposition to the scheme. In the weeks after the trial came into force, 3,574 people signed a [petition](https://www.change.org/p/the-mayor-of-bristol-marvin-rees-reverse-the-decision-to-close-bristol-bridge-baldwin-st-access-to-the-city-centre) calling for the scheme to be reversed, citing the impact on local businesses. This triggered a [counter-petition](https://www.change.org/p/b-keep-bristol-bridge-closed-to-car-traffic-and-support-a-car-free-healthy-city-centre) signed by 1,425 supporters of a "car-free healthy city centre". Hamid Parast, who owned Centre Cafe Lounge on Baldwin Street, claimed the scheme caused difficulties for deliveries, citing this as [one of the reasons for the cafe's closure](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/food-drink/complete-disaster-causes-bristol-cafe-5604539). But there has also been praise from Baldwin Street businesses. Brewdog bar, Oowee takeaway and Five Grains cafe spoke about how the trial had [created a more enjoyable environment for customers](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/shopping/businesses-baffled-bristol-area-ranked-5602350) and made it easier for cyclists to deliver food from the street's businesses. _**To keep up
