Bristol Palestine Alliance has organised the protest, calling for an immediate ceasefire. The protest is also calling on Bristolian Wael Arafat to end his six-week hunger strike for the Palestinian people. His adopted mother has been invited to the stage to read a speech on his behalf. Mr Arafat, originally from Gaza is currently in [Bath](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bath-and-north-east-somerset) hospital following a hunger strike provoked by an Israeli air strike on his home on October 22 resulting in the deaths of several members of his family. Neighbourhood](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article8796812.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/1_Ebln-Bus-Gate.jpg) View 2 Images How a bus gate might look in the planned East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood(Image: Bristol City Council) Bristol City Council has begun consulting the public again on its plans for an East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood. The plans involve new bus gates, bollards and one-way systems to prevent drivers from taking shortcuts through residential streets. ‌ Plans for a liveable neighbourhood, covering Barton Hill, Redfield and St George, have long been discussed. But the new consultation marks a key step forward in getting a pilot up and running. Members of the public can comment on the plans in support, or object to them. ‌ Some residential streets in the area are plagued by commuters trying to avoid congestion on nearby main routes into the centre, such as Church Road. However some drivers and local residents are opposing the plans, as their journeys will become longer. ‌ **Read more: [Supporters of Bristol liveable neighbourhood plan say changes have ‘plenty of fans’](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/supporters-bristol-liveable-neighbourhood-plan-8872971)** **Read more: [South Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood progresses as work begins to draw up plans](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/south-bristol-liveable-neighbourhood-progresses-8956362)** In [consultation documents](https://www.ask.bristol.gov.uk/east-bristol-liveable-neighbourhood-tro), a council spokesperson said: “Although motorised traffic would be prevented from travelling through the liveable neighbourhood, drivers would still have easy access to all homes and businesses by entering and exiting from main distributor roads. ‌ Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. You can check out at any time. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice) [Join us on WhatsApp](https://chat.whatsapp.com/JwmceTjpWjYACrvdGPRfyJ) “Emergency service vehicles will have exemptions to enable access through the liveable neighbourhood. It is expected that lower traffic volumes and exemptions will make it easier and quicker for emergency services to reach their destinations.” ![Image 3](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9063841.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Ebln-Jan-24-Map.jpg) View 2 Images A map showing all the proposed changes(Image: Bristol City Council) Bus gates block access at certain parts of the road network to general traffic, while keeping access for buses, taxis, bicycles, motorbikes, and public service vehicles. Exemptions would be made for families living in the area who have children with special needs or disabilities, as well as carers attending residents living in the area, and disabled residents with blue badges. ‌ Bollards and planters will also be used on certain roads to block motor vehicles. These are sometimes known as “modal filters” and “pocket parks”, and still maintain access for people walking or cycling. New double yellow lines will be painted on some roads to clamp down on problem parking. [_**Try BristolLive Premium for FREE with no ads and new features**_](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/try-bristollive-premium-free-no-8958271) The public consultation runs until February 20. Consultation documents setting out the reasons behind the scheme were translated into Arabic, Pashto, Polish, Somali and Urdu, and are available on the [council’s website](https://www.ask.bristol.gov.uk/east-bristol-liveable-neighbourhood-tro). It’s still unclear when exactly the council plans to roll out the liveable neighbourhood pilot. Article continues below The spokesperson added: “The overall aim of the East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood is to reduce motorised traffic, and in doing so, reduce air pollution, noise pollution and road accidents. [This would] create quieter and safer streets where residents may feel more comfortable to walk, cycle or wheel when making local journeys — encouraging more to leave their car at home.” Follow Bristol mayor [Marvin Rees](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/marvin-rees) remarked in his annual State of the City address in October 2021 how he sought to prohibit private cars from Park Street which had “the potential to reinvent public realm up to the Triangle and remove rat-runs from the Downs.” ‌ In the same speech, he invited people to comment on a consultation into transport changes along the number 2 bus route, which appeared to show a traffic ban could be extended to College Green. The consultation stated that buses, taxis, motorcycles, bikes and HGVs would still be able to access the city centre area. ‌ Beyond the drop-in information sessions and online presentations in December 2021 and January 2022, there have been no further updates about the consultation published by Travelwest. When Bristol Live approached [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) for an update, we received no official statement. Article continues below **READ MORE - [YouTuber visits 'smelly' Bristol car park to see if it's really that bad](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/youtuber-visits-smelly-bristol-car-9133681)** **READ MORE - ['Backlog' of Bristol CAZ appeals after council admits wording was wrong](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/backlog-bristol-caz-appeals-after-9104752)** Looking back on the plans, which were unveiled before the implementation of the Clean Air Zone, they saw radical changes that sought to ease congestion in [Bristol city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre) and encourage residents to use public transport or bicycles. As part of the proposed changes, the left-turn from Canons Road to College Green would be removed so the pedestrian crossing island could be widened. ‌ [![Image 8: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Less traffic would allow us to expand the public space available on Park Street and help increase its status as a destination within the city. "The College Green/Canons Road/St Augustines Parade junction would be remodelled to account for the left turn from Canons Road being removed. Responses to the previous engagement asked us to improve pedestrian facilities by reallocating road space at this junction. "We are proposing an improved crossing and waiting area as the numbers of pedestrians and cyclists is extremely high." Article continues below Proposals sought to create a bus gate at the top of Park Street and Berkeley Avenue would close to general traffic, with proposed new bus stops being installed at the top of Jacob Wells Road as well. It continues: "We were also asked to consider removing car traffic from Park Street to make it easier for buses and to reduce pollution and enable cyclists and pedestrians to have a more pleasant journey. "The bus gate at the top of Park Street would give priority to public transport, giving buses faster and more reliable access from and to the central area." ![Image 9: How the consultation sough to change College Green](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article6540761.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_College-Green-changesJPG.jpg) View 3 Images How the consultation sough to change College Green ‌ The consultation states that Park Street Avenue could be closed at both ends to stop rat running between Park Row and Park Street and to provide the opportunity for public space. A widened footway on the east side of Park Street would be made, it continues, and parking moved to the west side of the street to make conditions safer for cyclists travelling down Park Street. While Park Street is seen as a "pivotal section" of the number 2 bus route, a few alternative options were proposed including installing a bus gate only restricting traffic inbound from the north or from the south. Parking would be removed along Queens Road to allow for a segregated cycle lane to be created. ‌ The cycle lane would continue from Queens Road and join the junction of Triangle West/Queens Road to allow cyclists to reach the new cycle lane on the west side of Queens Road at the top of Park Street. The consultation added they proposed to close Richmond Hill and Park Place to traffic at the junction with Queens Road to allow for more public space and landscaped areas. A new cycle lane along Queens Road from St Paul’s Road, past Queen’s Avenue, would be added, with that stretch of Queens Road becoming one-way on each direction. A new cycle lane would be installed over the Bristol Bridge, together with a cycle lane, continuous and new widened footways, with loading bays and disabled bays along the west side of Victoria Street. The consultation looked at the possible closure of Parrys Lane on the Down, remove parking along Roman Road and convert the road to a walking and cycling route. The consultation stated: "Proposed new 24 hour outbound bus lane on Whiteladies Road between Wellington Park and York Street. Article continues below ![Image 10](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article6540605.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_TriangleJPG.jpg) View 3 Images Proposed changes in the Triangle area as seen in 2022 "The new bus lane would allow buses to bypass queuing traffic on the approach to the Blackboy Hill junction, reducing delays to services and improving reliability. It is proposed to remove through traffic and parking from Roman Road and convert it to a cycling and walking route." Cork**](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/authors/tristan-cork/) Chief Reporter 05:00, 16 Mar 2024 ![Image 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article8796812.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/1_Ebln-Bus-Gate.jpg) View 2 Images How a bus gate might look in the planned East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood (Image: Bristol City Council) Bristol’s first ‘liveable neighbourhood’ has finally been given the go-ahead after more than two years of consultation and talking about the project. The plan will aim to reduce traffic, improve travel infrastructure and make it easier and nicer to walk or cycle around an area in east Bristol around the main A420 Church Road in [Barton Hill](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/barton-hill), parts of Redfield and[St George](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/st-george). ‌ The project[has been controversial](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/latest-controversial-liveable-neighbourhood-scheme-9063832) - with many residents in the area saying the council weren’t listening to their concerns, while others have [called for the council to go ahead](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/supporters-bristol-liveable-neighbourhood-plan-8872971)with the scheme. It will start now and run as a pilot at first, while transport chiefs monitor the effects of how they tinker with the road network. ‌ The liveable neighbourhood scheme will see traffic filters, traffic calming, one-way streets, pocket parks and bus gates placed in various spots around Barton Hill, St George and Redfield. After three rounds of consultation since January 2022, the city council has decided to press on with [the most recent proposed scheme](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/changes-made-bristol-liveable-neighbourhood-8796795) as a trial. Article continues below **Read next; [Delay to East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood due to Barton House evacuation](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/delay-east-bristol-liveable-neighbourhood-8956932)** **Read more: [Latest on controversial liveable neighbourhood scheme in east Bristol](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/latest-controversial-liveable-neighbourhood-scheme-9063832)** More than 1,300 people submitted comments to support or object to what is planned, with council highways bosses working with residents, community groups, businesses and schools to design a range of measures to make this part of East Bristol more ‘liveable’. Supporters of the scheme say while it doesn’t mean there are no-go areas for people driving vehicles, it makes most journeys slightly longer, and is aimed at encouraging people to walk or cycle instead of drive. At the same time, the idea is that the area will become nicer to walk or cycle in. ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) Council transport chief Cllr Don Alexander said he was ‘delighted’ they were moving forward with the East Bristol pilot. “We’re aiming to deliver a safe, healthy, inclusive, and attractive environment where everyone can breathe clean air, have access to better quality green spaces, and feel a part of their community,” he said. ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9063841.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Ebln-Jan-24-Map.jpg) View 2 Images (Image: Bristol City Council) “To do this we need to change the layout of some local roads to make them safer and to discourage drivers using them as shortcuts. Elsewhere, this has been shown to boost active travel in neighbourhoods, reducing traffic and congestion on the roads, which brings with it all the health benefits of getting exercise and feeling a part of your community. Article continues below “It’s an exciting project and I am looking forward to seeing how the trial progresses, particularly with initial work underway on the [South Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood pilot](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/south-bristol-liveable-neighbourhood-progresses-8956362),” he added. If the pilot scheme is deemed successful, the trial measures would be replaced with permanent infrastructure that would also include extra street lighting, new crossings with traffic signals, sections of cycle track and street trees. The trial scheme will be installed later this year, after the council has put the job out to tender. In the meantime, 15 cycle hangars are being installed in 14 streets across the area, with the first four going in next week on Holmes Street, Avonvale Road, Victoria Avenue/Witchell Road and Diamond Road. The [South Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood pilot](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/south-bristol-liveable-neighbourhood-progresses-8956362) will see a larger area involved, stretching right from [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster) Bridge and Windmill Hill to Ashton Gate Stadium and take in Parson Street Station and Ashton Vale too. Bristol City Council) A new 'bus gate' in Bristol has resulted in drivers being fined more than £500,000 since enforcement began at the start of 2024. The bus gate on Cumberland Road has issued more than 22,000 penalty charge notices from January 2 to March 19, raising a whopping £513,369 for [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council). ‌ The gate has faced serious backlash from residents and locals who say it is damaging to the local economy. The gate prohibits any vehicles other than buses, cycles, taxis and motorcycles to enter [the city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre) via Cumberland Road. ‌ Some drivers have even blamed Google Maps for showing Cumberland Road as the [fastest route into town](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/traffic-travel). However, using the route and going through the bus gate will land drivers with a fine. In the heart of the city, camera-enforced bus gates are also in place on Bristol Bridge and at the entrance of Baldwin Street from the centre. These bus gates form part of the council's Bristol Transport Strategy and aim to reduce traffic and therefore vehicle emissions in a bid to help meet air quality and 2030 climate goals. To reach a carbon neutral status by 2030, 90 percent of cars must be electric and car journeys across Bristol must be reduced by 40 percent. Mar 2024 ![Image 7: No caption](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9197676.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/1_yellow-brick-road-3jpg.jpg) View 2 Images Residents are unhappy at the latest addition to Clevedon seafront(Image: Save our Seafront) North Somerset Council is set to spend nearly £500,000 to reverse most of the controversial "yellow brick road" scheme along Clevedon's seafront. The scheme sparked outrage when it replaced much-loved sea-view parking with a cycle lane, odd wiggly lines, and a buff road surface likened to the "yellow brick road" from the Wizard of Oz. ‌ After the 2023 local elections, new council leader Mike Bell pledged to fully review the contentious scheme. The council has now unanimously agreed to spend £425k to undo many of the scheme's most disliked features, a decision that locals have welcomed. ‌ At a council meeting on March 27, Hannah Young, the council's executive member for highways and transport, said: "The most difficult process in many ways has been looking at how we can move forward with the changes given the very very difficult financial position the council finds itself in, alongside councils across the country." Article continues below **READ MORE: [The Bristol nightlife of yesteryear that we all miss](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/history/bristol-nightlife-yesteryear-miss-7063388)** **READ MORE: [Candidate posting election leaflet has finger bitten off by dog](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/candidate-posting-election-leaflet-finger-9197498)** Under the plans — which she stressed were “not the absolutely finalised version” — much of the sea-facing parking on The Beach will be restored under the plan, the wavy lines, two-way cycle lane, and most of the yellow buff will be removed. The one-way system and 20mph speed limit will remain, and there will be a single contraflow cycle lane installed instead. ‌ [![Image 8: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Put your skills to the test. Whether you love word games, tricky cryptic crosswords, Sudoku, or our other brain teasers, you'll find a new favourite today! Play Now](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games/) The move has been welcomed by people in the town affected by the scheme. Cathy Hawkins, a founding member of the “save out seafront” campaign, said: “It just shows that if you fight to change something, it can be changed.” But she urged councillors to think again about installing a contraflow cycle lane. She warned: “Having to look both ways both for cars and for cyclists coming down the hill quite fast is an accident waiting to happen.” ![Image 9: A satellite image of Clevedon seafront, with the scheme clearly visible](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9197675.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_clevedonseafrontpng.png) View 2 Images A satellite image of Clevedon seafront, with the scheme clearly visible(Image: Google Maps) Article continues below Malcolm Simmonds, who has run Beach Pottery on the road for almost 40 years, thanked Ms Young for meeting with locals and working on the changes. He said the scheme has caused “chaos,” leading to people speeding on the road and people blocking the loading bays “essential” for his business. Mr Bell said: “This partnership administration believes in trying to do things with the community, not to the community. When we get things wrong we will hold our hands up and recognise that and try and put it right.” Michael Pryke (Clevedon Walton, Conservative) said he had some reservations about what was proposed but councillors needed to compromise. He said: “Clevedon needs a good news story and to finally be able to draw a line under this entire matter and this is what this report does today.” Article continues below But he said he had concerns over how the council was footing the bill of the project. He said: “Clevedon’s slipway, which is where this money was going to go, is now facing a lack of funding when it needs some serious TLC.” £50k which was to be spent on repairing the slipway will now instead be spent on the changes to the beach. Other sources of funding for the works include another unallocated £21k from the Great Lakes project, along with section 106 money from developers and local transport plan funding. The council is also taking £153k out of its capital and revenue reserves. Work on the seafront could start in the autumn, in order to avoid disrupting the seaside town in the summer, and it could be completed by the end of the year. the B3135 Cliff Road(Image: Sedgemoor District Council) The main road running through Cheddar Gorge could close to traffic on certain days to "enhance the visitor experience". Hikers, climbers and cyclists have long visited the Somerset beauty spot, which is about 50 minutes from Bristol, to take in the magnificent scenery among the limestone cliffs. Article continues below A trial scheme is now making progress to temporarily close the B3135 Cliff Road on one day a month, banning vehicles but maintaining access for [cyclists](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cycling), pedestrians and horse riders. The National Landscape Team has used funding from Defra to explore the idea to open up the road to a wider variety of users, [Somerset Live reports.](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/news/somerset-news/traffic-free-sundays-cheddar-gorge-9204413) Article continues below [](https://popup.taboola.com/en/?template=colorbox&utm_source=tmg-bristolpost&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=thumbnails-mid-1x1:Mid%20Article%20Thumbnails%20Outstream:)[](https://popup.taboola.com/en/?template=colorbox&utm_source=tmg-bristolpost&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=thumbnails-mid-1x1:Mid%20Article%20Thumbnails%20Outstream:) [](https://cos-rd.com/18/12457)[Amazon’s Worst Nightmare: Clever Trick Causing Many to Cancel Prime in 2025 Online Shopping Tools | [Sponsored](https://popup.taboola.com/en/?template=colorbox&utm_source=tmg-bristolpost&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=thumbnails-mid-1x1:Mid%20Article%20Thumbnails%20Outstream:)[Sponsored](https://popup.taboola.com/en/?template=colorbox&utm_source=tmg-bristolpost&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=thumbnails-mid-1x1:Mid%20Article%20Thumbnails%20Outstream:) Learn More](https://cos-rd.com/18/12457 "Amazon’s Worst Nightmare: Clever Trick Causing Many to Cancel Prime in 2025") Undo The results of a six-week public consultation on the idea have now been published, on behalf of the Mendip Hills National Landscape team, with Sunday coming out as the most popular choice. The new [report](https://mendiphills-nl.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/FINAL-Cheddar-Gorge-for-Everyone-Consultatio-Report-202403.pdf)explains: "The team is bringing forward proposals to temporarily close Cheddar Gorge to vehicular traffic, initially once a month, through an Experimental Traffic Regulation Order (ETRO). [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) There have been complaints about antisocial driving [ruining the experience of visiting the Gorge in recent years](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/cheddar-gorge-entirely-closed-police-1097817), with police even resorting to closing it on a couple of occasions as a result. The National Landscape Team received more than 1,700 responses to the consultation, with more than 80 per cent agreeing that the Gorge could be more accessible for pedestrians, cyclists, and other non-vehicular visitors. The majority of respondents (71 per cent) said they wanted to see the road closed on a Sunday, but Saturday was also a popular choice with 43 per cent selecting it. Seventeen per cent of respondents were not in favour of the road closure. The report said that having reviewed the feedback, the recommendation is for the road closure to begin initially all day on a Sunday, once a month. Around half of people who responded (48 per cent) said they would enjoy a traffic-free environment, but there was strong interest from rambling groups (47 per cent), cycling groups (46 per cent) and families (45 per cent) to use the Gorge on traffic-free days. Additionally, a third of respondents said they would like to see live music events held there and a quarter selected theatre performances. Article continues below 138205441690 Jim Hardcastle, manager of the Mendip Hills National Landscape Team, said: “We have received many comments expressing support from those who would be more likely to visit the Gorge on traffic free days to enjoy the beauty and tranquillity of the area. There were some respondents who raised valuable and interesting points which we will carefully consider. "These include the speed at which cyclists may come down the Gorge, the impact on local businesses, the provision of parking and space for vehicles to turn around, and concerns about the length of the diversion route and impact on other roads nearby. We are confident that we can take these concerns into account when deciding on the next steps in the process. “We are excited to take this project into the next phase, and look forward to improving this picturesque location by opening it up to a wider range of visitors. Over the next few months we will be working with partners and the Highway Authority to decide on the best options. Look out for updates from us later in the year.” Article continues below An Experimental Traffic Regulation Order trials changes in road usage patterns, enabling local bodies to test how effective these changes are in managing traffic, enhancing road safety and improving the environment. Businesses in Cheddar and the car parks at either end of Cheddar Gorge would remain open as usual during the order. Jim added: “There has also been some feedback that covers issues outside the scope of the temporary road closure. These include road improvements, support for local businesses and improved public transport. While these are out of our direct control, we appreciate this feedback being raised with us and will share it with partners who are well placed to respond.” Follow Bristol Live: * https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/brist: How cycling around Bristol could become safer after upcoming local elections Plans include new bike lanes along bridges over the River Avon, and 20mph speed limits in many parts of the city ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 05:00, 24 Apr 2024 A quarter of Bristolians cycle around the city at least once a week, on routes ranging from segregated bike paths to four-lane main roads. And ahead of the upcoming local elections, politicians from each of the big parties have promised to make cycling in Bristol safer. ‌ The promises include new bike lanes along bridges over the River Avon, 20mph speed limits on many roads, and a faster roll-out of bicycle hangars. Several residential side streets in two parts of Bristol could also see new bollards, to block drivers from using them as rat runs. ‌ Four politicians from each of the main parties spoke to cycling campaigners in Queen Square on Saturday, April 20, after the Kidical Mass Ride in Bristol. The [protest ride](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cglvg0lkergo#:~:text=A%20group%20of%20cyclists%20have,Bath%20and%20Bridgwater%20in%20Somerset.) saw many families with children cycle through the city centre, showing the strength of demand for safer routes. Article continues below **Read more:**[How transport and getting around Bristol could change from next month](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/how-transport-getting-around-bristol-9239460) **Read more:**[Socialists standing in Bristol local elections say main parties are ‘voice of big business’](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/socialists-standing-bristol-local-elections-9240240) [Labour](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/labour-party) Councillor Don Alexander, cabinet member for transport, said: “We’re just finishing now the [Old Market gap](https://www.bristol247.com/news-and-features/news/work-begin-complete-old-market-gap/). Along with the Old Market quietway and Victoria Street, it will complete the cycling infrastructure from the Bristol to [Bath](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bath-and-north-east-somerset) Railway Path through to the centre and down to Temple Meads, which will be a product of many, many years of work. ‌ We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) “The next thing we’ve got planned are [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster) Bridges and Bath Bridges, where designs are being worked up for active travel infrastructure. Our repairs of bridges across the New Cut have shown that we need to reactivate the plan for a new cycling and walking bridge across the New Cut.” Other plans include [relocating the cycling centre](https://www.bristol247.com/news-and-features/news/new-14m-cycling-centre-planned-for-lawrence-weston/) from South Bristol to make way for new apartments, and two liveable neighbourhood schemes, which will clamp down on drivers using residential side streets as cut-throughs to avoid main roads. Cllr Alexander added: “Let’s not forget training. Our Family Cycling Centre is having to move from its temporary site in [Hengrove](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/hengrove), so we’re setting aside £13 million for a new one in Lawrence Weston, which will be a lot better. That’s now in the planning stages. I’m very pleased to host that in my ward, it just so happens that that’s where there was a site, I promise you. Article continues below “More important than any of these specific schemes is the work of reimagining public space and what it could be. It doesn’t have to be what it always has been, primarily for cars, be they parked or moving. There are loads of other possibilities. “That’s where the [East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristols-first-liveable-neighbourhood-finally-9169812), for me, is so important, because it gives communities a space to discuss what could happen to their streets and the other things that could go in there that would be great for their health, active travel, and the planet, with sustainable drainage, cycle parking and street trees. “We will be moving to the trial stage in July or August, we hope. We’re also working on the [South Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/south-bristol-liveable-neighbourhood-progresses-8956362), and I’ve had requests from a number of other areas and I’m really delighted to have those requests, because I’m keen that we’re going to move on those as soon as we have the resources.” ‌ Greens said they would ensure all new cycle lanes meet national guidelines, and have in opposition successfully led to several changes benefiting people cycling and walking. This includes opposing plans to reopen a road to cars which was blocked off during the pandemic. Green Cllr Carla Denyer, co-leader of the national Green Party and MP candidate for Bristol Central, said: “Most people would agree that the government’s job, probably above all else, is to keep its people safe. And yet somehow, cycling and walking facilities to keep people safe, end up Cinderella-like, at the bottom of everybody’s to-do lists. “At the Green Party, we do things differently. Your Green Party councillors brought a motion to [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) a few months ago, about reducing the number of serious injuries and worse to zero in Bristol. Thanks to the hard work of our transport and active travel lead, David Wilcox, it has passed. ‌ “[That motion](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/calls-safer-roads-over-100-8590089) included a line that all new walking and cycling routes in Bristol must be LTN 1/20 compliant. What that means is that journeys will be safer for pedestrians, wheelchair users, mobility scooter users and cyclists of all ages.” LTN 1/20 refers to the strict guidelines setting out how new cycle lanes should be built, and are held up as the gold standard. This includes making cycle lanes wide enough, and making infrastructure feel safe to use, rather than just a painted lane on a busy main road. Cllr Denyer added: “There are also some concrete changes that have happened across the city that you might have already seen that David also helped make happen, like the bollards on Bristol Bridge that stop drivers using the cycle track. Over the last eight years, we’ve also been the ones stopping the council from backsliding on some measures on sustainable travel. ‌ “We stopped the mayor from reopening University Road just off the Triangle, after it had been successfully pedestrianised a few years earlier. And again led by David, we campaigned for extra roads to be made 20mph. But unfortunately we were blocked on that by both the mayor’s office and the Conservative police and crime commissioner. “We are, at the moment, limited on what we can do, because for now the Green councillors sit on the opposition benches. However, there is a local election coming up, so if you want that to change, you know what to do.” The Tories called for more cycling routes between different suburbs, and complained that currently most routes just head into the city centre. They also said cyclists need safer places to store their bicycles near bus stops or train stations, highlighting the problem of bike theft. Cllr Mark Weston, leader of the Conservative group, said: “Because things are more dispersed for us in the suburbs, it’s actually about having the connectivity between the modes of travel. For us the priorities we want to see are how do you cycle, safely store your bike, and then use either trains or buses to travel on. “Because we’re so dispersed, and the [Conservatives](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/conservative-party) tend to represent suburban wards, our priorities are slightly different. We want to see safe travel around schools. We also want you to be able to drive — sorry, cycle to the bus stops or the train stations, store your bike and have a reasonable chance of it actually being there when you come back. “One of things that we’re very agitated about is it always seems to be about getting the cyclists to the city centre. Actually, it’s the interconnectivity, those radial routes that go from say Henbury and Brenty to Lawrence Weston or [Southmead](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/southmead) or [Horfield](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/horfield), they’re often ignored. But they’re the actual journeys that are being used in our communities.” The [Liberal Democrats](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/liberal-democrats) praised recent progress in improving infrastructure for people walking and cycling, but said this needs to happen much faster. Bike hangars were one example, allowing people with little space at home to safely store bicycles on the road. Liberal Democrat Cllr Andrew Varney said: “We’re doing a lot of good stuff in Bristol, but unfortunately it’s just too slow. We need to see more rapid progress, and that’s what the Liberal Democrats support. We’ve got about 160 schools in Bristol, and only 11 school streets, so we need to see a much faster rollout of that. “Another example is bike hangars, a fantastic idea as a lot of people don’t have a garden or rear access, they live in a flat, they don’t have somewhere to store a bicycle. A bike hangar takes the space of one car but it provides parking for six bicycles. We’ve got about 30. It’s progress, but it’s too slow. Article continues below “We’ve got about 1,200 kilometres of highway over Bristol, but only about 20 kilometres of really decent segregated cycling infrastructure. We need to do much better than that, and we need to improve it much more quickly.”

Bath(Image: Keir Cooper) A coach in [Bath](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/all-about/bath) was forced to spend half an hour making a “a three point turn in inches” on Saturday after heading down Sydney Road — which the council recently bollarded up as part of its liveable neighbourhood programme. ‌ It is one of [Bath and North East Somerset Council’s five new trial schemes](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/news/somerset-news/major-changes-busy-bath-junction-9016496), which aim to make residential roads safer and more pleasant routes for walking and cycling. The road’s junction with Warminster Road was [reworked in April](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/news/local-news/roadworks-hit-bath-road-latest-9189967) and bollards were installed as the road turns into Sydney Place to prevent rat running, forcing traffic to take the Beckford Road route around Sydney Gardens to get into the city centre. ‌ But when large vehicles do turn down the road, it poses a new problem for the road. Keir Cooper, who saw the stuck coach on Saturday, said: “It took him about half an hour to turn round (a three point turn in inches). Mills, could be transformed into a sustainable housing community Not all Bristol Live readers are happy to hear of plans for a [disused training centre that may be knocked down](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/disused-training-centre-could-transformed-9298026#comments-wrapper) to make way for a car-free, sustainable housing community. The Matrix Training Facility, located off The Crescent in Sea Mills, has been closed for several years. However, guardians have occupied and maintained the site, cultivating various areas with raised beds and pots. Our readers have been discussing the project in our [comments section](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/incoming/a-community-increased-communal-space-9312150#comments-wrapper). ‌ Tiny House Community Bristol (THCB), a registered Community Benefit Society, has designated a site and an adjacent car park for transformation into a co-housing community featuring homes around a communal courtyard garden. The site would provide space for 13 dwellings along with a community roundhouse and family accommodation. ‌ The applicants aim to incorporate growing spaces, establish landscaping, and plant trees. The site will not offer regular car parking spaces, but will feature a disabled parking bay, along with access and turning space for emergency services. Residents have raised concerns about the impact on the local area including refuse collection and parking. https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/brist: Disabled resident ‘having sleepless nights’ over Bristol liveable neighbourhood plan Traffic restrictions will be rolled out later this year to make the area safer for walking, cycling and wheeling ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 00:01, 31 May 2024 Updated 08:48, 31 May 2024 A disabled woman is “having sleepless nights” over plans for a liveable neighbourhood in parts of east Bristol. The plans include blocking access along a main avenue leading to her house, instead forcing residents to navigate a narrow side street which is “not viable” for large vehicles. ‌ The [East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood](https://eastbristolliveableneighbourhoods.commonplace.is/) is expected to launch as a trial later this year. The pilot will install new bollards, planters and bus gates to stop drivers from using residential roads to cut through the area covering Barton Hill, Redfield and St George. ‌ While some locals support the trial, due to the safety benefits of fewer cars driving past their homes, others are concerned that the restrictions will unfairly affect elderly and disabled people living in the area, as well as others who rely on driving, such as parents on the school run. Article continues below **Read more: [How disasters like extreme floods could hit Bristol cutting off power and water](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/how-disasters-like-extreme-floods-9313448)** **Read more: [Bristol's first 'liveable neighbourhood' finally given go-ahead](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristols-first-liveable-neighbourhood-finally-9169812)** Parts of the trial could be changed if and when [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) makes the scheme permanent, to iron out any particular issues. A local councillor said the bollards could be moved to different locations, if there are specific problems about accessibility for disabled people. ‌ Melissa Topping lives on Victoria Avenue, one of the main roads through the area, and is disabled. She relies on a wheelchair-accessible vehicle to get around, but is concerned that new planters will force her to drive down a narrow side road, Byron Street, to get to her house. She said: “Nobody is listening to me, nobody is giving me any answers. They’re basically putting a pole halfway down Victoria Avenue with a lock at the bottom of it, so Victoria Avenue is no longer going to be a road for any traffic, let alone through-traffic. “They’re saying that everything can come down Byron Street to get to this end of Victoria Avenue, which really is not a viable street for large vehicles. I myself have a large vehicle, and I wouldn’t even attempt to drive it down Byron Street. It’s too narrow, there’s a funny camber on it as well, and the visibility isn’t good. Article continues below “I usually drive up Church Road to turn right onto Avonvale Road, turn right onto Victoria Avenue and go straight down, with no problem. And that’s what all large vehicles do, for the end of Victoria Avenue. There aren’t any that try to come down Byron Street, it’s not worth it.” Ms Topping also raised concerns that a fire engine couldn’t navigate down Byron Street, due to its narrow width and parked cars alongside both sides. She also claimed bin men struggle to access the street, although one rubbish truck could be seen collecting bins shortly after the interview. ‌ She added: “I’ve spoken to the refuse men. They’ve said those roads are an absolute nightmare, Byron Street being the worst of all because it’s the smallest. They often have to park at the end, and the dustmen have to run up and get the bins. “I’m going to be left in a situation where I’m going to go out one day in my vehicle, come home and not be able to get home. Out of 10 houses that I know of at the end of my street, six houses are either elderly or disabled. That means only four of the houses can use active travel, if they wanted, the rest of us can’t. “The council isn’t taking any consideration of that at all. I’ve not had any answers to my questions. Apparently the reason they’re doing it is to stop rat runners. But in order for them to stop rat runners, what they’re doing is stopping residents from being able to get to where they need to go.” ‌ Ms Topping recently met with Green Councillor Barry Parsons, and a council officer from the project team, to discuss her concerns. But she said she previously felt patronised by some of the responses from the council to her questions. She added: “It’s upsetting. The anxiety that I’ve had since I found out about this has been through the roof. I’ve had lots of sleepless nights, and lots of people I know here have too. Everybody is very concerned. ‌ “They seem to think I’m confused. They want to come and ease my confusion. I’m not confused, I’m concerned. They have been very patronising. It’s not like there’s a congested stream of traffic through there that they need to stop. “I would like for it all to be completely scrapped, or at least for them to halt it, hold a proper consultation, meet residents, and find out actually what we want in the area and where the traffic calming is needed.” According to Cllr Parsons, who represents [Easton](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/easton), driving down Byron Street is “certainly possible with a large vehicle”, although he admitted the narrow side street is “tight and awkward”. He added that the liveable neighbourhood scheme could even make the area more accessible for people with disabilities. He said: “Melissa contacted me a few weeks ago with her concerns. Specifically her issues were about access as a disabled person. It’s something I really wanted to make sure we addressed. I arranged to meet Melissa in person with a member of the project team so that she could share her issues and we could talk about some possible steps and a way forward. “It’s important that this scheme should be as accessible as possible. We should be designing these schemes with accessibility in mind, right from the start. They have a lot of potential to make our streets more accessible for disabled people, not less. “We all agree that Byron Street is tight, no question about it. But it’s certainly possible to access Byron Street with a large vehicle. It’s tight and it can be awkward, but it’s certainly possible.” The East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood plan is the first of its kind in Bristol. Another is in the early stages of planning for parts of [Bedminster, Ashton Gate and Totterdown](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/south-bristol-liveable-neighbourhood-progresses-8956362), which could potentially also be replicated in other parts of the city. Similar schemes have been rolled out elsewhere in the country, sometimes called “low traffic neighbourhoods” instead, such as in [Bath](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bath-and-north-east-somerset). The aim is to make travelling by walking, cycling or wheeling more attractive than driving cars, to help cut congestion, pollution and road accidents. Cllr Parsons added: “With all the elements of it, like the modal filters, they’re movable. When the trial comes in, we can have a look about how the different traffic cells are actually working. It might be that we need to move some of those. None of this stuff is set in stone. **Sign up to receive daily news updates and breaking news alerts straight to your inbox for free **[here](https://bit.ly/3r1T6AI)**.** “The point of the trial is we can check these things out and see how they work in practice. It might be possible to move that traffic filter somewhere else, and provide some alternative access point for Melissa. We’ve asked the project team to go away and look at that. “It’s supposed to make travelling by car a little bit less convenient compared to travelling by foot, wheelchair, bike or mobility scooter. It’s encouraging people to use alternatives to the car. And there’s a lot of things that make it difficult to get around with the way our streets are designed currently. “There’s pavements without dropped kerbs, and pavements with the surface damaged can make it really difficult for disabled people. There’s vehicles parked on the pavements, bins and fly-tipping blocking the pavement. Melissa is going to help us identify big priorities for opportunities and improvements, so we can make the streets more accessible.” Once the trial is finally rolled out, local residents can help monitor its impacts and provide feedback to the council. Cllr Parsons said he and other local councillors in the area were keen to hear any other concerns about the scheme. He said: “There’s going to be citizen monitoring of this scheme, which will mean that members of the public are going to be able to get involved in overseeing how it’s actually working in practice. We think there’s going to be opportunities for people to get involved with things like traffic counting devices and hosting air quality monitoring equipment. “I think well-designed schemes like this are absolutely good for the community overall, and good for disabled people. This is a trial pilot scheme, and part of what’s being piloted is the ways the council can be responsive to residents, and how people can get involved and shape how it develops. Article continues below “As local ward councillors, we’re on board with this scheme, and we think it’s a good thing overall. But we’re really keen to hear from people where they have concerns, or about something they think hasn’t been considered, or deserves looking at again. It’s supposed to be a community conversation.”

Mopeds and taxis continue to defy traffic ban in Bristol city centre Three months after it was first reported, more than 50 reports have been made ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- 12:31, 04 Jun 2024 More than 50 drivers and riders have been reported for [breaking traffic rules](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/crime) in a [pedestrianisation zone](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/old-city-king-street-pedestrianised-7147136) in [Bristol](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/). Several roads in the Old City area of the city centre are closed to traffic at specific times except for loading and deliveries. ‌ The pedestrianisation scheme includes Clare Street, Corn Street, Marsh Street, Small Street, St Nicholas Street and St Stephen's Street. [Avon and Somerset Police](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/avon-and-somerset-constabulary) says other locations have seen offences, including in Wapping Wharf, Cotham and on the Gaol Ferry Bridge. ‌ In February, Bristol Live reported that [delivery riders were mainly to blame](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/delivery-riders-bristol-city-centre-9119819) for the offences, which saw 15 moped riders reported in one afternoon. Police confirmed at the time that it would be revisiting the area over the coming months. ‌ **READ MORE: [Town left with no banks wins fight for new banking hub](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/town-left-no-banks-wins-9321332)** **READ MORE: [Wannabe Mad Max driver loses car after dangerous tyre modification](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/wannabe-mad-max-driver-loses-9320576)** Over three months on, updates shared by the force’s Old City Neighbourhood Policing team have shown 59 Traffic Offence Reports were issued since February 26 and one arrest has been made. Twenty-two warnings were issued and a total of four vehicles were seized, including one moped and one motorbike, and that taxis were defying the traffic ban. ‌ On Monday February 26, 16 TORs were issued to mopeds riders. The following day, a further 11 TORs were issued to 'a mixture of taxi drivers and moped riders'. A vehicle was seized for having no insurance and an arrest was made. **Looking for Bristol Court & Crime top stories in one place?**[_**Sign up for our newsletter here**_](https://bit.ly/3NrDmOP). On Wednesday, March 27, three TORs and three warnings were issued to riders of mopeds. The police said in that update: “Speaking with local businesses in the area they state that the decrease in moped use in the area is enhancing their customers’ experience and welcome the positive action taken by police.” ‌ On Thursday, April 11, a moped rider rode their vehicle over Gaol Ferry Bridge and 'narrowly avoided members of the public'. The rider, who did not have insurance, had the moped seized and was issued with a TOR and a warning. In February 2024, the Old City Docks Neighbourhood Policing team updated its priorities for the area to include tackling driving offences within the area. Controversial bus gate makes council £1million in six months New figures show drivers have been fined 34,393 times for going through the bus gate ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ **Neil Shaw** Assistant Editor 08:33, 05 Jun 2024 Updated 08:36, 05 Jun 2024 Bristol City Council has made more than £1million in fines from a controversial bus gate in less than six months, new figures show. The council raked in the equivalent of about £7,400 per day from the bus gate on Cumberland Road in Bristol between January 1 and May 14. ‌ So far, there have been 34,393 fines issued to drivers passing through it. The bus gate prioritises public transport over private vehicles by only allowing buses, cycles, taxis and motorcycles to enter the central areas of the city using Cumberland Road. ‌ Penalty charge notices for driving through the bus gate cost £35, with some drivers blaming Google Maps for still showing that the fastest way to get into town is along Cumberland Road. According to figures released under a Freedom of Information request, income from the bus gate grossed 20 times more than any other in the city during the same period. ‌ In total, the Cumberland Road bus gate has generated £1,010,335 in fines. The revenue made from fines across all 19 bus gates in the city was £1.39million in total, the [BBC](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bbc) reports. The second-highest earning bus gate was Victoria Street (Bristol Bridge) at £59,105 and then Baldwin Street (Junction High Street) at £53,550. These figures were released after a local man claimed the gate was 'unlawful' and 'defective'. Matt Sanders, a graphic designer from Windmill Hill in Bristol, has spent months compiling evidence about the bus gate. ‌ He claims the signage goes against national regulations, and has urged [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) to make urgent changes, as well as refund drivers who have been fined - in a 150-page dossier. He has since sent a copy of the report to every councillor in the city. The council previously defended the scheme and said it installed 14 warning signs when it was only obliged to display two. It said the bus gate was installed to improve air quality and give priority to public transport. Bristol City Council said the bus gate on Cumberland Road was completely legal. “National government regulations only require councils to display two signs for a bus gate, but we have installed 14 signs in the area for this one alongside clear ‘bus gate’ road markings,” a spokesperson said. Article continues below “To give extra warning, an electronic sign was put in place for a month shortly after the bus gate was installed in September 2023. People who continued to drive through this bus gate in error were issued with warning letters as a reminder, before the first Penalty Charge Notices were issued four months later in January 2024. “All vehicles can still travel eastbound on Cumberland Road up to the bus gate, which means that the SS Great Britain and other nearby Spike Island attractions can still be accessed from both directions. “Motorists should always follow road signs, rather than sat navs/navigation devices. You would need to contact those route providers directly about their software. While councils are not required to install red road surfacing at bus gates, we have taken this step at the Cumberland Road bus gate to further enhance its visibility,” he added.

Horsefair(Image: Michael Lloyd Photography) Major plans for new bus lanes and cycle paths in Bristol’s city centre will include “removing traffic” from the area. Next month, new details will be revealed about the five ways how the city centre’s streets are about to radically change. ‌ Pedestrians and cyclists will be given much more space, while buses will be rerouted and taxis banned from certain roads. New bus lanes will ensure passengers spend less time stuck in congestion, making services more reliable. ‌ Transport bosses at [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) are expecting their plans, which will go out for public consultation next month, to be controversial. Councillors on the transport policy committee were updated about the city centre proposals on Thursday, July 11. Article continues below **Read more:**[Radical plans to transform Bristol city centre unveiled](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/radical-plans-transform-bristol-city-8627319) **Read more:**[‘Fairer prices needed’ as fares on trains cost three times more in South Bristol](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/fairer-prices-needed-fares-suburban-9406310) Adam Crowther, head of city transport, said: “The city centre proposals will be pretty transformative for the whole walking, cycling and bus network. You’ll pretty much end up with a fully segregated cycle network that goes all the way around the city centre and north, south, east and west, two or three different routes. ‌ Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. It also delivers a large amount of bus priority throughout the city centre, fully completing the anti-clockwise loop and other routes getting full bus priority. “If I take a scheme forward that nobody’s complaining about, I probably haven’t done my job properly because someone will always be losing something in a transport scheme. You’re always taking some space that’s committed to something, and using it for something else. There’s a limit to the amount of space and there’s always going to be challenges.” ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9411533.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_Ddp-Horsefair.jpg) View 3 Images How the Horsefair could look after the changes (Image: Bristol City Council) Article continues below Five separate business cases are being worked up for the city centre. These include building new segregated cycle routes and bus lanes along Temple Way, Bond Street and Newfoundland Circus; and improving the [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster) Bridges roundabout for buses, cyclists and pedestrians. General traffic will be banned from using Redcliffe Street, with a new bus gate installed on Redcliffe roundabout. Cars instead will be diverted up Phippen Street and St Thomas Street. Cars and taxis will also be banned from going down Union Street, while a new cycle lane will be built for people cycling uphill. The work will be paid for from a government grant called the City Region Sustainable Transport Settlement. The projects form part of a wider vision for the city centre, known as the [Development and Delivery Plan](https://www.bristol.gov.uk/residents/planning-and-building-regulations/planning-policy-and-guidance/supplementary-planning-documents-practice-notes-and-other-planning-guidance). This also includes pedestrianising the Horsefair and banning buses and taxis, as well as opening up the lanes and internal courtyards between streets in the Broadmead area, providing more connections north to south. ‌ ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9411536.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Ddp-Union-St.jpg) View 3 Images How Union Street could look after the changes (Image: Bristol City Council) The cycle lane along Temple Gate, which runs past the Holiday Inn near Temple Meads, is also planned to be improved, but under a separate project. Currently the lane stops abruptly, with an inconveniently placed rack of bike stands, followed by outdoor seating outside a restaurant and a narrow pavement. This building is expected to be demolished and replaced soon, as part of the Temple Quarter regeneration project. The replacement will be built further back from the road, creating more space for a proper bike lane to connect up to the existing one and the Clarence Road lane. Article continues below Similar plans nearby include new segregated cycle lanes along Temple Way, between the Old Market roundabout and the junction with the Friary and Victoria Street by the Ovo building. Another plan is for a signalised crossing across Temple Way, connecting cyclists on Avon Street through the BT building and onto Cheese Lane, before coming out by Castle Park. After the meeting, Green Councillor Ed Plowden, chair of the transport committee, said: “I am really excited about these far-reaching plans and look forward to having a city that ultimately works better for everyone. Improving these major transport routes for public transport and active travel means we will have realistic options for people who want to travel sustainably, as we look to remove as much carbon from our transport network as we can. “This summer we’ll be asking people who live, work, visit and travel through [Bristol city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre) to give us their views on proposals that will transform the area. From making Broadmead more welcoming and attractive, to preparing the way for the central element of a future rapid transit route, the plans would change how most people travel through the city Bristol's city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/major-plans-bus-lanes-cycle-9411529#comments-wrapper) have sparked a lively discussion amongst Bristol Live readers. The project, which includes new bus lanes and cycle paths, aims to "remove traffic" from key areas, leading to mixed opinions. Next month, the public will get a closer look at the proposals, which outline five major changes to the city's streets. Readers and residents have been actively sharing their thoughts in our [comments section](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/incoming/the-city-centre-isnt-your-9414056#comments-wrapper). ‌ The scheme aims to improve the experience for pedestrians and cyclists by allocating them more space. Additionally, buses will follow new routes, and taxis will face restrictions on certain roads. The introduction of new bus lanes is expected to cut down on congestion, leading to more punctual and dependable bus services. ‌ Bristol City Council's transport plans, set to go out for public consultation next month, are anticipated to be controversial. On July 11, councillors on the transport policy committee were briefed on the city centre proposals and stated they will looking to Bristol residents to give their their views on the proposals. 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9239456.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/1_20240403-175307.jpg) View 2 Images The project aims to reduce traffic on residential roads(Image: Alex Seabrook) Drivers will be stopped from taking shortcuts through many residential streets in South Bristol as part of a new Liveable Neighbourhood project. Bollards and planters will be installed in certain parts of [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster), Southville and Windmill Hill, to reduce traffic next to where people live. Article continues below Transport bosses at [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) say the changes would “create a better balance” between how streets are used, making them safer, quieter and less polluted. The project is the second one in the city, with a [similar scheme](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristols-first-liveable-neighbourhood-finally-9169812) planned for Barton Hill, Redfield and St George. Article continues below A new [public consultation](https://www.ask.bristol.gov.uk/hub-page/sbln) is giving locals the opportunity to have their say about what changes should be made to the roads across an area stretching from Ashton Vale to Totterdown. Close to the city centre, this part of Bristol has high demand for better walking and cycling routes. Article continues below 138205439166 **Read more:**[Cyclists raise concerns about plan for shared path along the Bristol Portway](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/cyclists-raise-concerns-plan-shared-9412044) **Read more:**[Major plans for bus lanes and cycle paths in Bristol city centre and ‘removing traffic’](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/major-plans-bus-lanes-cycle-9411529) Green Councillor Tony Dyer, council leader and representing Southville, said: “This project is about creating better neighbourhoods for everyone to live in. We want to cut down on rat-runs and through-traffic to create safer streets for our children and make it easier and more pleasant to walk and cycle. South Bristol Liveable Neighbourhoods represents a huge investment in the area, and we want everyone to have a say to help us develop the plans for the next stage.” Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) At the moment, some drivers are directed by sat navs and apps to take a shortcut through narrow residential streets, instead of following main roads. Driving from West Street to Winterstoke Road, for example, it’s quicker to cut through down Chessel Street, Garnet Street and onto Luckwell Road, than following the Parson Street gyratory. These sorts of shortcuts would be designed out of the road network. Drivers would still be able to access every street in the area by vehicle, although some might have to take slightly longer routes. ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9415076.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_South-Bristol-Liveable-Neighbourhood-map.jpg) View 2 Images The area covered by the South Bristol Liveable Neighbourhoods(Image: Bristol City Council ) Article continues below 138205441690 Other changes could include improving pedestrian crossings, planting more trees, installing more benches, and upgrading lighting. The council hopes that reducing traffic will encourage more people to walk, cycle or scoot around the area instead of travelling by car. This would help reduce air pollution and get more people exercising. The consultation will run until October 13, and includes online maps, surveys and drop-in events. People living in the area are invited to tell the council what they like and what they want to improve. Three drop-ins sessions are planned at: the Southville Centre, Beauley Road, on August 5 from 12pm to 6pm; the Chessel Centre, Chessel Street, on August 14 from 2.30pm to 6.30pm; and the Windmill Hill Community Centre, Vivian Street, on August 19 from 10am to 2pm. Article continues below An [interactive map](https://www.ask.bristol.gov.uk/south-bristol-liveable-neighbourhoods-engagement/maps/south-bristol-liveable-neighbourhoods-interactive-map) also shows where people have suggested changes. Many people, for example, have already asked for changes on East Street, where drivers frequently flout a ban on general traffic. East Street, one of the main shopping centres in Bedminster, is restricted to buses and loading vehicles. But little enforcement appears to take place, and the ban is often ignored. Cyclists are also directed to cycle against the flow of traffic on East Street, with no separation from buses and cars coming the other way. And the road is sometimes too narrow to cycle past a bus. One respondent said: “I cycle on the East Street contra-flow daily and have had many near misses. It is constantly used by vehicles that are not designated to drive on the road. Many of the buses and taxis do not adhere to the speed limits and do not make space for cyclists coming in the opposite direction. Article continues below “The road is too narrow at points to allow vehicles and cyclists to safely pass. The current system is dangerous and it is only a matter of time before there is a serious accident.” Another added: “Please install a bus gate. Cars regularly use this area as a cut-through and are often very aggressive when challenged.” North Street has also received a lot of comments. The street, which is the other main shopping centre in Bedminster, has many stretches with narrow pavements, two lanes of traffic and two rows of parked cars. Article continues below One respondent said: “North Street should be one of the most pleasant and inviting places to spend time in this area. But it’s not a comfortable place to walk or cycle, with narrow pavements, dangerous conflicts with fast cars, and barebones greenery.” Another added: “North Street should have a segregated cycle path. At the moment the heavy traffic, frequent junctions and amount of parked cars make it feel very unsafe. Restricting on-street parking would allow enough space for this and pavement widening.” The [East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristols-first-liveable-neighbourhood-finally-9169812) has proved controversial, and a trial is expected to launch this summer. Many people living in the area support the plans, particularly due to fears over road safety, speeding cars and frequent crashes; while others oppose them due to the increased lengths of their journeys in a car or van.
