https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/news-: 'A massive improvement'" as council takes aim at South Bristol rat-run traffic The new Liveable Neighbourhood project will see the installation of bollards and planters ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 05:01, 18 Jul 2024 The news that motorists in South Bristol will be stopped from [using residential streets as shortcuts](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/ban-through-traffic-make-south-9414390#comments-wrapper)has sparked a lively discussion by readers in our [comments section](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/a-massive-improvement-bristol-city-9417326#comments-wrapper). The new Liveable Neighbourhood project will see the installation of bollards and planters in specific areas of [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster), Southville, and Windmill Hill, with the aim of reducing traffic near homes. ‌ Bristol City Council's transport chiefs believe these changes will "create a better balance" in street usage, resulting in safer, quieter, and less polluted environments. This is the second such initiative in the city, with a similar plan in the pipeline for Barton Hill, Redfield, and St George. ‌ Residents across Bristol are being given the chance to voice their opinions on proposed changes to roads in an area spanning from Ashton Vale to Totterdown. This central part of the city, known for its proximity to the vibrant core of Bristol has a pressing need for better pedestrian and cycle-friendly routes. ‌ **READ MORE:**[**First look at Bristol's new Ritorno Lounge**](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/food-drink/gallery/first-look-bristols-new-ritorno-9417887) **READ MORE: [P](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/food-drink/bristol-pub-well-known-sunday-9416971)****[ub well-known for Sunday roasts stops serving food](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/food-drink/bristol-pub-well-known-sunday-9416971)** Commenter AdvisoryService101 says: “Would be a massive improvement to quality of the area, motorists using residential streets as rat runs is a blight and any improvement that brings back enjoyment for the locals is a big win-win.” ‌ Chiefchupachup disagrees: "Rat runs' are not a thing, nor are shortcuts. If a route is the quickest one to the destination then it is 'the route'. Closing more and more streets will only result in more congestion. One more thing, why are these 'liveable neighbourhoods' being forced onto the poorest parts of the city? It's even mentioned in the article that routes may be longer. So there you have it, a stealth tax on the poor.” GenericNickname agrees: “Aside from the money required to implement any changes, money that doesn't exist, there are so many issues with this I could write a book. Bollards and planters will take away valuable parking spaces. Bollards will get bent up quickly and the planters require maintenance. The rat runs will go quiet, but the traffic will now be bottlenecked, with idle car engines running. The cars that do go down these roads will need to travel longer distances to get there, expending fuel etc. Could go on and on.” HanhamHeights replies: “Let's look at the evidence from existing LTNs. Funding comes from specific government grants for sustainable transport, not general council budgets. The schemes maintain resident parking, any losses are minimal and offset by improved street environments. Costs are low, many areas use community-maintained planters, adding greenery. Contrary to fears, LTNs reduce overall traffic, about 15% of car trips usually disappear and people adapt, combine trips, or switch modes." ‌ "Despite concerns, LTNs see a net decrease in air pollution, even on boundary roads. Slight increases for some car trips, yes. But it encourages shorter trips by foot or bike, reducing overall mileage. Most report no significant impact on emergency service response times. After initial adjustment, many areas see increased footfall and spending. It's not perfect, but data shows LTNs generally improve neighbourhoods. Worth keeping an open mind and looking at results from other areas.” KaptainVon thinks: “On the face of it the benefits of reducing pollution are good. However, anything like this requires sensible implementation and given that successive councils in Bristol have a long history of implementing traffic policies that are far from sensible and have often led to increased pollution in residential areas. In fact, from what is reported, existing residents' vehicles are likely to be emitting more pollution just to reach their homes.” The Opinion believes: “A road is a road and as long as people are driving safely down a residential street and paying for that road with road tax, people should be able to drive wherever they need to. If people don't like cars going down the road, Here's two options: firstly move to where there isn't a public road by your house or secondly have the whole street pavemented so cars can't drive on it.” Article continues below AnyTony is optimistic: “Very happy to see this covering a large area. A couple of years ago it seemed like it might only cover Windmill Hill. Investment in such schemes will make a massive improvement for people living in this wide area, though we need to vastly improve public transport alongside and continue to reduce private vehicles, for example rolling out more RPZs with tougher rules on 2nd or even 3rd household vehicles. "It isn't a 'ban all vehicles' approach, it is just to rebalance things to make it fairer to everyone living in and using the areas. Yes, this will be a big change, but public & social health really can't continue being yoked to such excessive private vehicle usage (whether ICE or electric). So, very positive & I hope it garners much support.” **How do you feel about the new plan? Do you think it will improve Bristol? Have your say in our [comments section](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/a-massive-improvement-bristol-city-9417326#comments-wrapper).**
https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/contr: Controversial Bath LTN has 'eroded trust in politicians' 'If you chose the wrong place for intervention you cause harm and at times outright danger' ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- **John Wimperis** Local Democracy Reporter 10:40, 25 Jul 2024 The closure of a busy [Bath](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/all-about/bath) road to through traffic as a liveable neighbourhood has “eroded trust in politicians” and caused more congestion and pollution, a former local GP has warned councillors. ‌ Bollards were installed across Sydney Road where it becomes Sydney Place in April as part of Bath and North East Somerset Council ’s liveable neighbourhood programme, which aims to make the street “a safer and more pleasant walking and cycling route.” But the scheme has been controversial — with around 4,000 people singing a petition against it — and has even [been debated in Parliament](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/news/somerset-news/jacob-rees-mogg-calls-bath-9301485). ‌ Sydney Road locals attended Bath and North East Somerset Council ’s previous full meeting in May to praise the scheme as making their road “freed from the tyranny of the motor vehicle.” But at the council’s most recent full meeting on Thursday July 18, four people from surrounding and impacted areas warned it had done more harm than good. ‌ **READ MORE:****[I went to the stunning coastal village two hours from Bristol known as 'Little Switzerland'](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/whats-on/reviews/went-stunning-coastal-village-two-9433034)** **READ MORE:****[New Harbourside cafe at apartment block](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/new-harbourside-cafe-apartment-block-9432896)** Dr Ian Orpen, who lives in Bathampton and [was a GP in Bath for 30 years](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/news/somerset-news/long-serving-bath-gp-reflects-2978564), told the meeting: “The Sydney Road LTN has been an object lesson in how not to make changes to how lives are led.” ‌ He said: “It has further eroded trust in politicians. To be clear, I have no objection to liveable neighbourhoods as I have seen, where they have been thought through, they bring real benefit. Also, I see the administration’s ambition in tackling the climate emergency as laudable.” But he warned: “If you choose the wrong place for intervention you cause harm and at times outright danger. ‌ “To suggest that Sydney Road, which at the time of the trial carried one third of the traffic from the A36 into Bath is a rat run, does not stand up to scrutiny. It was designated a trunk road until declassified at the request of the council. This technicality does not alter how the road is seen or is used by the public. The disbenefits of the scheme should have been obvious without a trial, such as displaced traffic onto neighbouring roads, thereby generating rat runs, congestion, and increased pollution. “Delivering change always generates opposition. It is deeply unfortunate that the council chose to ignore the views of many whose lives would be affected by the proposal.” The scheme is [officially in place on a trial period](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/news/local-news/exeter-scraps-controversial-ltn-could-9350823), while a [consultation](https://beta.bathnes.gov.uk/sydneyroadETRO) is run and traffic data collected. Dr Orpen added that the trial was taking place [while major roadworks were happening on the A36](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/news/somerset-news/major-road-close-until-2025-9403646), lowering the amount of traffic on the road and impacting the validity of the trial data. ‌ Alan Morely, who lives near the bottom of North Road which joins the A36 just before Sydney Road, said: “As a result of the closure, we now have more traffic queueing in front of our houses, particularly during school runs.” He added that people on the road had not realised that closing Sydney Road was a possibility when the scheme was designed, so took no part in the design workshops. But now he warned: “Some residents have seen a significant increase in the number of emergency vehicles using sirens. Others perceive an increase in the average road speed going up North Road and we also see [traffic turning in Sydney Road](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/news/somerset-news/coach-gets-stuck-road-closed-9295618) — Kennet House had its post knocked over — and we see e-scooters going through the bollards into oncoming traffic.” ‌ He said: “In general, people are in favour of liveable neighbourhoods as most of us walk and some cycle everywhere within the city. However, we cannot disinvest the motorcar so any measures to reduce its impact should be for the benefit of the majority and minimise disruption to daily lives.” Neil McCabe added: “56 households on New Sydney Place undoubtedly benefit from the LTN — however 163 households on Darlington Street, Sydney Place, and Beckford Road will directly suffer from a 50% increase in traffic and consequent pollution.” A statement read out on behalf of Daniell Selwood, who lives on the edge of the Bathwick Estate but was unable to attend the meeting, said: “Near misses are happening the whole time because of the Sydney Road LTN. We see it daily. It is a near miss at the moment, it is not always going to be a near miss.” ‌ It added: “Their liveable neighbourhood has become our unliveable neighbourhood.” Sydney Road is part of Bath and North East Somerset Council’s programme of liveable neighbourhoods (also called low traffic neighbourhoods or LTNs) which they are rolling out. Three are permanently in place — two in Bath and one in Queen Charlton — while the Sydney Road scheme is still in its trial period. ‌ Supporters of the scheme have urged the council to make it permanent. Malcolm Robinson, who lives on the road, told the council meeting in May : “The Sydney Road LN creates a small safe space to move around without fear of being run down by a rat runner from Bathampton trying to get to Waitrose before it closes.” [Three more roads are set to be closed to through traffic as part of the liveable neighbourhood programme in early August](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/news/local-news/more-bath-roads-become-ltns-9406663), with bollards set to be installed on Winifred’s Lane at the top of Cavendish Road and on Catharine Place, along with a major overhaul of Gay Street between Queen Square and the Circus. But there have been concerns the closure of Winifred’s Lane could [push this traffic past children’s schools](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/news/somerset-news/claim-traffic-plan-benefits-baths-9068860). Dr Orpen warned: “Intervention has not been thought through. It's going to drive traffic very dangerously round a junior school which a consultant paediatrician of 30 years standing in the area is very worried about the fact that this could cause fatalities.” ‌ But others say it could reduce issues. Neil Dickinson, a member of the Cavendish Road community speedwatch group, told the meeting that vehicles were going at “totally unacceptable” speeds on Cavendish Road and using it as a main road to the motorway. He said: “The residential roads and narrow unclassified lanes were never intended to be used in this way and something needed to happen. The [experimental traffic regulation order] by the council in the Lower Lansdown area is an excellent initiative by the council, as are the increased number of crossings in the area, and hopefully the proposed trial will see both the volume and speeds reduced significantly in the area.” Bollards will be installed on Winifred’s Lane on Monday August 5, the changes to Gay Street will be carried out on August 6 and 7, and on Thursday August 8 the council hopes to complete the scheme by installing a row of bollards across Catharine Place. It has been controversial to say the least.](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9302217.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_AD_BL_23-05-2024_cumberlandroad.jpg) View 2 Images Cumberland Road now has a bus gate with red asphalt. It has been controversial to say the least.(Image: Bristol Live) Council chiefs have defended the way they have implemented a controversial bus gate on a road in [Bristol city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre), which is on course to catch the most motorists of any camera in the country, despite a judge at a tribunal saying the signage was not ‘compromised’. ‌ At the start of August, Bristol Live revealed that [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) had [lost another key case in the Traffic Penalty Tribunal](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/controversial-bus-gate-sign-ruled-9454032) - this time over the signage for drivers who turn onto Cumberland Road and into the bus gate that was installed there just under a year ago. ‌ Now, the council said it has improved the signage at the spot, and said they were ‘pleased to have seen a significant drop’ in the number of drivers getting caught. The bus gate has netted the council more than £1 million in fines since they started issuing penalties at the start of 2024. Article continues below **Read next: [Controversial bus gate sign ruled as 'compromised' after netting over a £1m in fines](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/controversial-bus-gate-sign-ruled-9454032)** **Read more: [Clean Air Zone signs to Bristol Airport through 'Portway trap' confusing rules tribunal](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/clean-air-zone-signs-bristol-9364482)** The case the council[lost at the Traffic Penalty Tribunal](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/controversial-bus-gate-sign-ruled-9454032), which has led to calls for the council to refund thousands of drivers’ fines, revolved around the warning signs for drivers turning left from Gas Ferry Road, where the SS Great Britain and Aardman Animations are based, onto Cumberland Road and straight into the new bus gate. ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) The gate only allows taxis, bikes, buses and authorised vehicles through - private cars are banned and will be fined if they head east along Cumberland Road towards the [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster) Bridge roundabout. Bus gate [campaigner and motorist Matt Sanders](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/council-defends-bus-gate-unlawful-9303110) lodged an appeal on behalf of a friend who was one of thousands who turned left at that junction and were caught driving through the bus gate, and the Traffic Penalty Tribunal adjudicator agreed, saying the signage was ‘compromised’ and couldn’t be adequately seen by drivers at night. The TPT adjudicator didn’t make a judgement on any of the other signage, and Bristol City Council said it was confident all the signs were compliant and legal. Bristol Live asked council highway chiefs about the TPT ruling, and a spokesperson for the council declined to mention it at all in the response. Article continues below ![Image 8: Matt Sanders at the junction of Gas Ferry Road and Cumberland Road - he's holding up what he says should be the sign warning drivers of a bus gate immediately to the left, next to the sign the council erected. The Traffic Penalty Tribunal has ruled the council's sign, on the left, is 'compromised'](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9454885.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_TCBR020824signBRI.jpg) View 2 Images Matt Sanders at the junction of Gas Ferry Road and Cumberland Road - he's holding up what he says should be the sign warning drivers of a bus gate immediately to the left, next to the sign the council erected. The Traffic Penalty Tribunal has ruled the council's sign, on the left, is 'compromised'(Image: Matt Sanders) “The signage installed surrounding the Cumberland Road Bus Gate is compliant with the latest guidance and legislation from the Department for Transport, with the number of signs exceeding the requirements set out by the Traffic Signs Manual,” the council spokesperson claimed. “Before the formal enforcement took place, there was a grace period of six weeks during which warning letters were sent to all drivers who used the bus gate, to make them aware of the new bus gate and that in the future drivers going through it will receive fines. ‌ “We have continued to listen to drivers' feedback and since the bus gate’s installation we have introduced an electronic sign and when the [weather](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/weather) improved, red surfacing was also installed to further highlight the bus gate. The bus gate has not been put in place to generate income, it is there to help reduce air pollution and increase the number of bus travel options for residents. “We are pleased to have seen a significant drop in PCNs related to the Cumberland Road Bus Gate since its introduction and are confident that this number will continue to reduce. Drivers can find details of bus gates in Bristol on the council’s website,” she added. READ MORE: [Controversial bus gate makes council £1million in six months](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/controversial-bus-gate-makes-council-9324276)READ MORE: [Council defends bus gate from 'unlawful' claims](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/council-defends-bus-gate-unlawful-9303110) So many visitors to the SS Great Britain were complaining that they were getting caught driving back out of Gas Ferry Road the same way they came in, that the SS Great Britain installed its own warning signs, but the council maintained that - despite the TPT ruling - the signs were good enough. ‌ The council said it has installed a ‘descriptive sign’ telling all vehicles to turn right, and a spokesperson pointed out that any driver reaching the junction would be able to see the bus gate immediately to their left. “There is a limit to what additional measures the council could put in place over and above what had already been implemented,” the council spokesperson said. “Any refunds or leniency are considered on a case by case basis.” Earlier this year, a Traffic Penalty Tribunal adjudicator criticised Bristol City Council’s inadequate signage warning motorists of the Clean Air Zone on the A4 into the city from [Avonmouth](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/avonmouth), and ruled in a [driver’s favour, ordering the council to scrap the fine](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/clean-air-zone-signs-bristol-9364482) it issued to him. Article continues below Bristol Live has asked repeatedly for a council response over questions on the implications of that ruling - both in terms of repaying other motorists’ fines, and its plans to act on the TPT adjudicator’s ruling - but the council has failed to answer after nearly two months. Article continues below A decision on whether to reopen the end of Dean Lane in [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster), at the junction with Coronation Road, will now form part of the South Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood consultation, and there is a possibility local people could decide they want it to remain closed to cars and vans for good. Access from Dean Lane onto Coronation Road was stopped by the council to prevent the road past Holy Cross Primary School becoming a rat run alternative route for motorists detouring away from Malago Road to get to the city centre. Dean Lane has become a quiet residential road past the Southbank Club and Holy Cross Primary School, and there are [plans for a large pre-school and children's nursery](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/plan-convert-closed-church-huge-9275674) to be created in the empty Holy Cross Church now too. Residents who asked if Dean Lane would also be reopened now Malago Road has been reopened have been told it won’t be, at least for the time being. A council spokesperson told Bristol Live there was no update on the future of Dean Lane, and it will now form part of the South Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood consultation plan. That will see traffic calming measures to create a better environment for people to walk and cycle around Southville, Ashton and Bedminster, with measures like creating one-way streets of the kind that already widely exist in the area, most notably off Coronation Road in Southville and West Street in Bedminster. Early consultation meetings and drop-in sessions, [organised by the local community group Action Greater Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/community-group-run-south-bristol-9423332), began last week with an afternoon held at the Southville Centre. The next drop-in engagement session is happening on Wednesday this week, August 14, at the Chessel Centre in Bedminster between 2.30pm and 6.30pm. 7](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article3552917.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_ML_BRI191118busengine_161.jpg) View 3 Images Buses on the Horsefair in Broadmead(Image: Michael Lloyd Photography) Buses and taxis could be banned from driving down a major shopping street in the city centre with much more space provided for pedestrians. The Horsefair in Broadmead is used by several bus routes, all of which would be diverted if the plans go ahead. ‌ [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) is planning to pedestrianise the Horsefair and Penn Street to help accommodate an extra 5,000 people who are expected to be living in and travelling around Broadmead in the next few years. The council is now [consulting the public](https://www.ask.bristol.gov.uk/bristol-city-centre-transport-changes-consultation-2024) until September 30. ‌ The changes aim to make the city centre more welcoming and people-friendly, by making it nicer to walk, use a wheelchair, and ride a scooter or bicycle, according to the council. The Horsefair and Penn Street will have new landscaping, benches and space for art. Article continues below **Read more: [Update on three new train stations due to open in Bristol](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/update-three-new-train-stations-9428929)** **Read more: [Major overhaul to roundabout connecting South Bristol to rest of city](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/major-overhaul-roundabout-connecting-south-9478335)** The public consultation includes other changes, such as two miles of new cycling lanes, a new express bus route, and changing the [Bedminster Bridges roundabout](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/major-overhaul-roundabout-connecting-south-9478335) into a signal-controlled junction. Access to the Horsefair would be kept for emergency vehicles, and deliveries at quiet times of the day. Bus stops, disabled parking bays and taxi ranks would be removed. ‌ Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. [More info](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/privacy-notice/) Several bus routes currently run down the Horsefair, and these will be diverted through Fairfax Street and Broad Weir alongside the back of Castle Park. Fairfax Street, which runs underneath the Galleries, will be made wider, brighter and have shop fronts, with new lifts installed. New bus stops would be no more than a five-minute walk from their current locations. Overall, there will be an increase in disabled parking bays in the city centre, as part of separate plans to redevelop the Galleries shopping centre. ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9481857.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Broadmead-Changes.jpg) View 3 Images A diagram showing the planned changes(Image: Bristol City Council) Article continues below A new junction would be created next to Primark, connecting Union Street and the Haymarket. Taxis and motorcycles would be banned from Union Street, which would become two-way for buses and bicycles. This would allow a new ‘rapid transit route’ bus to run through the city centre. Terminated buses left empty would be moved out of shopping areas to Temple Way. A bus gate would be installed at the Redcliffe roundabout, banning general traffic from driving up Redcliff Street. This is to speed up the journey times for the new rapid bus route, so buses don’t get stuck behind long queues of cars. Traffic would be diverted up Phippen Street instead. Bus lanes would be created on Temple Way, as well as a new segregated cycle lane from the Old Market roundabout to the Temple Gate junction. Bus lanes would also be created on Bond Street, as well as a parallel cycling route running along Pembroke Street and Wilson Street. ‌ ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9411533.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_Ddp-Horsefair.jpg) View 3 Images How the Horsefair could look after the changes(Image: Bristol City Council) Green Councillor Ed Plowden, chair of the transport policy committee, said: “These plans are transformative and will impact almost everyone who travels to, or through, [Bristol city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre). Broadmead is changing as shopping patterns evolve. Empty shops and department stores can be used for new housing and associated infrastructure. “A vision for Broadmead is set out in the Bristol City Centre Development and Delivery Plan. This consultation focuses on the transport and movement elements that would support this vision and the aspiration for a new rapid transit route. Please do look at the proposals and give us your feedback. We want to make sure we get these far-reaching plans right for the city.” ‌ Several redevelopment projects are taking place around Broadmead in the next few years. The [Galleries shopping centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/galleries-demolition-plan-heralds-new-9297371) will be replaced with 450 flats, community spaces, shops, a 250-bed hotel and student flats with 750 beds. The [Debenhams department store](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-debenhams-demolished-giant-new-9244612) will be replaced with 500 new apartments, and the [Premier Inn on the Bearpit](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/two-giant-new-bristol-city-9148301) replaced with flats for 422 students. The City Centre Transport Changes project is funded by the government through the City Region Sustainable Transport Settlement. This money can only be used by the council to improve transport infrastructure, and not for fixing potholes or other services like housing. The public consultation runs until September 30, and can be filled on the [council’s website](https://www.ask.bristol.gov.uk/bristol-city-centre-transport-changes-consultation-2024). Council) A liveable neighbourhood scheme in east Bristol has been delayed yet again, with measures now due to be installed at the end of the year. [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) has said that the East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood trial will be installed in November and December. ‌ The East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood has been discussed for several years, but its rollout has been repeatedly pushed back. The plans involve new bus gates, bollards and one-way systems to prevent drivers from taking shortcuts through residential streets. ‌ Some preparatory works are set to get underway in the coming weeks. The council says the project aims to make the area safer, healthier and greener by achieving a better balance between how streets are used for transport and people. Article continues below **Read more: [High street bank could be turned into flats in latest Bristol plans](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/high-street-bank-could-turned-9529363)** **Read more: [Last remaining pub in Bristol neighbourhood saved from demolition](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/last-remaining-pub-bristol-neighbourhood-9532070)** Green Councillor Ed Plowden, chair of the transport policy committee, said: “I’m really excited that work to install Bristol’s first liveable neighbourhood trial will take place later this year as part of the pilot project. It will take a bit of getting used to, especially for anyone who is used to driving through the area. ‌ [![Image 8: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Put your skills to the test. Whether you love word games, tricky cryptic crosswords, Sudoku, or our other brain teasers, you'll find a new favourite today! Play Now](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games/) “That’s why we’re recommending watching our film and looking through the online resources in the lead up to the trial. There is also the option to book a travel planning session if you need some extra help as an individual or as an organisation. “We’re confident these upcoming changes will make the liveable neighbourhood a safer and healthier place to live with quiet streets that are less congested and polluted. It’s important to emphasise that all areas of the neighbourhood will still be accessible by motorised vehicles, but that routes may change.” In spring 2023, the council said the project was due to start in the autumn later that year. It was then pushed back to last winter, then this summer — and now the latest scheduled roll-out is November and December this year. Article continues below A [short video](https://eastbristolliveableneighbourhoods.commonplace.is/) has been produced by the council, explaining the changes and how they will affect people living in the area, including Barton Hill, Redfield and St George. It explains how walking, wheeling and cycling throughout the trial area will be safer and easier, while the routes people drive to their home or other areas within the liveable neighbourhood are likely to change. Online one-to-one travel planning sessions with transport officers [can be booked](https://eastbristolliveableneighbourhoods.commonplace.is/) ahead of the trial. These are tailored sessions to help people navigate the new routes. Organisations and businesses can also request that a member of the team visits them to take them through the trial changes. This can either be with management or members of staff, in person or online. Article continues below Next year the council will seek views on the trial, to explore what changes could be made before a permanent layout is rolled out. This will include more street lighting, new crossings with traffic signals, sections of cycle lanes and street trees. The project is funded by the government’s City Region Sustainable Transport Settlement, which is administered by the West of England Combined Authority. the outskirts of Bristol are unhappy with how their infrastructure has been neglected, despite expansion of the surrounding areas. Last week, Bristol Live reported that large trucks passing through Pilning had been [shaking one man's house](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/residents-nightmare-huge-trucks-shake-9517684), and now other residents have expressed their ongoing concerns of how the building-up of Bristol and [South Gloucestershire](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/south-gloucestershire) is affecting the village. Article continues below Pilning is your typical homely rural village, home to popular traditional family-run pubs The Plough Inn and The King's Arms, as well as a beautiful Victorian parish church. The village is served hourly by the Stagecoach 12 bus from Bristol Parkway to Severn Beach, but residents must travel on this route to Cribbs Causeway before being able to reach [Bristol city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre). Article continues below ![Image 8](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9532683.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_st-peters-church-pilningJPG.jpg) View 3 Images (Image: Google Maps) Article continues below 138329481766 One resident described the road past his house in Pilning as a "rat run", adding: "Whenever the A403 is closed from Pilning traffic lights, then the vehicles are diverted through Pilning and Easter Compton." **Read more:** * [Multiple fundraisers set up to 'save' Bristol's iconic Turbo Island from developers](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/multiple-fundraisers-set-up-save-9527059) * [Massive burst water main on edge of Bristol may take a week to repair](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/massive-burst-water-main-edge-9528244) Sign up to our daily newsletter for the latest local and breaking news in Bristol Subscribe We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and improve our understanding of you. Though trucks exceeding 7.5 tonnes should not pass through Easter Compton and Pilning, these restrictions were lifted whilst work was carried out on the A403, between August 21 and 31. The Western Approach Distribution Centre is just a four-minute drive from Pilning. One resident felt that traffic has "increased exponentially" since the [Tesco](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/tesco) and Amazon warehouses were built there. Pilning is home to a train station, which has previously been reported to be [one of the least used stations in the UK.](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/visited-bristol-railway-station-only-8056688) According to GWR, the station has an "extremely sparse service", only running two trains a week to Penzance. Article continues below 138205439166 ![Image 9](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9531871.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_photo_2018-12-11_14-25-35.jpg) View 3 Images (Image: Western Daily Press) South Gloucestershire Council's local plan leading up to 2040 sets out plans to build 20,490 new homes. In Pilning's neighbouring village Easter Compton, there are plans to build 790 homes, and residents are concerned that key roads such as the B4055 are not being upgraded despite this expansion. The construction of the new M49 motorway junction should help relieve pressure on local roads in the area. The latest update from South Gloucestershire Council was in March 2024, announcing that construction would begin this summer and last approximately 12 months. Article continues below A spokesperson for [South Gloucestershire Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/south-gloucestershire-council) said: “We are aware of local concerns around traffic in Pilning and our Highways Officers have liaised with residents, the Local Ward Member and Parish Council around ways of making improvements. Over recent years we’ve implemented a 20mph zone and various traffic calming schemes, including the installation of speed tables in the local area. “Monitoring of the reduced speed limits in place is encouraging and motorists and road users are responsible for adhering to these limits, along with the weight restrictions in place, as failure to do so may result in a criminal conviction. https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/local: Calls for public transport improvements as east Bristol gears up for liveable neighbourhood scheme The East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood trial, which will see new bus gates, bollards and one-way systems installed, has been delayed multiple times, but is now set to go forward ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 05:00, 10 Sep 2024 Bristol Live readers are unsurprised to hear that the [contraversial East Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood scheme has been hit with yet another delay](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/controversial-liveable-neighbourhood-east-bristol-9534869#comments-wrapper), with the council now saying it will be installed at the end of the year. The scheme, which has been in the pipeline for several years, involves new bus gates, bollards and one-way systems to deter drivers from using residential streets as shortcuts. Readers and residents have been having their say in our [comments section](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/local-news/readers-say-improve-public-transport-9539246#comments-wrapper). ‌ Initially set to start in autumn 2023, the project's launch has been repeatedly postponed - first to last winter, then this summer, and now finally to November and December this year. ‌ The council has stated that the project's goal is to create a safer, healthier, and greener environment by striking a better balance between transport and pedestrian use of the streets. In the coming year, the council plans to gather public opinion on the trial, with the aim of identifying potential modifications before implementing a permanent layout. ‌ **Read next** * [Bristol City Council to consider selling Bottle Yard Studios later this month](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/bristol-city-council-consider-selling-9539564) * [16-mile diversion as A-road roundabout on Bristol's outskirts to close](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/a403-severn-road-roundabout-closure-9525199) This could include additional street lighting, new signal-controlled crossings, sections of cycle lanes, and street trees. ‌ Commenter Junius1 writes: “It’s not just the few planned LTNs. Traffic volumes in Bristol, which is the fourth most congested city in the UK, need to be significantly reduced to improve people's health, travel times and air quality. The CAZ adopted for the city targeted nitrogen dioxide levels but not particulate matter, which is a serious threat to health. Bristol needs alternative forms of mass transport to encourage people out of cars. Unfortunately, it's local authority and the regional mayoral combined authority has signally failed to devise credible plans which can win government funds for this.” Darrow agrees: “I would happily leave my car at home - or even get rid of it - if there was a reliable public transport system in place. Until then I will have to continue to drive as cuts are being made to improving public transport routes!” HanhamHeights points out: “You've hit the nail on the head about public transport needing improvement - no argument there. But you're missing the point of LTNs. They're not trying to force you to ditch your car completely. LTNs are about making your immediate neighbourhood safer and more pleasant for short trips. They're designed to make walking or cycling the easy choice for those quick errands around your home. For longer journeys or when you really need your car, you can still use it. It might just mean a slightly different route out of your area.” ‌ Martymoo is unhappy: “Brilliant, I now have to go on a 2 and a half mile detour to take my neighbour to the health centre as she is immobile. Thanks so much.” BMushroom agrees: “Making people drive further, thus creating more pollution, is a win-win situation for - hang on, it'll come to me in a bit.” ‌ Chiefchupachup adds: “How is it greener and healthier when vehicles have to travel much farther distances? BCC in complete denial of that fact.” Jabbymisschief says: “Bad news for everyone living around the LTN. Church Road is already way to crambed with motor vehicles already. No functioning bus lane, bus service or even a safe cycle lane. Just nose to tail traffic right outside the ambulance station. Brilliant.” YosserBlues adds: “Accept that it's a fact of life that people have cars. The genie's out of that bottle and you're not going to turn it back now. So work with that by keeping traffic moving, and not all funnelled into the same areas, crawling, or stopping, belting out more fumes.” Article continues below HanhamHeights replies: “Ah, the old 'longer routes' must mean more pollution chestnut. Nice try, but real-world evidence says otherwise. LTNs actually reduce overall traffic. Turns out, when short car trips become a bit less convenient, people often decide walking or cycling isn't so bad after all. Some traffic just vanishes. People adapt, combine trips and find alternatives. It's called 'evaporation', and it's a beautiful thing. LTNs don't aim to eliminate cars, but to reduce unnecessary short trips. They spread traffic more evenly across main roads, not funnel it. Data shows they decrease overall traffic and emissions, not increase them. The 'keep traffic moving' approach you suggest actually induces more demand, leading to more congestion and pollution long-term.” **How do you feel about the plans for an LTN? Do you think it will improve the area or will it just cause issues for motorists? have your say in our [comments section](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/local-news/readers-say-improve-public-transport-9539246#comments-wrapper).**

centre.](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9558807.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/1_BRI_PG_160924transport-7.jpg) View 7 Images Cllr Ed Plowden says that the proposed changes would make Broadmead a "much better place" and advised drivers after the potential pedestrianisation to not "bother" driving into the city centre.(Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach PLC) “If you’re thinking of driving into [Bristol](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/) by car, don’t bother,” is how a councillor at the heart of the proposed [Bristol city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-centre) transport changes described how plans to pedestrianise and transform [Broadmead](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/broadmead) will affect vehicles in future. The changes proposed in Broadmead are part of a long-term project to prepare for 5,000 more people living in the area. ‌ The project, which will [see the city centre transformed](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/main-shopping-street-bus-route-9481861), will see bus stops replaced and moved, Union Street becoming a two-way bus gate that only permits buses and cyclists, and a new junction linking the Haymarket to Union Street once again. Further segregated cycle lanes would be installed along the Haymarket, and a [bus gate](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/transport) would be created at [Redcliffe](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/redcliffe) Way. ‌ The [plans](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/planning) are aimed at [removing traffic from the city centre](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/major-plans-bus-lanes-cycle-9411529)and making it easier for those dependent on using cars, including disabled people, to travel around Bristol. There are a planned three and a half kilometres of segregated cycle paths that will be installed - which [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) hope to begin by March 2027. Article continues below ![Image 8: One of the major changes will see a new junction created between Union Street and the Haymarket going around Primark.](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9558814.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_BRI_PG_160924transport-10.jpg) View 7 Images One of the major changes will see a new junction created between Union Street and the Haymarket going around Primark.(Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach PLC) [Animals killed in fire as blaze devastates South West family attraction](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/animals-killed-fire-blaze-devastates-10654057?int_source=nba) [Map shows where in Bristol snow is forecast as 'arctic blast' hits this week](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/where-will-snow-fall-bristol-10650459?int_source=nba) Broadmead is set to change drastically as The Horsefair and Penn Street will become pedestrianised, only allowing access to emergency services and deliveries for businesses at quiet times, and alongside plans to make Union Street a new bus gate, will introduce about “10 tennis courts of new traffic-free space”. The ongoing consultation period will end on September 30 and the council said that around 1,400 responses have been received. It added that it wants people to know that the council is acknowledging concerns and comments and hopes for more comments. ‌ [![Image 9: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Put your skills to the test. Whether you love word games, tricky cryptic crosswords, Sudoku, or our other brain teasers, you'll find a new favourite today! Play Now](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games/) “Much better place to be for everyone” -------------------------------------- ![Image 10: Cllr Ed Plowden says that the proposed changes would make Broadmead a "much better place".](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9558807.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/1_BRI_PG_160924transport-7.jpg) View 7 Images Cllr Ed Plowden says that the proposed changes would make Broadmead a "much better place".(Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach PLC) Councillor Ed Plowden, chair of the Transport and Connectivity Committee, exclusively told Bristol Live: “I think this will make it a much better place to be for everyone. Obviously change is difficult, there will be more people living in the area and hopefully working in the area and we want to recognise that Broadmead is changing and will be much more residential alongside the other uses, so we want to make it a great place to live and work.” Buses would be diverted so they go around Broadmead after The Horsefair and Penn Street are closed off to traffic. Services that use The Horsefair and Penn Street will be diverted via Fairfax Street and Broad Weir (the former will become brighter, lighter and have shop fronts as part of the Galleries development). Other services that use Baldwin Street and/or Victoria Street will use the new road network created by changes to Temple Way and Bond Street. Article continues below In addition to these changes, 47 disabled parking spaces would be closed and replaced by 47 disabled parking spaces and a further 20 once [the Galleries](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/the-galleries-bristol) development has finished. Four taxi ranks, with space for 16 taxis, would close and be replaced by four ranks providing space for 17, likewise once the Galleries development is finished, an additional two ranks with space for eight taxis will be available. ![Image 11: Fairfax Street, pictured, will become part of the route for many of the buses that go through Broadmead.](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9558815.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_BRI_PG_160924transport-3.jpg) View 7 Images Fairfax Street, pictured, will become part of the route for many of the buses that go through Broadmead.(Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach PLC) Cllr Plowden added: “Getting buses to go through Fairfax Street will make it a much more pleasant environment underneath the Galleries to get on and off the bus. At the moment it is not the best but we are very mindful of the fact that we make all the buses and connections close. We are looking at the disabled parking spaces and the taxi ranks - there will be no loss in numbers.” ‌ “We’re putting together a whole package of measures to make sustainable transport, whether that is buses, [cycling](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/cycling) or walking, the natural option. It will be a lot easier to cycle and walk. “It may not work for everyone but we are thinking, in particular, about the needs of disabled people and people who really are dependent on their cars. From my point of view I hope that by freeing up the road space and getting as many people as we can to use other methods of transport that are more efficient for the city, that will free up space for those that are car dependent.” **_Sign up to receive daily news updates and breaking news alerts straight to your inbox for free [here](https://bit.ly/3r1T6AI)._** ‌ Traffic like a balloon - “we are trying to let the air out gently” ------------------------------------------------------------------ ![Image 12: The list of changes to Broadmead featured on a map.](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9481857.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Broadmead-Changes.jpg) View 7 Images The list of changes to Broadmead featured on a map.(Image: Bristol City Council) Cllr Plowden also recognised concerns that the transport project could push traffic elsewhere across the city. He said: “It is difficult and it would be really nice if there was a magic wand and you could change the transport system straight away, but what we’re trying to do is piece together, in a strategic way, a way of making it easier for people to get around the city without feeling that they have to do it in a car. “So rather than squeezing a balloon and pushing out the traffic somewhere else, we are trying to let the air out gently to make it easier for everyone to get around. And those who are still dependent on cars, hopefully there will be less congestion and it will be easier for them.” ‌ The councillor added that he hopes removing traffic from the city centre streets will help improve the reliability of buses and improve transport as a whole. After the pedestrianisation is completed, he advised: "If you're thinking of driving into Bristol, don't bother." Lessons learned from Cumberland Road bus gate --------------------------------------------- ![Image 13: The bus gate on Cumberland Road has proved controversial as Cllr Plowden says lessons have been learned.](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9302217.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_AD_BL_23-05-2024_cumberlandroad.jpg) View 7 Images The bus gate on Cumberland Road has proved controversial as Cllr Plowden says lessons have been learned.(Image: Bristol Live) The project helps support the idea of a rapid transit service by connecting the southwest of the city to the northeast via a potential bus route. In Broadmead, this would be achieved by the new Union Street and the junction to the Haymarket. Bus gates would be installed at Union Street, the [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster) Bridges and at Redcliffe Street next to Portwall Lane, alongside additional bus lanes at Bond Street and [Temple Way](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/temple-way). The Cumberland Road bus gate, which became active at the start of this year, has proved controversial as [signage was exposed for being “inadequate” by a judge and appeals were successful against being fined](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/council-loses-two-more-cumberland-9533359). ![Image 14: Union Street is set to become a two-way bus gate only allowing cyclists and buses to use the road.](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9558821.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_BRI_PG_160924transport-2.jpg) View 7 Images Union Street is set to become a two-way bus gate only allowing cyclists and buses to use the road.(Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach PLC) Cllr Plowden said that the council has learned lessons and has called for a more consistent approach to the aesthetic of bus gates in the city. He said: “The Bristol Bridge bus gate is working well now, you don’t see many cars being caught out unknowingly. We’re trying to have a consistent way of creating bus gates in Bristol so it looks really familiar to people as they get to know what a bus gate looks like. “It should be the same everywhere in Bristol as far as possible. Obviously we need to take a case by case approach with putting them in and making sure there is good warning and good places to turn around so they don’t get caught out by it. I want to make sure that they are really recognisable.” Despite the concerns over the project, Cllr Plowden said: “I think this project will be transformative and I think it will really change the way we move about the city but also the way we live in the city centre. It’s going to make it a really good place for people to be, for people to go shopping, but also for people to spend time and enjoy their time here, whether visiting or living in the new developments.” The overall estimated cost of the project is not yet known and the phase schedule is to be confirmed as the council works with key stakeholders to determine when construction and demolition can begin. cyclists and buses to use the road.](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9558821.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_BRI_PG_160924transport-2.jpg) View Image Union Street is set to become a two-way bus gate only allowing cyclists and buses to use the road.(Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach PLC) The contentious plans to [pedestrianise Broadmead and give it a makeover](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/pedestrianisation-broadmead-planned-transport-changes-9575992#comments-wrapper) have sparked a flurry of debate amongst Bristol Live readers in our [comments section](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/locals-fear-broadmead-pedestrianisation-plans-9579873). Remarks made by Councillor Ed Plowden, who heads the Transport and Connectivity Committee, have stirred up even more controversy. ‌ At first glance, removing traffic from the city centre seems like a brilliant idea, however, when you delve deeper into the plans - which include turning Union Street into a two-way bus gate, pedestrianising The Horsefair and Penn Street, and introducing new cycle lanes throughout the city centre - it becomes a highly complex issue. ‌ While touring the area with reporters, Councillor Plowden remarked: "If you're thinking of driving into Bristol by car, don't bother," in reference to how cars would navigate the city centre. This comment drew criticism from a [Labour](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/labour-party) councillor who argued that it would "create a no-go zone for disabled people". Article continues below Bus routes would be redirected, additional disabled parking spaces would be established, and more bus gates would be set up at [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster) Bridges and Redcliffe Street. Despite the project's insistence that it is not anti-car, it might feel that way. But what's the use when buses are notoriously unreliable and, for some, extremely infrequent? [Animals killed in fire as blaze devastates South West family attraction](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/animals-killed-fire-blaze-devastates-10654057?int_source=nba) [Couple caught having daytime sex in car on the Downs sparks warning](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/couple-caught-having-daytime-sex-10654009?int_source=nba) Many people steer clear of buses due to their well known reputation. We at Bristol Live have been advocating for improved bus services in Bristol. If buses aren't serving everyone adequately now, how will they cope when cars are phased out? Commenter Jonty2 thinks: “The conclusion is that there is virtually no ambition or foresight left at the Council. The centre and Broadmead should have been pedestrianised decades ago. Cyclists should also dismount unless in a dedicated cycle lane. Maybe put the waste of money changes to the centre towards affording Council housing at [Hengrove](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/hengrove) Park and the Caravan clubs housing sites?” ‌ Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. As a disabled OAP I would love to go to shops to buy clothing (nothing better than trying on for fit, and feel the material), but all these student flats will kill any shops wanting to open there. I can't get to [South Gloucestershire](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/south-gloucestershire) (Cribbs) as my mobility scooter cannot go on the bus, and if my taxi cannot take me to Broadmead (if there was still something to go there for) then any shops will be totally out of reach. I am surely not the only one who would have this problem.” Fisherman19 agrees: “Just give up really and get about the best you can, the council is the same as always, it's all grand plans, consultants, computer graphics, and passing the buck. Cyclists moan they don't get enough cycle lanes which they don't use, and now after years of intimidating pedestrians they themselves are getting intimidated by high speed electric bikes, don't ask for sympathy it's your turn now.” Article continues below Susiep retorts: “We pedestrians know that one of us dies every 9 days on a UK pavement having been hit by a motor vehicle, and one of us dies on a pavement every 851 days having been hit by a bicycle. We pedestrians know what actually presents the greatest risk to us.” Magrathean adds: “I love cycling and I love my bikes. But most people will not be interested in cycling, especially in poor [weather](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/weather). It will remain a minority. But a reality like that doesn't get through to policy makers with their heads in the clouds.” Katiem writes: “30 years ago I used to drive into the centre to go shopping. I hate buses for various reasons. I now walk. As I get older I expect I won't bother to go into the centre. The shops are not exactly tempting. The centre will continue to die and become residential and high rise. High rise cities are awful and no-one truly gives us a choice.” ‌ **Sign up to receive daily news updates and breaking news alerts straight to your inbox for free **[here](https://bit.ly/3r1T6AI)**.** Junius1 says: “No-one- especially politicians- can guarantee that Broadmead will not become a disaster zone as a result of all the development planned. It's all a big gamble that it might turn out alright in the end.” Robofbristol writes: “If this stupid scheme to ban cars from Broadmead goes ahead, I'm buying shares in Cribbs Causeway! Broadmead will become a ghost city. Us motoring majority must face up to the fact governments both national and local no longer represent our views and would like rid of private car ownership altogether. They are taking away our freedom bit by bit.” ‌ Paulgc agrees: “[Bath](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bath-and-north-east-somerset) will love these plans!” Wesfrench adds: “So will Cribbs Shopping Centre - free parking, no gangs of youths, good motorway links!” ReesIsToast suggests: “Flatten the lot and build a new, mixed-residential/commercial space with two or three central-feature spaces that are for entertainment. Public transport can pass through but private vehicles cannot.” Paulgc asks: “What about deliveries to the few shops that are left or getting items home if you buy anything?” Article continues below HanhamHeights replies: “Deliveries will be unaffected by these plans. schools(Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto) Cars with cameras on top of them could patrol Bristol streets near schools to clamp down on parents parking dangerously. Some parents ignore parking restrictions outside schools “putting children at risk”, according to one councillor who has called for better enforcement. ‌ [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) is responsible for enforcing rules on parking, but struggles with enforcement outside schools during drop-off and pick-up times. The high number of schools that need to be patrolled, and the short amount of time that’s affected, both make enforcement challenging. ‌ One solution could be camera cars, used in other council areas successfully, to be rolled out at a wider level in Bristol. Questions were raised about school safety during a meeting of the member forum on Tuesday, October 8. Article continues below [Labour](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/labour-party) Councillor Katja Hornchen said: “There’s an issue with school parking, which I’m sure is not only in [Brislington](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/brislington) East. I live on the border with [South Gloucestershire](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/south-gloucestershire) and I can assure you, as a teacher in South Gloucestershire, they [camera cars] work very efficiently because people are frightened of them.” [Animals killed in fire as blaze devastates South West family attraction](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/animals-killed-fire-blaze-devastates-10654057?int_source=nba) [Couple caught having daytime sex in car on the Downs sparks warning](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/couple-caught-having-daytime-sex-10654009?int_source=nba) The council also struggles to hire enough civil enforcement officers, with vacancies in the team left empty for years. Camera cars however would allow for officers to enforce parking rules outside several schools much more quickly. Green Cllr Ed Plowden said: “School enforcement may better lend itself to camera enforcement, and this is something that officers have on their roadmap. Although there would be an initial capital cost for the purchase and the set up of the cameras, they could be more effective to operate in the long term. ‌ Get the latest Bristol Live breaking news on WhatsApp Our community members are treated to special offers, promotions and adverts from us and our partners. That’s not really a yes or no, but it’s certainly something that’s in consideration.” Another issue is the partial ban on council using camera cars more generally to enforce parking rules, put in place by the Coalition government. Eric Pickles, former communities secretary, announced the ban a decade ago “in a victory for drivers and shoppers”. This means tickets have to be fixed to windscreens by parking wardens, rather than just using the cars to catch drivers breaking the rules and then sending a parking ticket in the post. Exceptions were made for critical routes, such as schools, bus lanes and bus stops. Article continues below Cllr Plowden added: “Back in 2014, Eric Pickles stopped any council enforcing parking with the use of cameras. Since then there’s a number of roads in Bristol that have really ground to a halt, making it extremely difficult for bus operators to operate. “There’s a whole load of places where we see that you could have an enforcement officer go right along the street, and when they came back again it would still be clogged up with poor parking. That would be a great quick-win for the new incoming government to reverse that. “It was something that Eric Pickles did on a whim. That would enable us to do a lot more parking enforcement across the city and support more sustainable travel.” Follow Bristol Live: * [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/bristol.live) * [X School](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9590586.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/0_Parents-slam-dangerous-colourful-school-road-markings-that-look-like-Twister.jpg) View 3 Images Colourful school road markings installed by a town council near Oakfield Academy and Critchill School(Image: Tom Wren / SWNS) Serious concerns over the effectiveness of a Safer School Streets initiative have been raised. The scheme aims to create safer student walking and cycling routes by implementing time-bound road closures near local schools. ‌ The schemein Frome, which began on April 22, closes certain roads near Trinity First, Oakfield Park, Avanti Park, and Critchill School during peak school hours: between 8.10 am and 9am. and from 2.45 pm to 3.30 pm. ‌ However, speaking at Frome’s October council meeting, Alan Whitmore, a resident of Oakfield Road, voiced frustration over perceived lax enforcement and questioned whether the scheme was implemented correctly and enforceable. Article continues below “I live on Oakfield Road opposite Oakfield Academy. My grandchildren attend Avanti Park School, and my questions tonight are about the Safer School Streets for Frome,” Mr Whitmore said. [Animals killed in fire as blaze devastates South West family attraction](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/animals-killed-fire-blaze-devastates-10654057?int_source=nba) [Map shows where in Bristol snow is forecast as 'arctic blast' hits this week](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/where-will-snow-fall-bristol-10650459?int_source=nba) “Can I ask if the appropriate regulations have been made to make this scheme legally enforceable? Could I also ask what enforcement of the restriction times for this scheme has taken place in the restricted areas?” ![Image 8: Map of streets included in the Frome Safer School Streets trial](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9203033.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Map-of-streets-included-in-the-Frome-Safer-School-Streets-trial-Sustrans-290324.png) View 3 Images Map of streets included in the Frome Safer School Streets trial(Image: Sustrans) ‌ [![Image 9: games page](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games-full.png) Ready for a Daily Challenge? Put your skills to the test. Whether you love word games, tricky cryptic crosswords, Sudoku, or our other brain teasers, you'll find a new favourite today! Play Now](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/games/) Mr Whitmore continued by sharing personal observations of frequent non-compliance. “I have seen widespread ignoring of the restriction times on Oakfield Road. I’ve seen many vehicles turn up to collect people during restricted times. Some sit with engines idling, sometimes 15 to 30 minutes before the restriction time,” he added, questioning the overall adherence to the project’s safety objectives. In response, Peter Wheelhouse, the Economic Development & Regeneration Manager & Deputy Town Clerk of Frome Town Council assured Mr Whitmore and other attendees that enforcement efforts are underway, though they primarily fall under police jurisdiction. “The important thing for me to say is that those restrictions can only be formally enforced by the police, and we have had regular contact with them around ensuring that this is enforced,” he explained. Article continues below Mr Wheelhouse acknowledged that while local authorities are stretched, there are efforts to monitor and enforce the scheme with NSL officers, contracted through Somerset Council Parking Services, who have recently been instructed to oversee parking compliance in the area. On the financial side, Mr Whitmore raised concerns over the program’s cost, referencing a media report which claimed that the coloured road markings at two schools cost around £146,000. ![Image 10: Colourful school road markings installed by a town council near Oakfield Academy and Critchill School](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9590591.ece/ALTERNATES/s615b/0_Parents-slam-dangerous-colourful-school-road-markings-that-look-like-Twister.jpg) View 3 Images Colourful school road markings installed by a town council near Oakfield Academy and Critchill School(Image: Tom Wren / SWNS) ‌ Mr Wheelhouse disputed this figure, saying it was ‘spurious’ and clarifying that the cost of road markings was closer to £62,000. “The sum in the contract with our contractor was closer to £62,000 for that particular element of the scheme,” he stated, adding that funding for the trial did not come from the town council’s budget but from Active Travel England through a grant obtained by Sustrans. Mr Whitmore then pressed for details on the exact nature of enforcement actions by NSL wardens. “When you say the wardens are out, what are they doing? Are they advising? Are they giving warnings? Are they giving parking tickets?” he asked. Mr Wheelhouse responded by saying that wardens are authorised to issue tickets and will do so where offences are observed. “You can fully expect to see wardens on the street over the coming weeks handing out tickets where it’s required,” he said. Article continues below At the meeting, another member acknowledged the community’s mixed reception of the trial. “It is a trial,” the speaker noted, “an 18-month trial. If we need to make tweaks or changes, we’re very open to that. It’s all about trying and seeing how it goes, then iterating if necessary.” Mr Wheelhouse concluded by encouraging residents to continue providing feedback. “Please keep the reports coming in. We must receive feedback from the community about what’s happening on the ground,” he said, emphasising the council’s commitment to assessing the scheme’s impact through ongoing data collection and an evaluation scheduled for December. ![Image 11](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article5866306.ece/ALTERNATES/s1168v/0_WhatsApp-Phone.jpg) ### Somerset Live WhatsApp Breaking News and Top Stories **Join Somerset Live’s WhatsApp community for top stories and breaking news sent directly to your phone** [Somerset Live](https://www.somersetlive.co.uk/) is now on WhatsApp and we want you to join our community. No people.](https://i2-prod.bristolpost.co.uk/article9626691.ece/ALTERNATES/s615/1_GettyImages-1521892242.jpg) View Image Drivers are not happy(Image: Getty) The recent introduction of a 20mph speed limit across Wales, effective from September 17, 2023, has seen journey times lengthen across the nation, sparking considerable debate. The legislation aims to reduce accident risk and severity, encouraging alternative modes of transport such as walking, cycling or scootering. It is also hoped it will provide additional benefits for mental and physical well-being. ‌ Research conducted by Transport for Wales discovered that from September 2023 to April 2024, average vehicle speeds on main 20mph roads dropped by around 4.3mph. 58% of vehicles are now travelling at - or below - 24mph compared to 20% previously. Average journey times have increased on most assessed routes but generally not by more than two minutes. Journey time variability has decreased on most routes, suggesting improved journey time reliability. In addition, air quality monitoring has not shown any significant difference in nitrogen dioxide concentrations in 20mph areas compared to non-20mph areas. ‌ A range of views has emerged following this report on Wales' default speed restriction, with some expressing frustration over the implications of the newly enforced measure. Critics include Bikelanesnotcancercare, who commented: "It only takes 1 car doing 20mph then all cars behind it must do 20mph, this is not a personal choice but enforced by some old gopher making a point. This leads to anger and frustration which in turn leads to other very serious social and health problems", reports [Wales Online](https://www.walesonline.co.uk/news/wales-news/anger-frustration-stress-levels-through-30119276). This can take an age, particularly during rush hour and school times. RCTCBC have done nothing to aliviate this. They could easily put in passing places, stop people parking on junctions, yellow lines, etc!" Blackhand18 believed: "Certainly hasn't helped my mental or physical health. To the contrary, my stress levels hit the roof following a car moving at a snail's pace and constantly changing gears moving from 30mph to 20mph to 40mph all within yards is damaging my car and my ankle joints. Barrian believed: "All smoke and mirrors. If the air quality had improved then they would be shouting about it. How about showing the comparison of the new 20 mph zones before and after the introduction? It says no material difference between 20 and 30 roads. Most 30 roads are in less urban areas now so that isn't comparable plus I asked what the difference was between the pre 20 and the post 20 data. I also notice no mention of carbon dioxide or carbon monoxide emissions. I wonder why? For a full analysis of the data all this must be compared and not the cherry picking that the Senedd has put in the press release." Sharkman wrote: "Being behind sad people doing 17mph not even 20 is leading to guess what? Worse driving and more people getting angrier." But Williisnt responded saying: "If 20 is the legal limit then driving at 17mph is about right. That's not sad, that's driving safely and legally within the law." Numbersontheleft wrote: "I pick up my grandson 4 times a week. The journey is 10 miles and most roads are now 20mph. https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/brist: Unpopular plans to close road into South Bristol neighbourhood could be scrapped Only three roads lead in and out of the area, one of which was due to be closed to cars --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 11:26, 21 Oct 2024 Unpopular plans to close a road leading into a South Bristol neighbourhood are set to be scrapped this week. One of three routes into a part of Totterdown was due to close, as part of wider road safety improvements, but local drivers complained their journeys would be longer. ‌ Bellevue Road is the last turning left at the northern end of the A37 Wells Road. [Bristol City Council](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bristol-city-council) was planning to close the junction to cars, after concerns about a history of collisions there. The area would also have been improved for pedestrians and cyclists. ‌ But the closure would mean leaving just two roads out of Totterdown, either down Oxford Street onto St John’s Lane or Windsor Terrace onto St Luke’s Road. Drivers struggle to pass each other in the very narrow streets in the area, and the closure was expected to add to congestion. ‌ The plan formed part of a [wider project](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/news/bristol-news/major-changes-key-south-bristol-8407858) along the Wells Road and Number 2 bus corridor, with bus lanes and pedestrian crossings, the rest of which will still be rolled out. Councillors on the transport policy committee will vote on approving a full business case on Thursday, October 24. A [committee report](https://democracy.bristol.gov.uk/documents/s102029/Committee%20Report%20Final%20Final.pdf) said: “This element will not be taken forward as part of this scheme following consultation. The issues we are trying to resolve at this location will be considered as part of the South Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood, and outcomes from this consultation will be fed into [that project].” **Sign up to receive daily news updates and breaking news alerts straight to your inbox for free **[here](https://bit.ly/3r1T6AI)**.** ‌ The [South Bristol Liveable Neighbourhood](https://www.bristol.gov.uk/residents/people-and-communities/liveable-neighbourhoods/south-bristol-liveable-neighbourhood) covers Totterdown, [Bedminster](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/bedminster) and Southville, and is likely to include bollards to prevent rat-running, better crossings, and new trees. The council is in the early stages of consulting the public about the plans, with detailed proposals expected next spring. Last month Green Councillor Lisa Stone, representing the Windmill Hill ward which includes Totterdown, wrote in an opinion piece for Bristol24/7 that a local survey showed a clear response against closing the Bellevue Road junction. She added that the former [Labour](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/labour-party) administration “did not listen to residents”. ‌ She said: “I would like to see the evidence which suggests that there is a problem with this junction and for the bus company to meet with me to discuss these issues. If necessary I would like to see some simple yellow hatching on the bus lane at this junction, to be enforced with CCTV. “As for reducing air pollution, the offered alternative routes show that cars will need to be driven longer distances around the area, and this would create a lot of issues that simply do not outweigh the benefits. Not only that, I can see that there would be possible issues for emergency vehicles getting in and out of this area as well. “This plan has simply not been thought through and the previous Labour administration clearly did not listen to any recommendations coming from local residents. If they had, I feel that this proposal would look remarkably different and would have reached the same aims, but with a better outcome.” ‌ However transport consultants from AtkinsRéalis, who produced a [full business case](https://democracy.bristol.gov.uk/documents/s102030/Appendix%20A%20A37%20A4018%20South%20FBC%20-%20V3.0%20Redacted.pdf) for the wider project, said the junction had “low levels of safety”. Several collisions were reported there between 2018 and 2023, according to data from the Department for Transport, with a “high proportion involving pedestrians or cyclists”, the business case said. The plans were first proposed under the former Labour administration. Labour Cllr Don Alexander, former cabinet member for transport, said the closure had been properly considered, and the junction had a “proven history of danger to cyclists”. Writing on X/ [Twitter](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/all-about/twitter), he said: “It had been thought through — this junction has a proven history of presenting a danger to cyclists and motorcyclists. Nobody should put personal political advantage over the facts.” Article continues below
